You tell us who you are, and we use it.

I want to address you by the name and pronouns you use. If your chosen name or pronouns differ from what appears on the official roster, please email me at tdr@umass.edu at the start of the term, and I will use them in all communication and feedback. UMass Amherst allows students to designate a chosen name and a pronoun in SPIRE, which then propagates to Canvas and class rosters, and I encourage you to set these if you have not already. If I ever get your name or pronouns wrong, a quick, private email is welcome and I will fix it.

Student Support Resources
The course is hard by design; you do not have to navigate it alone.

Help with the course material comes first from the instructor by email at tdr@umass.edu, and from the CICS supplemental instruction and tutoring resources offered through the Manning College advising office, which you can find on the CICS undergraduate advising pages. This might not apply to six week summer sessions. Beyond the course, the University offers support for the rest of your life as a student. The Center for Counseling and Psychological Health (CCPH) provides confidential mental health support and can be reached at (413) 545-2337, with a counselor available at that number at any hour. The Dean of Students Office helps students navigate personal emergencies, illness, and other circumstances that disrupt coursework, and can advocate on your behalf with instructors. The Writing Center offers free help with written communication, useful for the project poster and your reflections. The W.E.B. Du Bois Library provides research and technical resources, and the University offers food, housing, and financial assistance for students facing insecurity through the Dean of Students Office. Asking for help in time is a strength, and it is what these resources exist for.

+# COMPSCI 426 Agent Instructions
+
+These rules apply to all AI-assisted work in this repository for COMPSCI 426:
+Scalable Web Systems, Summer Session II 2026.
+
+## Course Mission
+
+- Build and measure simulated scalable web systems, not production deployments.
+- Stay aligned with the course stack: devcontainers, Docker, Docker Compose,
+  JavaScript/Node.js services, Caddy, Redis, k6, Prometheus, and Grafana.

+  patterns over clever or oversized implementations.
+- Use `syllabus.md` for course schedule, grading, sprint deliverables, policies,
+  and staff contact details.
+
+## What Belongs Here
+
+- Knowledge Unit exercises and notes.
+- Homework source code, load tests, and submission notes.
+- Sprint and project code, docs, posters, demo scripts, and reflections.
+- Docker Compose files, service code, k6 scripts, observability config, and
+  generated synthetic test data.
+- AI disclosure records under `ai/chats/`.
+
+Do not store unrelated classwork, secrets, API keys, private credentials, large
+binary dumps, personal Canvas exports, or production data.
+
+## Agentic Coding Workflow
+
+- Read the assignment or sprint prompt first, then check `syllabus.md`.
+- Inspect the repo before editing. Prefer `rg`, `fd`, `jq`, and `tree` when
+  available.
+- Work in small, reviewable changes with clear commits or PRs when appropriate.
+- Keep code runnable in the course devcontainer.
+- Use Docker Compose for multi-service work; do not install databases or
+  infrastructure directly on the host.
+- Keep services domain-relevant but simulated: synthetic data, injected latency,
+  scripted failures, and measurable behavior are expected.
+- Add or update tests, k6 scripts, health checks, logs, or metrics when changing
+  behavior that depends on them.
+- Verify with the same command a grader or teammate would run.
+- Before large edits, show a diff summary or explain the intended file changes.
+
+## Implementation Standards
+
+- Prefer maintainable JavaScript over clever abstractions.
+- Make HTTP endpoints explicit and easy to test with `curl`.

+  logs, and Prometheus metrics when the sprint requires them.
+- Use Caddy for load balancing/reverse proxy requirements.
+- Use Redis for caching, queues, pub/sub, and related sprint requirements.
+- Use k6 to measure p50, p95, p99 latency, throughput, and error rate.
+- Document how to start the full system with one command.

+
+- Use branches and pull requests for team work.
+- Keep commit history useful: small commits, meaningful messages, no secrets.

+This file keeps course facts that agents may need while working in this repo.

+

+

+
+- Devcontainers, Docker, Docker Compose, Git, and GitHub workflows.
+- Distributed-system properties: latency, reliability, idempotency, delivery

+  consistent hashing, scatter/gather.

+- Event-driven systems: Redis queues, pub/sub, dead letter queues, workers.

+- Failure diagnosis: thundering herd, versioning errors, cascading failure.

# COMPSCI 426 Agent Instructions

These rules apply to all AI-assisted work in this repository for COMPSCI 426:
Scalable Web Systems, Summer Session II 2026.

## Course Mission

- Build and measure simulated scalable web systems, not production deployments.
- Stay aligned with the course stack: devcontainers, Docker, Docker Compose,
  JavaScript/Node.js services, Caddy, Redis, k6, Prometheus, and Grafana.
- Prefer simple, observable systems that clearly demonstrate distributed-systems
  patterns over clever or oversized implementations.
- Use `syllabus.md` for course schedule, grading, sprint deliverables, policies,
  and staff contact details.

## What Belongs Here

- Knowledge Unit exercises and notes.
- Homework source code, load tests, and submission notes.
- Sprint and project code, docs, posters, demo scripts, and reflections.
- Docker Compose files, service code, k6 scripts, observability config, and
  generated synthetic test data.
- AI disclosure records under `ai/chats/`.

Do not store unrelated classwork, secrets, API keys, private credentials, large
binary dumps, personal Canvas exports, or production data.

## Agentic Coding Workflow

- Read the assignment or sprint prompt first, then check `syllabus.md`.
- Inspect the repo before editing. Prefer `rg`, `fd`, `jq`, and `tree` when
  available.
- Work in small, reviewable changes with clear commits or PRs when appropriate.
- Keep code runnable in the course devcontainer.
- Use Docker Compose for multi-service work; do not install databases or
  infrastructure directly on the host.
- Keep services domain-relevant but simulated: synthetic data, injected latency,
  scripted failures, and measurable behavior are expected.
- Add or update tests, k6 scripts, health checks, logs, or metrics when changing
  behavior that depends on them.
- Verify with the same command a grader or teammate would run.
- Before large edits, show a diff summary or explain the intended file changes.

## Implementation Standards

- Prefer maintainable JavaScript over clever abstractions.
- Make HTTP endpoints explicit and easy to test with `curl`.
- All custom services should eventually expose health endpoints, structured JSON
  logs, and Prometheus metrics when the sprint requires them.
- Use Caddy for load balancing/reverse proxy requirements.
- Use Redis for caching, queues, pub/sub, and related sprint requirements.

# COMPSCI 426 Syllabus Reference

This file keeps course facts that agents may need while working in this repo.
Use `AGENTS.md` for operating rules.

## Course Basics

- Course: COMPSCI 426, Scalable Web Systems.
- Term: Summer Session II 2026.
- Dates: Monday, July 6, 2026 through Friday, August 14, 2026.
- Mode: online, asynchronous.
- Credits: 3.
- Instructor: Tim Richards, `tdr@umass.edu`.
- TA: Miles (Mingzhe) Li, `mingzhel@umass.edu`.
- Canvas: https://umamherst.instructure.com/courses/38093
- Exams: none.
- Group work: yes.
- Expected workload: about 22-23 hours per week for 6 weeks.

## Course Focus

Students build, monitor, break, and load test distributed web-system
simulations. The course is concept-first and experiential: build or observe a
pattern first, then name it.

Core topics:

- Devcontainers, Docker, Docker Compose, Git, and GitHub workflows.
- Distributed-system properties: latency, reliability, idempotency, delivery
  semantics, consistency, and failure modes.
- Single-node patterns: sidecar, ambassador, adapter.
- Serving patterns: replication, Caddy load balancing, caching, sharding,
  consistent hashing, scatter/gather.
- Measurement with k6: latency percentiles, throughput, error rates.
- Event-driven systems: Redis queues, pub/sub, dead letter queues, workers.
- Coordination: locks, leases, ownership election, concurrent data changes.
- Observability: structured logs, metrics, tracing, Prometheus, Grafana.
- Failure diagnosis: thundering herd, versioning errors, cascading failure.

## Required Technology

- Course devcontainer.
- VS Code, Docker Desktop, and VS Code Remote Containers extension.
- Node.js and JavaScript for services.
- Docker CLI and Docker Compose.
- k6 for load testing.
- Caddy as reverse proxy and load balancer.
- Redis, MongoDB, PostgreSQL, Prometheus, and Grafana where assignments require.
- Textbook: Designing Distributed Systems, 2nd Edition, Brendan Burns.

Do not install course infrastructure directly on the host unless explicitly
required. A Chromebook or tablet is not sufficient because the course requires a
local containerized development environment.

## Assessment Weights

- Participation: 5%.
- Weekly quizzes: 20%.
- Homework: 30%.
- Sprints: 25%.
- Final project deliverables: 20%.
- Exercises: expected practice, 0%.

There is no extra credit. Final percentage is rounded once at the end.

Grade scale:

| Letter | Range |
| --- | --- |
| A | 93-100 |
| A- | 90-92 |
| B+ | 87-89 |
| B | 83-86 |
| B- | 80-82 |
| C+ | 77-79 |
| C | 73-76 |
| C- | 70-72 |
| D+ | 67-69 |
| D | 60-66 |
| F | below 60 |

## Weekly Schedule

Week 0, Jun 29-Jul 3:

- KU 0A: Development Environment Setup.
- KU 0B: GitHub and Team Setup.

Week 1, Jul 6-Jul 10:

- KU 01: Why Distributed Systems?
- KU 02: APIs, Latency, Reliability, and Percentiles.
- KU 03: Idempotency, Delivery Semantics, and Data Consistency.
- Homework 1.
- Project Sprint 0: Team Formation and Project Concept.

Week 2, Jul 13-Jul 17:

- KU 04: Docker Fundamentals.
- KU 05: Docker Compose.
- KU 06: Sidecar Pattern.
- KU 07: Ambassador Pattern.
- Homework 2.
- Project Sprint 1: Project Definition and Scalability Framing.

Week 3, Jul 20-Jul 24:

- KU 08: Adapter Pattern.
- KU 09: Replicated Services, Caching, and Rate Limiting.
- KU 10: Sharded Services.
- KU 11: Scatter/Gather.
- Homework 3.
- Project Sprint 2: First Containerized System.

Week 4, Jul 27-Jul 31:

- KU 12: Resilience and Failure Modes.
- KU 13: Functions, Event-Driven Processing, and Decorator Pattern.
- KU 14: Work Queue Systems.
- KU 15: Event-Driven Batch Processing.
- Homework 4.
- Project Sprint 3: Serving Patterns and First Load Test.

Week 5, Aug 3-Aug 7:

- KU 16: Coordinated Batch Processing.
- KU 17: Ownership Election.
- KU 18: Observability.
- Project Sprint 4: Async Processing and Resilience.

Week 6, Aug 10-Aug 14:

- Project Sprint 5: Observability, Final Measurement, and Delivery.
- Final project deliverables.

## Sprint Deliverables

Sprint 0:

- Shared GitHub repository with collaborators.
- README with team roster.
- Short domain paragraph and initial scalability challenge.

Sprint 1:

- Refined domain and scalability problem with Computing for the Common Good
  framing.
- Initial service list with one sentence per service.
- Latency and reliability requirements.

Sprint 2:

- At least two containerized services under Docker Compose.
- Each service has an HTTP endpoint returning domain-relevant simulated data.
- At least one sidecar or ambassador pattern.
- `docker-compose.yml` starts the system with one command.

Sprint 3:

- At least one replicated service behind Caddy.
- Redis caching on at least one service path with simulated hits and misses.
- k6 load test for replicated service.
- Written p50, p95, and p99 latency summary.

Sprint 4:

- Async processing path using Redis work queue or pub/sub.
- Health endpoints on all services.
- Docker Compose healthcheck configuration.
- Scripted failure or slowdown scenario and response description.

Sprint 5:

- Prometheus metrics exposed by all custom services.
- Prometheus scraping in Docker Compose.
- Grafana dashboard with request rate, error rate, and p95 latency.
- Structured JSON logs from all custom services.
- Final k6 load test and bottleneck interpretation.
- Complete README and one-command startup.
- Recorded demo, 10 minutes or less.
- One-page project poster PDF.
- Individual reflection from each team member.

## Homework, Quizzes, and Participation

- Homework is submitted through Gradescope and autograded.
- Homework can be resubmitted before the deadline; final submission is graded.
- Homework may be up to 2 days late with 10% deduction per day.
- Homework after 2 days late is not accepted.
- Sprint deliverables and final capstone are hard deadlines.
- Weekly quizzes are on Canvas, about 20 questions, 45 minutes, up to 3 attempts.
- Highest quiz score counts.
- Final-week quiz is cumulative.
- Participation is weekly: Week 0 public introduction, Weeks 1-5 private
  reflections.

## Project Final

The project is a simulated scalable web system. It should use synthetic data,
injected latency, scripted failures, coordinated services, async pipelines,
caching, observability, and load testing. Public deployment is not required.

Final deliverables:

- GitHub repository URL.
- Recorded video demonstration.
- Project poster PDF.
- Individual written reflection.

## AI Policy

AI tools are allowed. Any AI use must be disclosed for the submission where it
was used. Required disclosure:

- Transcript of all relevant AI interactions.
- Full prompts sent and full responses received.
- Inline comments at code generated or substantially modified by AI.

Undisclosed AI use or missing transcripts may be treated as an academic honesty
violation.

## Communication Policy

Email course questions to `tdr@umass.edu` from verified UMass email.

Subject format:

```text
[426] Short specific subject
```

Include:

- Category: Logistics, Assignment, Technical, Grading, Extension,
  Accommodation, or Personal.
- Exact deliverable name, such as Sprint 3 or KU 11 Sharded Services.
- Repo link and relevant PR, commit, or Gradescope run for technical questions.
- Verbatim error message.
- What has already been tried.
- The precise question.

Requests about deadlines, accommodations, or situations affecting work should be
sent before the deadline. Staff aim to respond within one business day on
weekdays; do not expect weekend or holiday responses.

## Other Policies

- Individual work, quizzes, homework, and individual reflections must be your
  own.
- Team collaboration is expected within the assigned project team.
- Across teams, concept discussion is allowed, but copying code or submissions
  is not.
- Disability accommodations should be arranged early through Disability
  Services and by emailing the instructor.
- Course interactions must be respectful and inclusive.

Welcome! This guide will get your development environment up and running, even if you have never used Docker or a dev container before. Read through each section in order the first time, it only takes about 10 minutes.

What is this, exactly?
When you open the development environment folder in VS Code, it automatically builds a Linux environment that runs inside your computer. Think of it like a virtual machine, but lighter and faster. Inside that environment you get:

Node.js (latest LTS) and all the tools you need for web development
Optional databases (PostgreSQL, Redis, MongoDB, MySQL, and more) that you can turn on with a single command
A pre-configured terminal with shortcuts that make common tasks faster
Everything needed for web development, no manual installation required
No matter whether you are on macOS, Windows, or Linux, everyone on the team gets the exact same environment. "It works on my machine" stops being an excuse.

A note before you dive in: This document covers a lot of ground, and that is intentional. It is meant to be a reference you return to throughout the course, not something you need to absorb all at once. You will not use everything here, and that is completely fine. Many of the services, shortcuts, and tools listed are available if and when a homework or exercise calls for them. If you have never touched a terminal or typed a command before, do not worry. The terminal may look unfamiliar at first, but you will get comfortable with it gradually as we work through things together. Just follow the steps in order, and if something is confusing, set it aside for now. It will make more sense in context when we get there.

Step 1: Install the prerequisites
You need three things installed on your computer before you start. Click each link and follow the instructions for your operating system.

Docker DesktopLinks to an external site. Docker is the engine that runs the dev environment. The Desktop app gives you a graphical dashboard too.

Windows users: during installation, choose "Use WSL 2" if asked. After installing, open Docker Desktop once and let it finish starting up before moving on.

Visual Studio CodeLinks to an external site. The code editor.

Dev Containers extensionLinks to an external site. This VS Code extension makes the "open in container" magic work. Click the link, then click Install, and VS Code will open and install it automatically.

Once all three are installed, make sure Docker Desktop is running (look for the Docker whale icon in your taskbar or menu bar) before continuing.

Step 2: Download the development environment
Go to the Gantry Dev Container ReleasesLinks to an external site.. Under "Assets," download the latest release by selecting the file named gantry-<version>.zip. Do not download the "Source code" archives, that is not the release build. Save the file somewhere you can find it, such as your Desktop or your own folder for this course.

Step 3: Extract the archive
Extract gantry-<version>.zip to your chosen folder location. Do not leave it in your Downloads folder, the container will store your course work inside this folder, so treat it as your course workspace.

On macOS: double-click gantry-<version>.zip to extract it. A folder named gantry-<version> will appear alongside the archive.

On Windows: right-click gantry-<version>.zip and choose "Extract All." Select your destination folder and click Extract. A folder named gantry-<version> will appear in the destination folder.

On Linux: open a terminal and run unzip gantry-<version>.zip. A folder named gantry-<version> will appear in the destination folder. You may also use a zip extracting application provided by the particular Linux distribution you are using (e.g., Ubuntu, Fedora, Arch)

Step 4: Open the Development Environment in VS Code
Open VS Code.

Go to File → Open Folder and select the development environment folder.

VS Code will show a notification in the bottom-right corner (this may take a moment).

Click "Reopen in Container". If you missed the notification, open the Command Palette (Ctrl+Shift+P on Windows/Linux, Cmd+Shift+P on Mac), type "Reopen in Container", and press Enter.

Wait for the build to finish. The first time takes 3–5 minutes while it downloads everything. You will see a progress bar in the bottom-right corner. Subsequent openings are almost instant. It is helpful to be on a fast WiFi connection for this part.

When the build finishes, VS Code reloads and you are now inside the development environment.

Step 5: Open the terminal
The terminal is how you run code and commands. Inside VS Code:

Go to Terminal → New Terminal in the menu bar, or press Ctrl+` (backtick).
The Gantry banner confirms everything is working. The $ at the end of the last line is the prompt, it is waiting for you to type a command.

New to the terminal? The terminal works by typing a command and pressing Enter. Commands are case-sensitive. If something goes wrong, you can usually press Ctrl+C to stop whatever is running.

Common Tasks
The following examples cover common tasks. Run them in the VS Code terminal (Terminal → New Terminal in the menu bar, or press Ctrl+` (backtick)).

Run a Node.js script
Let's confirm Node.js is ready.

node --version
You should see something like v22.x.x. Now create and run a tiny script:

echo 'console.log("Hello from the dev container!")' > hello.js
node hello.js
Expected output:

Hello from the dev container!
Install npm packages and run a project
If you have a package.json file in your workspace:

npm install
npm run dev
The npm run dev command starts your project (exact behavior depends on the project). Press Ctrl+C to stop it.

Shortcuts that save typing:

Instead of	You can type
npm install	ni
npm run dev	nrd
npm run	nr
npm start	ns
npm test	nt
Start a database and connect to it
Databases are off by default to save memory. Turn one on when you need it.

Start PostgreSQL:

dc-up postgres
You will see Docker pulling the image and starting the container. Once it says the container is healthy, connect to it:

psql-dev
You are now inside the PostgreSQL shell. Try a quick command:

\l
This lists all databases. You should see devdb in the list. Type \q to exit.

Start Redis:

dc-up redis
redis-dev ping
Expected output: PONG

Start MongoDB:

dc-up mongo
mongo-dev
You are now in the MongoDB shell. Type show dbs to list databases. Type exit to leave.

Stop everything when you're done:

dc-down
Check what is running
dps
This shows all running containers in a tidy table format. If nothing is running, you will see an empty table. To see the logs from a running service (like postgres), use:

dc-logs postgres
Press Ctrl+C to stop watching logs.

Make an HTTP request and read JSON
The environment comes with several tools for working with HTTP APIs.

curl https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/todos/1
The output is JSON but it is hard to read. Pipe it through jq to pretty-print it:

curl https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/todos/1 | jq .
Or use the built-in shortcut jcurl which does both steps at once:

jcurl https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/todos/1
You can also use xh (a friendlier HTTP tool):

xh https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/todos/1
Check what ports are listening
When your app is running, you might want to see what ports are in use:

ports
This lists every port that has something listening on it.

Available Services
Start any service with dc-up <name>. Stop everything with dc-down.

Service	Start command	What it is

Redis	dc-up redis	In-memory cache and key-value store
MongoDB	dc-up mongo	Document (NoSQL) database
MySQL	dc-up mysql	Relational database (MySQL flavour)
RabbitMQ	dc-up rabbitmq	Message queue. Management UI on port 15672
Elasticsearch	dc-up elastic	Full-text search engine
Memcached	dc-up memcached	Simple in-memory cache
MinIO	dc-up minio	S3-compatible object storage. Console on port 9001
Redpanda	dc-up redpanda	Kafka-compatible event streaming
Mailpit	dc-up mailpit	Local email catcher. Web UI on port 8025
Adminer	dc-up adminer	Web-based database GUI (port 8080)
Nginx	dc-up nginx	Web / reverse proxy server
Caddy	dc-up caddy	HTTPS-capable web / reverse proxy server
Prometheus	dc-up prometheus	Metrics collection (port 9090)
Grafana	dc-up grafana	Metrics dashboards. admin / admin (port 3030)

dc-up postgres redis mongo
Quick-Connect Shortcuts
Once a service is running, these shortcuts drop you straight into its CLI (command line interface):

Command	What it does
psql-dev	Opens the PostgreSQL shell connected to devdb
redis-dev	Opens redis-cli connected to the Redis container
mongo-dev	Opens mongosh connected to MongoDB devdb
mysql-dev	Opens the MySQL shell connected to devdb
Opening a Shell Inside a Service Container
Need to run commands directly inside a database container (for example, to run admin commands)?

dexb postgres
Replace postgres with any running service name. This opens a bash shell inside that container. Type exit to come back.

Customizing Your Terminal
You can add your own aliases, functions, and environment variables without touching any shared files and without restarting the container.

Open the file .bashrc.user in your workspace root (VS Code's Explorer panel, it is a hidden file, so look for it there or open it from the terminal).

Add your customizations. Example:

# My personal shortcuts
alias serve='npx http-server . -p 8080'
alias cls='clear'
export MY_API_KEY="abc123"
Apply changes without restarting by running:
reload-env
Your changes are now active in the current terminal.

MongoDB	mongo	27017	dev	devpassword	devdb

Troubleshooting
The "Reopen in Container" notification never appeared
Open the Command Palette (Cmd+Shift+P / Ctrl+Shift+P), type Dev Containers: Reopen in Container, and press Enter. If that option doesn't appear, make sure the Dev Containers extension is installed and Docker Desktop is running.

The build failed or got stuck
Make sure Docker Desktop is open and running (check the taskbar/menu bar icon).
Open the Command Palette and choose Dev Containers: Rebuild Container.
If it fails again, open Docker Desktop and check that you have at least 4 GB of memory allocated to Docker (Settings → Resources).
A service won't start
Check Docker is running, then try:

dc-logs <service>
This shows the service's error output. Common fix: the service might need a moment to initialize. Try dc-up <service> again after 10 seconds.

psql-dev / redis-dev says "connection refused"
The service is not running yet. Start it first:

dc-up postgres   # or redis, mongo, etc.
Wait a few seconds for it to become ready, then try again.

My app can't connect to the database
Make sure you are using the service name as the host (e.g. postgres, redis, mongo), not localhost. Inside the dev container, services talk to each other by name. See the connection table above.

I can't push to GitHub
Run this inside the container terminal:

gh auth status
If it says you are not authenticated, run:

gh auth login
Follow the prompts. After authenticating, git push will work automatically.

I accidentally ran something and the terminal is frozen
Press Ctrl+C to cancel the current command. If that doesn't work, close the terminal tab and open a new one from Terminal → New Terminal.

Everything is broken, I want to start fresh
Open the Command Palette and choose Dev Containers: Rebuild Container. This rebuilds the environment from scratch. Your files in the workspace folder are never deleted.

# COMPSCI 426 Agent Instructions

These rules apply to all AI-assisted work in this repository for COMPSCI 426:
Scalable Web Systems, Summer Session II 2026.

## Course Mission

- Build and measure simulated scalable web systems, not production deployments.
- Stay aligned with the course stack: devcontainers, Docker, Docker Compose,
  JavaScript/Node.js services, Caddy, Redis, k6, Prometheus, and Grafana.
- Prefer simple, observable systems that clearly demonstrate distributed-systems
  patterns over clever or oversized implementations.
- Use `syllabus.md` for course schedule, grading, sprint deliverables, policies,
  and staff contact details.

- Knowledge Unit exercises and notes.
- Homework source code, load tests, and submission notes.
- Sprint and project code, docs, posters, demo scripts, and reflections.
- Docker Compose files, service code, k6 scripts, observability config, and
  generated synthetic test data.
- AI disclosure records under `ai/chats/`.

Do not store unrelated classwork, secrets, API keys, private credentials, large
binary dumps, personal Canvas exports, or production data.

## Agentic Coding Workflow

- Read the assignment or sprint prompt first, then check `syllabus.md`.
- Inspect the repo before editing. Prefer `rg`, `fd`, `jq`, and `tree` when
  available.

- Keep code runnable in the course devcontainer.
- Use Docker Compose for multi-service work; do not install databases or
  infrastructure directly on the host.
- Keep services domain-relevant but simulated: synthetic data, injected latency,
  scripted failures, and measurable behavior are expected.
- Add or update tests, k6 scripts, health checks, logs, or metrics when changing
  behavior that depends on them.
- Verify with the same command a grader or teammate would run.

- Prefer maintainable JavaScript over clever abstractions.
- Make HTTP endpoints explicit and easy to test with `curl`.

# COMPSCI 426 Syllabus Reference

This file keeps course facts that agents may need while working in this repo.
Use `AGENTS.md` for operating rules.

## Course Basics

- Course: COMPSCI 426, Scalable Web Systems.
- Term: Summer Session II 2026.
- Dates: Monday, July 6, 2026 through Friday, August 14, 2026.
- Mode: online, asynchronous.
- Credits: 3.
- Instructor: Tim Richards, `tdr@umass.edu`.
- TA: Miles (Mingzhe) Li, `mingzhel@umass.edu`.
- Canvas: https://umamherst.instructure.com/courses/38093
- Exams: none.
- Group work: yes.
- Expected workload: about 22-23 hours per week for 6 weeks.

## Course Focus

Students build, monitor, break, and load test distributed web-system
simulations. The course is concept-first and experiential: build or observe a
pattern first, then name it.

Core topics:

- Devcontainers, Docker, Docker Compose, Git, and GitHub workflows.
- Distributed-system properties: latency, reliability, idempotency, delivery
  semantics, consistency, and failure modes.
- Single-node patterns: sidecar, ambassador, adapter.
- Serving patterns: replication, Caddy load balancing, caching, sharding,
  consistent hashing, scatter/gather.
- Measurement with k6: latency percentiles, throughput, error rates.
- Event-driven systems: Redis queues, pub/sub, dead letter queues, workers.
- Coordination: locks, leases, ownership election, concurrent data changes.
- Observability: structured logs, metrics, tracing, Prometheus, Grafana.
- Failure diagnosis: thundering herd, versioning errors, cascading failure.

## Required Technology

- Course devcontainer.
- VS Code, Docker Desktop, and VS Code Remote Containers extension.
- Node.js and JavaScript for services.
- Docker CLI and Docker Compose.
- k6 for load testing.
- Caddy as reverse proxy and load balancer.
- Redis, MongoDB, PostgreSQL, Prometheus, and Grafana where assignments require.
- Textbook: Designing Distributed Systems, 2nd Edition, Brendan Burns.

Do not install course infrastructure directly on the host unless explicitly
required. A Chromebook or tablet is not sufficient because the course requires a
local containerized development environment.

## Assessment Weights

- Participation: 5%.
- Weekly quizzes: 20%.
- Homework: 30%.
- Sprints: 25%.
- Final project deliverables: 20%.
- Exercises: expected practice, 0%.

| Letter | Range |

| B | 83-86 |

| C+ | 77-79 |
| C | 73-76 |
| C- | 70-72 |
| D+ | 67-69 |
| D | 60-66 |
| F | below 60 |

Week 0, Jun 29-Jul 3:

- KU 0A: Development Environment Setup.
- KU 0B: GitHub and Team Setup.

- KU 01: Why Distributed Systems?
- KU 02: APIs, Latency, Reliability, and Percentiles.
- KU 03: Idempotency, Delivery Semantics, and Data Consistency.
- Homework 1.
- Project Sprint 0: Team Formation and Project Concept.

Week 2, Jul 13-Jul 17:

- KU 04: Docker Fundamentals.
- KU 05: Docker Compose.
- KU 06: Sidecar Pattern.
- KU 07: Ambassador Pattern.
- Homework 2.
- Project Sprint 1: Project Definition and Scalability Framing.

Week 3, Jul 20-Jul 24:

- KU 08: Adapter Pattern.
- KU 09: Replicated Services, Caching, and Rate Limiting.
- KU 10: Sharded Services.
- KU 11: Scatter/Gather.
- Homework 3.
- Project Sprint 2: First Containerized System.

Week 4, Jul 27-Jul 31:

- KU 12: Resilience and Failure Modes.
- KU 13: Functions, Event-Driven Processing, and Decorator Pattern.
- KU 14: Work Queue Systems.
- KU 15: Event-Driven Batch Processing.
- Homework 4.
- Project Sprint 3: Serving Patterns and First Load Test.

Week 5, Aug 3-Aug 7:

- KU 16: Coordinated Batch Processing.
- KU 17: Ownership Election.
- KU 18: Observability.
- Project Sprint 4: Async Processing and Resilience.

Week 6, Aug 10-Aug 14:

- Project Sprint 5: Observability, Final Measurement, and Delivery.
- Final project deliverables.

## Sprint Deliverables

Sprint 0:

- Shared GitHub repository with collaborators.
- README with team roster.
- Short domain paragraph and initial scalability challenge.

Sprint 1:

- Refined domain and scalability problem with Computing for the Common Good
  framing.
- Initial service list with one sentence per service.
- Latency and reliability requirements.

Sprint 2:

- At least two containerized services under Docker Compose.
- Each service has an HTTP endpoint returning domain-relevant simulated data.
- At least one sidecar or ambassador pattern.
- `docker-compose.yml` starts the system with one command.

Sprint 3:

- At least one replicated service behind Caddy.
- Redis caching on at least one service path with simulated hits and misses.
- k6 load test for replicated service.
- Written p50, p95, and p99 latency summary.

Sprint 4:

- Async processing path using Redis work queue or pub/sub.
- Health endpoints on all services.
- Docker Compose healthcheck configuration.
- Scripted failure or slowdown scenario and response description.

Sprint 5:

- Prometheus metrics exposed by all custom services.
- Prometheus scraping in Docker Compose.
- Grafana dashboard with request rate, error rate, and p95 latency.
- Structured JSON logs from all custom services.
- Final k6 load test and bottleneck interpretation.
- Complete README and one-command startup.
- Recorded demo, 10 minutes or less.
- One-page project poster PDF.
- Individual reflection from each team member.

- Homework is submitted through Gradescope and autograded.

- Homework may be up to 2 days late with 10% deduction per day.
- Homework after 2 days late is not accepted.
- Sprint deliverables and final capstone are hard deadlines.
- Weekly quizzes are on Canvas, about 20 questions, 45 minutes, up to 3 attempts.
- Highest quiz score counts.
- Final-week quiz is cumulative.
- Participation is weekly: Week 0 public introduction, Weeks 1-5 private
  reflections.

## Project Final

The project is a simulated scalable web system. It should use synthetic data,
injected latency, scripted failures, coordinated services, async pipelines,
caching, observability, and load testing. Public deployment is not required.

Final deliverables:

- GitHub repository URL.
- Recorded video demonstration.
- Project poster PDF.
- Individual written reflection.

## AI Policy

AI tools are allowed. Any AI use must be disclosed for the submission where it
was used. Required disclosure:

- Transcript of all relevant AI interactions.
- Full prompts sent and full responses received.
- Inline comments at code generated or substantially modified by AI.

violation.

## Communication Policy

Email course questions to `tdr@umass.edu` from verified UMass email.

Subject format:

```text
[426] Short specific subject
```

Include:

- Category: Logistics, Assignment, Technical, Grading, Extension,
  Accommodation, or Personal.
- Exact deliverable name, such as Sprint 3 or KU 11 Sharded Services.
- Repo link and relevant PR, commit, or Gradescope run for technical questions.
- Verbatim error message.
- What has already been tried.
- The precise question.

Requests about deadlines, accommodations, or situations affecting work should be
sent before the deadline. Staff aim to respond within one business day on
weekdays; do not expect weekend or holiday responses.

## Other Policies

- Individual work, quizzes, homework, and individual reflections must be your
  own.
- Team collaboration is expected within the assigned project team.
- Across teams, concept discussion is allowed, but copying code or submissions
  is not.
- Disability accommodations should be arranged early through Disability
  Services and by emailing the instructor.
- Course interactions must be respectful and inclusive.

+## Suggested Technical Reference
+
+The course development environment is the Gantry devcontainer. It gives all
+students the same Linux-based workspace inside VS Code with Node.js, Docker
+tools, optional databases, HTTP tools, load testing tools, and shell shortcuts.
+
+Setup flow:
+
+1. Install Docker Desktop, Visual Studio Code, and the VS Code Dev Containers
+   extension.
+2. Start Docker Desktop before opening the project.
+3. Download the latest Gantry release zip named `gantry-<version>.zip`; do not
+   use the GitHub "Source code" archives.
+4. Extract it outside Downloads and treat the extracted folder as the course
+   workspace.
+5. Open the folder in VS Code and choose `Dev Containers: Reopen in Container`.
+6. Wait for the first build to finish; first build usually takes 3-5 minutes.
+7. Open a terminal in VS Code. The Gantry banner confirms the container is ready.
+
+Terminal basics:
+
+- Commands are case-sensitive.
+- Press `Ctrl+C` to stop a stuck or running command.
+- Use `Terminal -> New Terminal` or `Ctrl+\`` in VS Code.
+- Rebuild a broken environment with `Dev Containers: Rebuild Container`; files
+  in the workspace are not deleted.
+
+Common Node commands:
+
+| Task | Command |
+| --- | --- |
+| Check Node | `node --version` |
+| Install packages | `npm install` or `ni` |
+| Run dev script | `npm run dev` or `nrd` |
+| Run npm script | `npm run` or `nr` |
+| Start project | `npm start` or `ns` |
+| Run tests | `npm test` or `nt` |
+| Install with pnpm | `pnpm install` or `pni` |
+| Run pnpm script | `pnpm run` or `pnr` |
+
+Docker/service shortcuts:
+
+| Shortcut | Purpose |
+| --- | --- |
+| `dc-up <service>` | Start one or more services |
+| `dc-down` | Stop all services |
+| `dc-logs <service>` | Watch service logs |
+| `dps` | Show running containers |
+| `dexb <service>` | Open bash inside a running service container |
+| `dlog <container>` | Follow raw Docker logs |
+| `dprune` | Clean stopped containers/images |
+
+Available services:
+
+| Service | Start | Notes |
+| --- | --- | --- |
+| PostgreSQL | `dc-up postgres` | User `dev`, password `devpassword`, DB `devdb` |
+| Redis | `dc-up redis` | Cache and key-value store |
+| MongoDB | `dc-up mongo` | Document database |
+| MySQL | `dc-up mysql` | User `dev`, password `devpassword`, DB `devdb` |
+| RabbitMQ | `dc-up rabbitmq` | Queue; management UI on port 15672 |
+| Elasticsearch | `dc-up elastic` | Full-text search |
+| Memcached | `dc-up memcached` | Simple in-memory cache |

+| Redpanda | `dc-up redpanda` | Kafka-compatible event streaming |
+| Mailpit | `dc-up mailpit` | Local email catcher; UI on port 8025 |
+| Adminer | `dc-up adminer` | Database GUI on port 8080 |
+| Nginx | `dc-up nginx` | Web/reverse proxy |
+| Caddy | `dc-up caddy` | HTTPS-capable web/reverse proxy |
+| Prometheus | `dc-up prometheus` | Metrics collection on port 9090 |
+| Grafana | `dc-up grafana` | Dashboards on port 3030, `admin`/`admin` |
+| Jaeger | `dc-up jaeger` | Tracing UI on port 16686 |

+Quick-connect shortcuts:
+
+| Command | Purpose |
+| --- | --- |

+| `redis-dev` | Redis CLI |
+| `mongo-dev` | MongoDB shell connected to `devdb` |
+| `mysql-dev` | MySQL shell connected to `devdb` |
+
+HTTP and network tools:
+
+| Command | Purpose |
+| --- | --- |
+| `curl <url>` | Make HTTP request |
+| `curl <url> \| jq .` | Pretty-print JSON |

+| `xh <url>` | Friendlier HTTP client |
+| `GET`, `POST`, `PUT`, `DELETE` | Shortcut HTTP verbs |
+| `wstest ws://localhost:3000` | WebSocket test |
+| `ports` | Show listening ports |

+| Redis | `redis` | 6379 | | | |
+| MySQL | `mysql` | 3306 | `dev` | `devpassword` | `devdb` |
+| RabbitMQ | `rabbitmq` | 5672 | `dev` | `devpassword` | |
+| Elasticsearch | `elastic` | 9200 | | | |
+| Memcached | `memcached` | 11211 | | | |
+| MinIO | `minio` | 9000 | `minioadmin` | `minioadmin` | |
+| Redpanda | `redpanda` | 9092 | | | |
+| SMTP/Mailpit | `mailpit` | 1025 | | | |
+
+Example PostgreSQL URL:
+
+```text
+postgresql://dev:devpassword@postgres:5432/devdb
+```
+

+
+Personal shell customization belongs in `.bashrc.user`, not shared project
+files. Use `reload-env` after editing it. Do not commit secrets from personal
+customizations.
+
+Troubleshooting:
+
+- If `Reopen in Container` does not appear, use the command palette and confirm

+- If the container build fails, try `Dev Containers: Rebuild Container` and

+- If GitHub push fails, run `gh auth status`, then `gh auth login` if needed.

+`lsof`, Git, GitHub CLI, Docker, and Docker Compose.

# COMPSCI 426 Agent Instructions

These rules apply to all AI-assisted work in this repository for COMPSCI 426:
Scalable Web Systems, Summer Session II 2026.

## Course Mission

- Build and measure simulated scalable web systems, not production deployments.
- Stay aligned with the course stack: devcontainers, Docker, Docker Compose,

binary dumps, personal Canvas exports, or production data.

## Suggested Technical Reference

The course development environment is the Gantry devcontainer. It gives all
students the same Linux-based workspace inside VS Code with Node.js, Docker
tools, optional databases, HTTP tools, load testing tools, and shell shortcuts.

Setup flow:

1. Install Docker Desktop, Visual Studio Code, and the VS Code Dev Containers
   extension.
2. Start Docker Desktop before opening the project.
3. Download the latest Gantry release zip named `gantry-<version>.zip`; do not
   use the GitHub "Source code" archives.
4. Extract it outside Downloads and treat the extracted folder as the course
   workspace.
5. Open the folder in VS Code and choose `Dev Containers: Reopen in Container`.
6. Wait for the first build to finish; first build usually takes 3-5 minutes.
7. Open a terminal in VS Code. The Gantry banner confirms the container is ready.

Terminal basics:

- Commands are case-sensitive.
- Press `Ctrl+C` to stop a stuck or running command.
- Use `Terminal -> New Terminal` or `Ctrl+\`` in VS Code.
- Rebuild a broken environment with `Dev Containers: Rebuild Container`; files
  in the workspace are not deleted.

| Task | Command |
| --- | --- |
| Check Node | `node --version` |
| Install packages | `npm install` or `ni` |
| Run dev script | `npm run dev` or `nrd` |
| Run npm script | `npm run` or `nr` |
| Start project | `npm start` or `ns` |
| Run tests | `npm test` or `nt` |
| Install with pnpm | `pnpm install` or `pni` |
| Run pnpm script | `pnpm run` or `pnr` |

Docker/service shortcuts:

| Shortcut | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `dc-up <service>` | Start one or more services |
| `dc-down` | Stop all services |
| `dc-logs <service>` | Watch service logs |
| `dps` | Show running containers |
| `dexb <service>` | Open bash inside a running service container |
| `dlog <container>` | Follow raw Docker logs |
| `dprune` | Clean stopped containers/images |

Open VS Code.

ok so what od i do here tep 4: Open the Development Environment in VS Code
Open VS Code.

Go to File → Open Folder and select the development environment folder.

VS Code will show a notification in the bottom-right corner (this may take a moment).

Click "Reopen in Container". If you missed the notification, open the Command Palette (Ctrl+Shift+P on Windows/Linux, Cmd+Shift+P on Mac), type "Reopen in Container", and press Enter.

Wait for the build to finish. The first time takes 3–5 minutes while it downloads everything. You will see a progress bar in the bottom-right corner. Subsequent openings are almost instant. It is helpful to be on a fast WiFi connection for this part.

When the build finishes, VS Code reloads and you are now inside the development environment.

Do this on your Mac:

1. Open VS Code.

2. In VS Code, go to:

   `File -> Open Folder...`

3. Select this folder:

   `/Users/austinfairbanks/school/cs426`

4. After it opens, wait a few seconds for a popup in the bottom-right that says something like:

   `Reopen in Container`

   Click it.

5. If no popup appears:

   Press `Cmd+Shift+P`, type:

   `Dev Containers: Reopen in Container`

   then press Enter.

6. Wait for the build to finish. The first time may take 3-5 minutes or longer because Docker downloads/builds the environment.

You’ll know it worked when VS Code reloads and the bottom-left corner shows something like `Dev Container` or `Gantry`. Then open a terminal with:

`Terminal -> New Terminal`

The terminal should show the Gantry banner.

- Editing, planning, writing docs, saving AI chats: Codex outside is fine.


The Terminal: A Primer
Talk to your computer with words, not clicks

You have probably spent most of your computing life using a graphical interface — clicking icons, dragging windows, navigating menus. The terminal is a completely different way of talking to your computer, and it requires a different mental model. This primer explains what the terminal is, why it exists, why it matters for a course like this one, and what you need to know to use it without confusion.

What the Terminal Is
Your operating system — macOS, Windows, Linux — is a layer of software that manages the hardware underneath your applications. Every time you create a file, open a browser, or install a program, the operating system is doing the actual work. A graphical interface gives you buttons and menus to make requests to the operating system. The terminal does the same thing, but through text.

When you open a terminal, you see a cursor waiting for input. That interface is called the command line. You type a command, press Enter, and the operating system executes it. The output, if there is any, appears as text below your command. Then the cursor reappears and waits for the next one. That is the entire interaction model.

The program that reads your input and coordinates with the operating system is called a shell. On macOS and Linux, the default shell is usually bash or zsh. On Windows with WSL, you also get bash. The shell is not the terminal window itself — the terminal is the visual container, and the shell is the program running inside it. The distinction rarely matters in practice, but you will see both words used in documentation.

Why the Terminal Exists and Why It Matters
The terminal is not a relic from before graphical interfaces were invented. It is still the primary tool for technical work because it is fast, precise, scriptable, and universal.

Most of the tools used in professional software development — version control, build systems, test runners, package managers, servers, deployment scripts — are built to be operated from the command line. They have no graphical interface at all, or their graphical interface exposes far less than the command line does. git, npm, node, docker, psql: every tool you will use in this course is a command-line program. You will install packages by typing npm install. You will run your server by typing node server.js. You will interact with a database by typing commands. None of this happens through a menu.

There is a second reason the terminal matters: it is the same everywhere. A command that works on your laptop works on your classmates' laptops and on a remote server in a data center. When you deploy an application to production, there is no graphical interface available — there is only a shell. Learning to work in the terminal now means the jump to professional environments is not a surprise later.

Terminology You Need to Know
Before touching any commands, you need a shared vocabulary.

The file system is the structure your operating system uses to organize all stored data. Everything — your documents, your code, your programs — lives somewhere in the file system.

A directory is a container that holds files and other directories. You may know this concept as a "folder." In the terminal, the word "directory" is standard. Directories nest inside each other, forming a tree.

The root directory is the top of that tree. On macOS and Linux it is written as /. On Windows with WSL it is also / inside the Linux environment. Everything else in the file system is inside the root directory, directly or indirectly.

Your home directory is the directory assigned to your user account. On macOS it is typically /Users/yourname. On Linux it is typically /home/yourname. The ~ character is shorthand for your home directory in most shells.

The working directory is the directory the terminal is currently "inside." When you open a terminal, it starts in your home directory. When you run a command, the command executes relative to the working directory unless you specify otherwise. Understanding what your working directory is at any moment is one of the most important habits in terminal use.

A path is the address of a file or directory in the file system. An absolute path starts from the root and describes the full address: /home/yourname/cs326/project/server.js. A relative path starts from the current working directory: if your working directory is /home/yourname/cs326, then project/server.js is a relative path to the same file.

A command is a text instruction you give to the shell. Commands are usually short programs that live somewhere on your file system. When you type a command name, the shell searches a list of known locations to find and run it.

An argument is additional information passed to a command. When you type node server.js, node is the command and server.js is an argument telling it which file to run.

A flag (also called an option) is a special kind of argument that modifies a command's behavior. Flags usually start with - or --. For example, ls -l runs ls with the -l flag, which changes the output format.

A script is a text file containing a sequence of commands. Instead of typing ten commands manually, you put them in a script file and run the whole file at once. Scripts are how automation works in the terminal.

Permissions control who is allowed to read, write, or execute a file. Every file and directory in the file system has a set of permissions attached to it. Permissions matter when you try to run a script or access a file and the operating system refuses — understanding permissions tells you why and how to fix it.

Standard output (stdout) is where a command sends its normal output — the text you see printed in the terminal after a command runs. Standard error (stderr) is a separate channel for error messages. Both appear in the terminal by default, but they can be separated and redirected independently.

A process is a running instance of a program. When you run node server.js, you start a process. That process runs until it finishes or you stop it. Pressing Ctrl+C in the terminal sends a signal to the current process telling it to stop.

The Commands You Need First
These are the commands you will use constantly. Learn what they do before you need them in an activity.

pwd: Print the working directory.
Outputs the absolute path of the directory the terminal is currently in. When you are disoriented, run this first.

pwd
ls: List files and directories.
Shows the files and directories inside the working directory. Running ls -l shows a detailed view including permissions, owner, size, and modification date.

ls
ls -l
cd: Change directory.
Moves the terminal's working directory to the path you specify.

cd cs326
cd ..
cd ~
cd /home/yourname/cs326
cd .. moves up one level to the parent directory. cd ~ moves to your home directory. cd with no argument also moves to your home directory.

mkdir: Make a directory.
Creates a new directory with the name you provide.

mkdir project
mkdir -p project/src/routes
The -p flag creates intermediate directories as needed. Without it, mkdir project/src/routes fails if project or project/src do not already exist.

touch: Creates an empty file if it does not exist, or update the modification timestamp.
Commonly used to create placeholder files.

touch server.ts
cp: Copy file or directory.
Copies a file from one location to another.

cp server.ts server.backup.ts
cp -r src src-backup
The -r flag copies recursively, which is required when copying a directory.

mv: Move file or directory.
Moves a file to a new location, or renames it if the destination is in the same directory.

mv server.ts app.ts
mv server.js src/server.js
rm: Remove file or directory.
Deletes a file or directory. This is permanent — there is no trash or undo.

rm server.backup.ts
rm -r src-backup
The -r flag removes a directory and everything inside it recursively. Use it carefully.

cat: Concatenate a file.
Prints the contents of a file to the terminal. Used constantly for quickly reading short files.

cat package.json
less: Pages content from a file.
Shows the contents of a file one screen at a time, letting you scroll through output that is too long to read in a single terminal view. Unlike cat, it does not dump everything at once. Use the arrow keys or j/k to scroll, space to jump a full page, and q to exit.

less server.ts
less package.json
You will use less any time a file is long enough that cat makes it scroll past before you can read it. It is also how man displays its pages internally, the same navigation keys apply (see below).

echo: Print text to standard output.
Useful in scripts and for quick checks.

echo "hello"
echo $PATH
clear: Clear the terminal screen.
Your command history is not deleted; the display is just scrolled. It clears things up.

man: Manual.
Open the manual page for a command. On macOS and Linux, nearly every command has a manual page. Use the arrow keys or j/k to scroll, space to jump a full page, and q to exit. Press q to exit.

man ls
man cp
Running a Script
Basics
A script is an executable text file. To run one, you call it like a command:

node server.js
Some scripts are written for the shell directly, not for a runtime like Node. Those files typically end in .sh. To run a shell script, you first need to make sure it has execute permission, then call it:

chmod +x setup.sh
./setup.sh
chmod +x adds execute permission to the file. The ./ prefix tells the shell to look for the file in the current directory — without it, the shell only searches its known program locations and will not find your script.

The Shebang (#!)
The first line of a shell script that tells the operating system which interpreter to use to run the file. When you execute a script, the operating system reads the first two characters. If they are #!, it treats the rest of that line as the path to the program that should run the script.

#!/bin/bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
#!/usr/bin/env node
#!/usr/bin/env python3
Without a shebang, the operating system does not know what kind of script it is looking at. It may refuse to run it, or it may guess wrong. With a shebang, running ./setup.sh works exactly the same as running bash setup.sh — the shebang makes the file self-describing.

The second form, #!/usr/bin/env node, is more portable than a hardcoded path like #!/usr/local/bin/node. The env program searches your PATH for the named interpreter, so the script works regardless of where Node is installed on a given machine. You will see this form in most modern scripts that target Node or Python.

The shebang line is ignored as a comment by the interpreter itself, # starts a comment in bash, Python, and most scripting languages, so it causes no errors when the interpreter processes the rest of the file.

Here is a simple Node script that prints a greeting to the terminal:

#!/usr/bin/env node
const name = process.argv[2] ?? "stranger";
console.log(`Hello, ${name}!`);
Save this as greet.js, make it executable, and run it:

chmod +x greet.js
./greet.js
./greet.js Alice
Output:

Hello, stranger!
Hello, Alice!
process.argv is an array Node populates with the command-line arguments passed to the script. The first two entries are always the path to Node and the path to the script itself, so index 2 is where your first real argument lives. The ?? operator supplies a default if no argument was given.

Without the shebang, you would have to type node greet.js Alice every time. With it, ./greet.js Alice works -- the script knows how to run itself.

Permissions in Brief
When you run ls -l, each entry starts with a string like -rwxr-xr--. That string encodes the permissions on the file. The characters map to three groups: the owner, the group, and everyone else. For each group, there are three possible permissions: read (r), write (w), and execute (x). A - means that permission is not granted.

You will encounter permissions issues most often when trying to run a script that the operating system refuses to execute. The fix is usually chmod +x filename, which adds execute permission for the owner. The course activities will tell you when this is necessary.

What Happens When Something Goes Wrong
The terminal is unforgiving in one specific way: it does what you say, not what you meant. If you mistype a filename, it will tell you the file does not exist. If you run a command in the wrong directory, the results will be wrong. If you delete something with rm, it is gone.

Developing three habits will prevent most problems. First, always know your working directory. Run pwd whenever you are uncertain. Second, use ls before and after operations that create or move files. Third, read error messages carefully -- they almost always tell you exactly what went wrong. "No such file or directory" means your path is wrong. "Permission denied" means you do not have the right access level. "Command not found" means the program is not installed or not on your PATH.

There is no way to learn the terminal except by using it. The commands above will get you through everything in this course. You will be slow at first and faster within a week.

A Note on This Course
In this course you will use the terminal constantly. Every activity, every project sprint, every interaction with git, npm, node, and the Gantry container runs through the command line. If you setup the development environment and reach the integrated terminal inside VS Code, you are already in the right place. The shell running there is the same shell described in this primer. Every command here works exactly the same inside that terminal as it would in a standalone terminal application.

# Terminal Primer

Source: COMPSCI 426 Canvas page, "Terminal".

The terminal is a text interface for giving commands to the operating system.
The terminal window is the visual container; the shell, usually bash or zsh on
macOS/Linux, is the program that reads commands and runs them.

## Why It Matters

The course relies on command-line tools including `git`, `npm`, `node`,
`docker`, and database CLIs such as `psql`. Professional development, remote
servers, build systems, tests, deployments, and automation are also primarily
command-line driven.

## Core Vocabulary

- File system: the tree of stored files and directories.
- Directory: a folder that can contain files and other directories.
- Root directory: top of the tree, written `/` on macOS/Linux.
- Home directory: user directory, commonly `/Users/yourname`; `~` is shorthand.
- Working directory: where the shell currently is.
- Path: address of a file or directory.
- Absolute path: starts at root, such as `/Users/austin/project/server.js`.
- Relative path: starts from the working directory, such as `src/server.js`.
- Command: a text instruction run by the shell.
- Argument: extra input to a command, such as `server.js` in `node server.js`.
- Flag/option: modifies behavior, usually starts with `-` or `--`.
- Script: text file containing commands or code to run.
- Permissions: read/write/execute rules for files and directories.
- stdout: normal command output.
- stderr: error output.
- Process: a running program. `Ctrl+C` asks the current process to stop.

## First Commands

Print current working directory:

```bash
pwd
```

List files:

```bash
ls
ls -l
```

Change directories:

```bash
cd cs426
cd ..
cd ~
cd /Users/austinfairbanks/school/cs426
```

Create directories:

```bash
mkdir project
mkdir -p project/src/routes
```

Create or update a file timestamp:

```bash
touch server.ts
```

Copy files/directories:

```bash
cp server.ts server.backup.ts
cp -r src src-backup
```

Move or rename:

```bash
mv server.ts app.ts
mv server.js src/server.js
```

Remove files/directories:

```bash
rm server.backup.ts
rm -r src-backup
```

`rm` is permanent. There is no trash or undo.

Print a short file:

```bash
cat package.json
```

Read a longer file one screen at a time:

```bash
less server.ts
less package.json
```

Inside `less`, use arrow keys or `j`/`k` to scroll, Space for a page, and `q`
to quit.

Print text:

```bash
echo "hello"
echo "$PATH"
```

Clear the screen:

```bash
clear
```

Open manual pages:

```bash
man ls
man cp
```

Manual pages use the same navigation keys as `less`; press `q` to exit.

## Running Scripts

Run a Node script:

```bash
node server.js
```

Run a shell script:

```bash
chmod +x setup.sh
./setup.sh
```

`chmod +x` adds execute permission. The `./` prefix means "run the file in this
directory" instead of searching installed command locations.

## Shebangs

A shebang is the first line of an executable script. It tells the operating
system which interpreter to use.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
#!/usr/bin/env node
#!/usr/bin/env python3
```

The `/usr/bin/env` form is portable because it finds the interpreter from
`PATH`.

Example executable Node script:

```js
#!/usr/bin/env node
const name = process.argv[2] ?? "stranger";
console.log(`Hello, ${name}!`);
```

Run it:

```bash
chmod +x greet.js
./greet.js
./greet.js Alice
```

Expected output:

```text
Hello, stranger!
Hello, Alice!
```

## Permissions

`ls -l` shows permissions like `-rwxr-xr--`. The groups are owner, group, and
everyone else. Each group can have read (`r`), write (`w`), and execute (`x`).
A `-` means that permission is absent.

When a script will not run because of permissions, the usual fix is:

```bash
chmod +x filename
```

## Debugging Terminal Problems

Use these habits:

- Run `pwd` when unsure where you are.
- Run `ls` before and after creating, moving, or deleting files.
- Read error messages literally.
- `No such file or directory` usually means the path is wrong.
- `Permission denied` means access or execute permissions are missing.
- `Command not found` means the program is missing or not on `PATH`.
- Press `Ctrl+C` to stop the current process.

## Course Note

In COMPSCI 426, terminal use is constant. Git, npm, Node, Docker, Gantry,
database tools, services, load tests, and project sprints all use the command
line. The integrated terminal inside the VS Code devcontainer is the expected
place to run course commands.

# Course Docs

This folder stores imported Canvas/course reference pages for COMPSCI 426.

Use these files as lookup references when a task depends on a specific course
page. Do not treat every file here as always-active instructions; `AGENTS.md`
contains the operating rules and `syllabus.md` contains the high-level course
reference.

## Index

- `terminal-primer.md`: terminal concepts, shell vocabulary, core commands,
  script execution, permissions, and troubleshooting habits.

ᯓ The Project
The Project
What You Are Building
The capstone of this course is a simulated scalable web system built by your team over six weeks. The system is a simulation: its data is synthetic, its latency is injected, its failures are scripted, and its computation is modeled. This is a deliberate design choice, not a shortcut. A production system built from scratch in six weeks is not realistic, and that is not the goal. The goal is design, engineering, and measurement. Simulation lets your team practice every pattern covered in the course, break the system intentionally, and measure it under realistic load, without the operational complexity of real data pipelines or live traffic.

Every pattern you study in the units is first presented as a simulation. By the time you reach the project, you will know exactly how to model latency, inject failures, and observe behavior, because the units showed you how. The project is where those techniques are applied to a coherent system of your team's own design.

Computing for the Common Good
Your project domain must serve a real community or address a genuine societal need. This is not a theme layer on top of the technical work; it shapes what services exist, what the latency and reliability requirements mean, and who is affected when the system fails. A system that routes community food pantry inventory across multiple locations has different failure consequences than one that serves movie recommendations, and reasoning about those consequences is part of the design work.

Domains that fit this framing include, for example: a public health outbreak alert and notification service; a community library catalog with digital resource lending; a municipal transit real-time information and disruption alert system; an emergency shelter capacity and resource tracking system; or a neighborhood mutual aid request coordination platform. Domains that do not fit include commercial recommendation engines, advertising platforms, social media analytics, or entertainment applications.

When choosing a domain, ask: who benefits if this system is reliable and fast, and who is harmed when it is not? If the answer involves a specific real community, you are in the right territory.

What the System Must Demonstrate
Every project, regardless of domain, must demonstrate the following:

Reliability: Services have health check endpoints. The system can recover from at least one scripted failure scenario.
Latency: At least one service path is measured under load with k6. Results are reported as p50, p95, and p99 percentiles.
Resiliency: The system handles at least one simulated failure (a slow service, a crashing service, or a queue backlog) without total collapse.
Observability: At least two services expose Prometheus metrics. A Grafana dashboard displays request rate, error rate, and p95 latency. At least one service writes structured log output.
Patterns: The system must implement patterns covered in the course across its services. [TBD: minimum required pattern list and count]
Technical Constraints
The same constraints that apply to the course units apply to the project:

JavaScript only, using the course subset: arrow functions, no classes, ES6 modules, functional iteration preferred.
All services and infrastructure are orchestrated with Docker Compose. The entire system must start with a single docker compose up command.
Services are written in Node.js with Express for HTTP.
Load testing uses k6. Caching and async processing use Redis. Reverse proxying and load balancing use Caddy.
No new tools may be introduced unless approved in advance.
Team Structure
Teams are assigned by the instructor. Team size depends on the course version: 2–3 members in the 6-week summer or winter version, 3–7 members in the 13-week regular semester. Each team targets one custom service per team member plus one shared service (team_size + 1, minimum 3): a 2-person summer team targets 3 services; a 3-person team targets 4; a 5-person semester team targets 6. Infrastructure containers (Caddy, Redis, Prometheus, Grafana) do not count. Services are added incrementally: 2 in Sprint 2, at least one more in Sprint 4, reaching the full target by Sprint 5.

Each team member is expected to contribute meaningfully and independently. Contribution is assessed from objective GitHub evidence: commits, pull requests authored and reviewed, and merge history. Because the later sprints are more integrative than the earlier ones, sprint grading is trajectory-weighted across the term. [TBD: trajectory-weighting formula.]

Non-contributing members do not receive credit for work they did not do. [TBD: non-contributing member policy and process.]

Repository
Your team shares one GitHub repository, created during Sprint 0. All work is committed to this repository. The instructor has read access throughout the term and uses the commit and pull request history to assess individual contribution.

[TBD: required repository directory structure and naming conventions.]

Sprint Overview
Sprint	Schedule	Grade entry	Weight	Title
0	Week 1	Sprint 1	½	Team Formation and Project Concept
1	Week 2	Sprint 2	½	Project Definition and Scalability Framing
2	Week 3	Sprint 3	full	First Containerized System
3	Week 4	Sprint 4	full	Serving Patterns and First Load Test
4	Week 5	Sprint 5	full	Async Processing and Resilience
5	Week 6	Project Final (20%)	—	Observability, Final Measurement, and Delivery
Sprint 0 and Sprint 1 each count as half a sprint toward the Sprints grade (30%). Sprints 2, 3, and 4 each count as a full sprint. Sprint 5 is graded separately as the Project Final (20%).

Deadlines
Sprint deadlines are hard. Late sprint work is not accepted, because your teammates and the instructor depend on each stage being in place on time. If something will prevent you from meeting a sprint deadline, contact the instructor through the support form before the deadline, not after.

Alternative formats

tools.description:
Available model overrides (optional; inherited parent model is preferred):
- `gpt-5.5`: Frontier model for complex coding, research, and real-world work. Reasoning efforts: low, medium (default), high, xhigh. Service tiers: priority.
- `gpt-5.4`: Strong model for everyday coding. Reasoning efforts: low, medium (default), high, xhigh. Service tiers: priority.
- `gpt-5.4-mini`: Small, fast, and cost-efficient model for simpler coding tasks. Reasoning efforts: low, medium (default), high, xhigh.
- `gpt-5.3-codex-spark`: Ultra-fast coding model. Reasoning efforts: low, medium, high (default), xhigh.
        Spawn a sub-agent for a well-scoped task. Returns the spawned agent id plus the user-facing nickname when available. Spawned agents inherit your current model by default. Omit `model` to use that preferred default; set `model` only when an explicit override is needed.
This spawn_agent tool provides you access to sub-agents that inherit your current model by default. Do not set the `model` field unless the user explicitly asks for a different model or there is a clear task-specific reason. You should follow the rules and guidelines below to use this tool.

Do not spawn sub-agents unless the user explicitly asks for sub-agents, delegation, or parallel agent work.
Agent-role guidance below only helps choose which agent to use after spawning is already authorized; it never authorizes spawning by itself.

### Designing delegated subtasks
- Subtasks must be concrete, well-defined, and self-contained.
- Delegated subtasks must materially advance the main task.
- Do not duplicate work between the main rollout and delegated subtasks.
- Avoid issuing multiple delegate calls on the same unresolved thread unless the new delegated task is genuinely different and necessary.
- Narrow the delegated ask to the concrete output you need next.
- For coding tasks, prefer delegating concrete code-change worker subtasks over read-only explorer analysis when the subagent can make a bounded patch in a clear write scope.
- When delegating coding work, instruct the submodel to edit files directly in its forked workspace and list the file paths it changed in the final answer.
- For code-edit subtasks, decompose work so each delegated task has a disjoint write set.

### After you delegate
- Call wait_agent very sparingly. Only call wait_agent when you need the result immediately for the next critical-path step and you are blocked until it returns.
- Do not redo delegated subagent tasks yourself; focus on integrating results or tackling non-overlapping work.
- While the subagent is running in the background, do meaningful non-overlapping work immediately.
- Do not repeatedly wait by reflex.
- When a delegated coding task returns, quickly review the uploaded changes, then integrate or refine them.

### Parallel delegation patterns
- Run multiple independent information-seeking subtasks in parallel when you have distinct questions that can be answered independently.
- Split implementation into disjoint codebase slices and spawn multiple agents for them in parallel when the write scopes do not overlap.
- Delegate verification only when it can run in parallel with ongoing implementation and is likely to catch a concrete risk before final integration.
- The key is to find opportunities to spawn multiple independent subtasks in parallel within the same round, while ensuring each subtask is well-defined, self-contained, and materially advances the main task.

agent_type.description:
Optional type name for the new agent. If omitted, `default` is used.
Available roles:
default: {
Default agent.
}
explorer: {
Use `explorer` for specific codebase questions.
Explorers are fast and authoritative.
They must be used to ask specific, well-scoped questions on the codebase.
Rules:
- In order to avoid redundant work, you should avoid exploring the same problem that explorers have already covered. Typically, you should trust the explorer results without additional verification. You are still allowed to inspect the code yourself to gain the needed context!
- You are encouraged to spawn up multiple explorers in parallel when you have multiple distinct questions to ask about the codebase that can be answered independently. This allows you to get more information faster without waiting for one question to finish before asking the next. While waiting for the explorer results, you can continue working on other local tasks that do not depend on those results. This parallelism is a key advantage of delegation, so use it whenever you have multiple questions to ask.
- Reuse existing explorers for related questions.
}
worker: {
Use for execution and production work.
Typical tasks:
- Implement part of a feature
- Fix tests or bugs
- Split large refactors into independent chunks
Rules:
- Explicitly assign **ownership** of the task (files / responsibility). When the subtask involves code changes, you should clearly specify which files or modules the worker is responsible for. This helps avoid merge conflicts and ensures accountability. For example, you can say "Worker 1 is responsible for updating the authentication module, while Worker 2 will handle the database layer." By defining clear ownership, you can delegate more effectively and reduce coordination overhead.
- Always tell workers they are **not alone in the codebase**, and they should not revert the edits made by others, and they should adjust their implementation to accommodate the changes made by others. This is important because there may be multiple workers making changes in parallel, and they need to be aware of each other's work to avoid conflicts and ensure a cohesive final product.
}

+# Terminal Primer Summary
+
+Use this summary for terminal basics, beginner explanations, script execution,
+permissions, command-line vocabulary, and debugging shell errors.
+
+## Integral Points
+
+- The terminal is a text interface for making operating-system requests.
+- The shell is the program inside the terminal that reads and runs commands.
+- Course tools are command-line driven: `git`, `npm`, `node`, `docker`,
+  database CLIs, Gantry helpers, services, and k6.
+- The working directory matters; run `pwd` when disoriented.
+- Paths can be absolute from `/` or relative to the current working directory.
+- Arguments pass data to commands; flags/options modify behavior.
+- A process is a running program; `Ctrl+C` stops the current foreground process.
+
+## Core Commands
+
+- `pwd`: print working directory.
+- `ls`, `ls -l`: list files.
+- `cd`: change directory.
+- `mkdir`, `mkdir -p`: create directories.
+- `touch`: create empty file or update timestamp.
+- `cp`, `cp -r`: copy files/directories.
+- `mv`: move or rename.
+- `rm`, `rm -r`: permanently delete files/directories.
+- `cat`: print short files.
+- `less`: page through long files; `q` exits.
+- `echo`: print text.
+- `clear`: clear terminal display.
+- `man`: open command manual pages.
+
+## Scripts and Permissions
+
+- Run Node scripts with `node file.js`.
+- Run shell scripts with `chmod +x script.sh` then `./script.sh`.
+- Use shebangs such as `#!/usr/bin/env bash`, `#!/usr/bin/env node`, or
+  `#!/usr/bin/env python3`.
+- `ls -l` shows read/write/execute permissions.
+
+## Debugging Habits
+
+- Check `pwd`.
+- Use `ls` before and after file operations.
+- Read errors literally.
+- `No such file or directory` usually means the path is wrong.
+- `Permission denied` usually means access or execute permissions are missing.
+- `Command not found` means the program is missing or not on `PATH`.
+

+
+- JavaScript only.
+- Arrow functions only: `const fn = () => ...`.

+

# Terminal Primer Summary

Use this summary for terminal basics, beginner explanations, script execution,
permissions, command-line vocabulary, and debugging shell errors.

## Integral Points

- The terminal is a text interface for making operating-system requests.
- The shell is the program inside the terminal that reads and runs commands.
- Course tools are command-line driven: `git`, `npm`, `node`, `docker`,
  database CLIs, Gantry helpers, services, and k6.
- The working directory matters; run `pwd` when disoriented.
- Paths can be absolute from `/` or relative to the current working directory.
- Arguments pass data to commands; flags/options modify behavior.
- A process is a running program; `Ctrl+C` stops the current foreground process.

## Core Commands

- `pwd`: print working directory.
- `ls`, `ls -l`: list files.
- `cd`: change directory.
- `mkdir`, `mkdir -p`: create directories.
- `touch`: create empty file or update timestamp.
- `cp`, `cp -r`: copy files/directories.
- `mv`: move or rename.
- `rm`, `rm -r`: permanently delete files/directories.
- `cat`: print short files.
- `less`: page through long files; `q` exits.
- `echo`: print text.
- `clear`: clear terminal display.
- `man`: open command manual pages.

## Scripts and Permissions

- Run Node scripts with `node file.js`.
- Run shell scripts with `chmod +x script.sh` then `./script.sh`.
- Use shebangs such as `#!/usr/bin/env bash`, `#!/usr/bin/env node`, or
  `#!/usr/bin/env python3`.
- `ls -l` shows read/write/execute permissions.

## Debugging Habits

- Check `pwd`.
- Use `ls` before and after file operations.
- Read errors literally.
- `No such file or directory` usually means the path is wrong.
- `Permission denied` usually means access or execute permissions are missing.
- `Command not found` means the program is missing or not on `PATH`.
