Add this to the context Unit 04: Docker Fundamentals
Introduction
Chapter 1 of the textbook positions containers as the foundational technology that makes distributed system patterns possible. Before containers, the patterns the book describes existed as ideas but not as reusable, portable artifacts: you could implement a sidecar in code, but the deployment unit was just "some process" that had to be configured, versioned, and reproduced by hand on every machine it ran on. Containers changed that. When a service and everything it depends on are packaged into a single image, you have something that runs identically anywhere Docker is installed, that can be composed with other services by name, and that other teams can depend on without knowing what it is built from.

Units 1 through 3 covered the logical challenges of distributed services: concurrency, measurement, and safe retries. Before any of those patterns can run in production, each service needs to be packaged as an image. A Node.js server that works on your machine may fail on a teammate's machine, in CI, or in production, because none of its dependencies are written down anywhere. This unit fixes that. You will write a Dockerfile, build it into an image, and run it as a container. By the end, those words stop being vocabulary and become two specific things you watched happen.

Before You Start
Read: Docker's overview of images and containers — https://docs.docker.com/get-started/docker-overview/Links to an external site.
References
Dockerfile reference — https://docs.docker.com/engine/reference/builder/Links to an external site.
docker build — https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/image/build/Links to an external site.
docker run — https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/container/run/Links to an external site.
docker ps / docker logs / docker rm — https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/container/Links to an external site.
Notes
The starting problem
Here's a tiny web server.

// server.js
import http from 'node:http';

http.createServer((req, res) => {
  res.writeHead(200, { 'Content-Type': 'text/plain' });
  res.end('Hello from a plain Node process\n');
}).listen(3000, () => console.log('Listening on port 3000'));
You also need a package.json so Node treats the file as an ES module:

{
  "type": "module"
}
Run it with node server.js, then visit localhost:3000 or run curl localhost:3000. It works, but notice everything it's quietly depending on: this exact machine has Node installed, at some version, with nothing else conflicting. None of that is written down anywhere. If you sent server.js to a teammate, it would either work by luck or fail in some way that has nothing to do with the code itself.

Extending the example
Write down exactly what this code needs to run, in a file called a Dockerfile, then build that description into an image.

# Dockerfile
FROM node:24
WORKDIR /usr/src/app
COPY . .
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
Each line does one specific thing. FROM node:24 starts from a base image that already has Node 24 installed. WORKDIR sets the directory inside the image where the following commands run. COPY . . brings everything from your current directory into the image. EXPOSE documents which port the container expects to be reached on. CMD is the command that runs when a container starts from this image.

Build it, then run it:

docker build -t hello-server .
docker run -p 3000:3000 hello-server
docker build reads the Dockerfile and produces an image named hello-server. docker run starts a container — a running instance of that image — and -p 3000:3000 connects port 3000 on your machine to port 3000 inside the container. Visit localhost:3000 again. Same response as before, but now it's coming from inside an isolated container built from a file that says exactly what it needs.

Managing containers and images
docker run blocks your terminal because the container's output goes there. To start a container in the background, add -d (detached mode). Give it a name with --name so you can refer to it by something other than its ID:

docker run -d --name my-server -p 3000:3000 hello-server
Check what's running:

docker ps
docker ps lists every running container: its ID, image, when it started, and the port mapping. To include containers that have stopped, use docker ps -a.

To see the output from a detached container:

docker logs my-server
When you're done, stop the container and remove it:

docker stop my-server
docker rm my-server
docker stop sends a signal that gives the process a moment to shut down cleanly. docker rm removes the stopped container — until you do this, the container still exists on disk (visible in docker ps -a) even after it stops. To skip the two steps, docker rm -f my-server stops and removes in one command.

Images accumulate too. To see what images are installed on your machine:

docker images
To remove an image (only works if no containers — running or stopped — are using it):

docker rmi hello-server
To remove all unused images at once:

docker image prune
Naming the pattern
An image is a packaged, read-only blueprint: your code plus everything it depends on to run, frozen into a single artifact. A container is a running instance of that image, the way a process is a running instance of a program. You can start several containers from the same image at once, and they won't interfere with each other — each one gets its own isolated filesystem and process space.

The Dockerfile is the recipe that produces the image, and each instruction in it becomes a layer that Docker can cache. That's why rebuilding an image after a small code change is usually much faster than the first build: Docker reuses unchanged layers and only reruns the steps that changed.

Two things worth keeping straight: EXPOSE just documents intent inside the Dockerfile. The -p flag on docker run is what actually connects a port on your machine to a port inside the running container. EXPOSE without -p doesn't open anything.

This is the foundation everything from Unit 6 onward sits on top of. Multi-container patterns — sidecars, proxies, workers — are just multiple containers, each one a running instance of some image, deliberately sharing a little while staying isolated in every other way.

Exercise
Task: Make the port configurable without rebuilding the image. Update server.js to read the port from process.env.PORT, defaulting to 3000 if it isn't set. Then run two containers from the same image at once, on two different host ports.

Starting point: server.js and Dockerfile from the Notes above.

You'll know it works when:

docker run -d --name server-3000 -e PORT=3000 -p 3000:3000 hello-server
docker run -d --name server-3001 -e PORT=3001 -p 3001:3001 hello-server
docker ps — both containers are listed as running
docker logs server-3000 — shows "Listening on port 3000"
docker logs server-3001 — shows "Listening on port 3001"
curl localhost:3000 and curl localhost:3001 both return a response
Cleanup: docker stop server-3000 server-3001 then docker rm server-3000 server-3001
Real World
Most Node.js projects have npm dependencies. That changes the Dockerfile in one important way: you need to install them inside the image before copying your source code.

Create an Express app:

// server.js
import express from 'express';

const app = express();
const port = process.env.PORT || 3000;

app.get('/', (req, res) => {
  res.send('Hello from Express in a container\n');
});

app.listen(port, () => console.log(`Listening on port ${port}`));
{
  "type": "module",
  "dependencies": {
    "express": "^4.18.0"
  }
}
Run npm install once locally to generate package-lock.json. Then write the Dockerfile:

FROM node:24
WORKDIR /usr/src/app
COPY package*.json .
RUN npm install
COPY . .
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
The key change is the order: copy package*.json first, run npm install, then copy the rest of the source. Docker caches each layer — so as long as package.json doesn't change, npm install is skipped on every subsequent rebuild. If you copied everything first and then ran npm install, any change to any file would invalidate the install layer and force a full reinstall.

Add a .dockerignore file to prevent the local node_modules from being copied into the image (which would overwrite what npm install just put there):

node_modules
Build and run:

npm install
docker build -t hello-express .
docker run -p 3000:3000 hello-express
curl localhost:3000 returns the response from Express running inside the container. The image contains Node, Express, and your code — nothing else — and it will run identically anywhere Docker is installed.

Home Exercise
Task: Make the greeting in the Express app configurable without rebuilding the image. Read a GREETING environment variable (defaulting to Hello) and include it in the response. Run the same image twice with different greetings.

Starting point: The Express app from the Real World section above.

You'll know it works when:

docker run -e GREETING=Hello -p 3000:3000 hello-express
docker run -e GREETING=Hola -p 3001:3000 hello-express
produces different responses:

curl localhost:3000   # Hello from Express in a container
curl localhost:3001   # Hola from Express in a container
Looking Ahead
Unit 5 shows how to stop typing long docker run commands by hand and instead describe several containers — like the app and sync containers from Unit 6 — in a single docker-compose.yml file. as a doucment for unit 4.

You will write a Dockerfile, build it into an image, and run it as a container. By the end, those words stop being vocabulary and become two specific things you watched happen.

Before You Start
Read: Docker's overview of images and containers — https://docs.docker.com/get-started/docker-overview/Links to an external site.
References
Dockerfile reference — https://docs.docker.com/engine/reference/builder/Links to an external site.
docker build — https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/image/build/Links to an external site.
docker run — https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/container/run/Links to an external site.
docker ps / docker logs / docker rm — https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/container/Links to an external site.
Notes
The starting problem
Here's a tiny web server.

// server.js
import http from 'node:http';

http.createServer((req, res) => {
  res.writeHead(200, { 'Content-Type': 'text/plain' });
  res.end('Hello from a plain Node process\n');
}).listen(3000, () => console.log('Listening on port 3000'));
You also need a package.json so Node treats the file as an ES module:

{
  "type": "module"
}
Run it with node server.js, then visit localhost:3000 or run curl localhost:3000. It works, but notice everything it's quietly depending on: this exact machine has Node installed, at some version, with nothing else conflicting. None of that is written down anywhere. If you sent server.js to a teammate, it would either work by luck or fail in some way that has nothing to do with the code itself.

Extending the example
Write down exactly what this code needs to run, in a file called a Dockerfile, then build that description into an image.

# Dockerfile
FROM node:24
WORKDIR /usr/src/app
COPY . .
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
Each line does one specific thing. FROM node:24 starts from a base image that already has Node 24 installed. WORKDIR sets the directory inside the image where the following commands run. COPY . . brings everything from your current directory into the image. EXPOSE documents which port the container expects to be reached on. CMD is the command that runs when a container starts from this image.

Build it, then run it:

docker build -t hello-server .
docker run -p 3000:3000 hello-server
docker build reads the Dockerfile and produces an image named hello-server. docker run starts a container — a running instance of that image — and -p 3000:3000 connects port 3000 on your machine to port 3000 inside the container. Visit localhost:3000 again. Same response as before, but now it's coming from inside an isolated container built from a file that says exactly what it needs.

Managing containers and images
docker run blocks your terminal because the container's output goes there. To start a container in the background, add -d (detached mode). Give it a name with --name so you can refer to it by something other than its ID:

docker run -d --name my-server -p 3000:3000 hello-server
Check what's running:

docker ps
docker ps lists every running container: its ID, image, when it started, and the port mapping. To include containers that have stopped, use docker ps -a.

To see the output from a detached container:

docker logs my-server
When you're done, stop the container and remove it:

docker stop my-server
docker rm my-server
docker stop sends a signal that gives the process a moment to shut down cleanly. docker rm removes the stopped container — until you do this, the container still exists on disk (visible in docker ps -a) even after it stops. To skip the two steps, docker rm -f my-server stops and removes in one command.

Images accumulate too. To see what images are installed on your machine:

docker images
To remove an image (only works if no containers — running or stopped — are using it):

docker rmi hello-server
To remove all unused images at once:

docker image prune
Naming the pattern
An image is a packaged, read-only blueprint: your code plus everything it depends on to run, frozen into a single artifact. A container is a running instance of that image, the way a process is a running instance of a program. You can start several containers from the same image at once, and they won't interfere with each other — each one gets its own isolated filesystem and process space.

The Dockerfile is the recipe that produces the image, and each instruction in it becomes a layer that Docker can cache. That's why rebuilding an image after a small code change is usually much faster than the first build: Docker reuses unchanged layers and only reruns the steps that changed.

Two things worth keeping straight: EXPOSE just documents intent inside the Dockerfile. The -p flag on docker run is what actually connects a port on your machine to a port inside the running container. EXPOSE without -p doesn't open anything.

This is the foundation everything from Unit 6 onward sits on top of. Multi-container patterns — sidecars, proxies, workers — are just multiple containers, each one a running instance of some image, deliberately sharing a little while staying isolated in every other way.

Exercise
Task: Make the port configurable without rebuilding the image. Update server.js to read the port from process.env.PORT, defaulting to 3000 if it isn't set. Then run two containers from the same image at once, on two different host ports.

Starting point: server.js and Dockerfile from the Notes above.

You'll know it works when:

docker run -d --name server-3000 -e PORT=3000 -p 3000:3000 hello-server
docker run -d --name server-3001 -e PORT=3001 -p 3001:3001 hello-server
docker ps — both containers are listed as running
docker logs server-3000 — shows "Listening on port 3000"
docker logs server-3001 — shows "Listening on port 3001"
curl localhost:3000 and curl localhost:3001 both return a response
Cleanup: docker stop server-3000 server-3001 then docker rm server-3000 server-3001
Real World
Most Node.js projects have npm dependencies. That changes the Dockerfile in one important way: you need to install them inside the image before copying your source code.

Create an Express app:

// server.js
import express from 'express';

const app = express();
const port = process.env.PORT || 3000;

app.get('/', (req, res) => {
  res.send('Hello from Express in a container\n');
});

app.listen(port, () => console.log(`Listening on port ${port}`));
{
  "type": "module",
  "dependencies": {
    "express": "^4.18.0"
  }
}
Run npm install once locally to generate package-lock.json. Then write the Dockerfile:

FROM node:24
WORKDIR /usr/src/app
COPY package*.json .
RUN npm install
COPY . .
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
The key change is the order: copy package*.json first, run npm install, then copy the rest of the source. Docker caches each layer — so as long as package.json doesn't change, npm install is skipped on every subsequent rebuild. If you copied everything first and then ran npm install, any change to any file would invalidate the install layer and force a full reinstall.

Add a .dockerignore file to prevent the local node_modules from being copied into the image (which would overwrite what npm install just put there):

node_modules
Build and run:

npm install
docker build -t hello-express .
docker run -p 3000:3000 hello-express
curl localhost:3000 returns the response from Express running inside the container. The image contains Node, Express, and your code — nothing else — and it will run identically anywhere Docker is installed.

Home Exercise
Task: Make the greeting in the Express app configurable without rebuilding the image. Read a GREETING environment variable (defaulting to Hello) and include it in the response. Run the same image twice with different greetings.

Starting point: The Express app from the Real World section above.

You'll know it works when:

docker run -e GREETING=Hello -p 3000:3000 hello-express
docker run -e GREETING=Hola -p 3001:3000 hello-express
produces different responses:

curl localhost:3000   # Hello from Express in a container
curl localhost:3001   # Hola from Express in a container
Looking Ahead
Unit 5 shows how to stop typing long docker run commands by hand and instead describe several containers — like the app and sync containers from Unit 6 — in a single docker-compose.yml file. as a doucment for unit 4.

# Unit 4 Summary: Docker Fundamentals

Use this summary when working on Unit 4 Docker concepts, Dockerfiles,
image/container commands, port mappings, environment variables, or containerized
Node/Express services.

## Integral Points

- Containers package a service and its dependencies into a portable image.
- Images make services reproducible across teammates, CI, and production.
- An image is a read-only blueprint; a container is a running instance of an
  image.
- A Dockerfile is the recipe that builds an image.
- Docker caches Dockerfile layers, so instruction order matters.
- `EXPOSE` documents the container port; `docker run -p host:container` actually
  publishes the port.
- Environment variables let you change runtime behavior without rebuilding the
  image.
- `.dockerignore` prevents local junk, especially `node_modules`, from being
  copied into the image.

## Before Starting

- Read: Docker overview of images and containers.
- References:
  - Dockerfile reference
  - `docker build`
  - `docker run`
  - `docker ps`, `docker logs`, `docker rm`

## Minimal Node Example

Files:

- `server.js`: plain Node HTTP server listening on port 3000.
- `package.json`: `{ "type": "module" }`.

```Dockerfile
FROM node:24
WORKDIR /usr/src/app
COPY . .
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
```

Commands:

```bash
docker build -t hello-server .
docker run -p 3000:3000 hello-server
```

- Detached run with name:
  `docker run -d --name my-server -p 3000:3000 hello-server`
- Running containers: `docker ps`
- All containers, including stopped: `docker ps -a`
- Logs: `docker logs my-server`
- Stop: `docker stop my-server`
- Remove stopped container: `docker rm my-server`
- Force stop/remove: `docker rm -f my-server`

- Remove image: `docker rmi hello-server`
- Prune unused images: `docker image prune`

Make `PORT` configurable:

```js

```

```bash

```

# Unit 04: Docker Fundamentals

Source: COMPSCI 426 Canvas page pasted by the user.

## Introduction

Chapter 1 of the textbook positions containers as the foundational technology that makes distributed system patterns possible. Before containers, the patterns the book describes existed as ideas but not as reusable, portable artifacts: you could implement a sidecar in code, but the deployment unit was just "some process" that had to be configured, versioned, and reproduced by hand on every machine it ran on. Containers changed that. When a service and everything it depends on are packaged into a single image, you have something that runs identically anywhere Docker is installed, that can be composed with other services by name, and that other teams can depend on without knowing what it is built from.

Units 1 through 3 covered the logical challenges of distributed services: concurrency, measurement, and safe retries. Before any of those patterns can run in production, each service needs to be packaged as an image. A Node.js server that works on your machine may fail on a teammate's machine, in CI, or in production, because none of its dependencies are written down anywhere. This unit fixes that. You will write a Dockerfile, build it into an image, and run it as a container. By the end, those words stop being vocabulary and become two specific things you watched happen.

## Before You Start

Read: Docker's overview of images and containers — https://docs.docker.com/get-started/docker-overview/Links to an external site.

## References

Dockerfile reference — https://docs.docker.com/engine/reference/builder/Links to an external site.
docker build — https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/image/build/Links to an external site.
docker run — https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/container/run/Links to an external site.
docker ps / docker logs / docker rm — https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/container/Links to an external site.

## Notes

### The starting problem

Here's a tiny web server.

```js
// server.js
import http from 'node:http';

http.createServer((req, res) => {
  res.writeHead(200, { 'Content-Type': 'text/plain' });
  res.end('Hello from a plain Node process\n');
}).listen(3000, () => console.log('Listening on port 3000'));
```

You also need a package.json so Node treats the file as an ES module:

```json
{
  "type": "module"
}
```

Run it with node server.js, then visit localhost:3000 or run curl localhost:3000. It works, but notice everything it's quietly depending on: this exact machine has Node installed, at some version, with nothing else conflicting. None of that is written down anywhere. If you sent server.js to a teammate, it would either work by luck or fail in some way that has nothing to do with the code itself.

### Extending the example

Write down exactly what this code needs to run, in a file called a Dockerfile, then build that description into an image.

```Dockerfile
# Dockerfile
FROM node:24
WORKDIR /usr/src/app
COPY . .
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
```

Each line does one specific thing. FROM node:24 starts from a base image that already has Node 24 installed. WORKDIR sets the directory inside the image where the following commands run. COPY . . brings everything from your current directory into the image. EXPOSE documents which port the container expects to be reached on. CMD is the command that runs when a container starts from this image.

Build it, then run it:

```bash
docker build -t hello-server .
docker run -p 3000:3000 hello-server
```

docker build reads the Dockerfile and produces an image named hello-server. docker run starts a container — a running instance of that image — and -p 3000:3000 connects port 3000 on your machine to port 3000 inside the container. Visit localhost:3000 again. Same response as before, but now it's coming from inside an isolated container built from a file that says exactly what it needs.

### Managing containers and images

docker run blocks your terminal because the container's output goes there. To start a container in the background, add -d (detached mode). Give it a name with --name so you can refer to it by something other than its ID:

```bash
docker run -d --name my-server -p 3000:3000 hello-server
```

Check what's running:

```bash
docker ps
```

docker ps lists every running container: its ID, image, when it started, and the port mapping. To include containers that have stopped, use docker ps -a.

To see the output from a detached container:

```bash
docker logs my-server
```

When you're done, stop the container and remove it:

```bash
docker stop my-server
docker rm my-server
```

docker stop sends a signal that gives the process a moment to shut down cleanly. docker rm removes the stopped container — until you do this, the container still exists on disk (visible in docker ps -a) even after it stops. To skip the two steps, docker rm -f my-server stops and removes in one command.

Images accumulate too. To see what images are installed on your machine:

```bash
docker images
```

To remove an image (only works if no containers — running or stopped — are using it):

```bash
docker rmi hello-server
```

To remove all unused images at once:

```bash
docker image prune
```

An image is a packaged, read-only blueprint: your code plus everything it depends on to run, frozen into a single artifact. A container is a running instance of that image, the way a process is a running instance of a program. You can start several containers from the same image at once, and they won't interfere with each other — each one gets its own isolated filesystem and process space.

The Dockerfile is the recipe that produces the image, and each instruction in it becomes a layer that Docker can cache. That's why rebuilding an image after a small code change is usually much faster than the first build: Docker reuses unchanged layers and only reruns the steps that changed.

Two things worth keeping straight: EXPOSE just documents intent inside the Dockerfile. The -p flag on docker run is what actually connects a port on your machine to a port inside the running container. EXPOSE without -p doesn't open anything.

This is the foundation everything from Unit 6 onward sits on top of. Multi-container patterns — sidecars, proxies, workers — are just multiple containers, each one a running instance of some image, deliberately sharing a little while staying isolated in every other way.

You’re basically on base. The only correction: Docker containers are not really VMs. They’re isolated processes using the host kernel, built from an image. For this course that distinction mostly matters because containers are lighter, faster to start, and meant to be composed into multi-service systems.

From Unit 4, the fundamental things to keep sharp are:

- **Image vs container**
  - Image = packaged blueprint: code + runtime + dependencies.
  - Container = running instance of that image.
  - You can run many containers from one image.

- **Dockerfile is the recipe**
  - `FROM` chooses the base runtime.
  - `WORKDIR` sets the directory inside the image.
  - `COPY` moves files into the image.
  - `RUN` executes build-time commands like `npm install`.
  - `CMD` is the default runtime command.

- **Build-time vs runtime**
  - `docker build` creates the image.
  - `docker run` starts a container from the image.
  - Env vars like `PORT`/`GREETING` are runtime config, so you can change behavior without rebuilding.

- **Ports**
  - `EXPOSE 3000` is documentation inside the image.
  - `-p 3001:3000` is what actually maps your host port `3001` to container port `3000`.

- **Layer caching**
  - Copy `package*.json`, run `npm install`, then copy source.
  - That way source changes do not force dependency reinstall.
  - `.dockerignore` should exclude `node_modules`.

The course-relevant takeaway:

> Docker turns “this service works on my machine” into “this service is a reproducible artifact that can run with other services.”

If you already know that, you don’t need to grind this page. Just make sure you can write a basic Dockerfile and explain `image/container`, `EXPOSE/-p`, and build-time/runtime config.

content.text: How does it work a little under thoe hood - how is it simialr and differnet form a vm

payload.message: How does it work a little under thoe hood - how is it simialr and differnet form a vm

Docker is VM-like in the user experience, but not in the machinery.

A VM virtualizes hardware. You run a hypervisor, the hypervisor pretends to be a whole computer, then the guest OS boots its own kernel inside that fake computer.

```text
Your Mac hardware
-> macOS
-> hypervisor
-> guest Linux kernel
-> Linux userspace
-> your app
```

A container virtualizes the operating-system environment, not the hardware. The process runs on a kernel that already exists, but Linux features isolate what it can see and do.

```text
Linux kernel
-> isolated process namespace/filesystem/network/cgroups
-> your app
```

Under the hood, Docker mainly uses:

- **Images / layers**
  An image is a stack of filesystem layers. Each Dockerfile instruction creates or reuses a layer. That is why `COPY package*.json` then `RUN npm install` can be cached.

- **Namespaces**
  These isolate what a process can see:
  - process namespace: container sees its own process tree
  - network namespace: container has its own network interface/ports
  - mount namespace: container sees its own filesystem
  - user namespace: can remap users/permissions
  - hostname namespace: container can have its own hostname

- **cgroups**
  Control resource usage: CPU, memory, process limits, etc.

- **Union filesystem**
  Lets Docker stack read-only image layers plus a writable container layer on top. When a container writes a file, it writes to its own writable layer, not back into the image.

- **Port forwarding / NAT**
  `-p 3001:3000` tells Docker to forward traffic from your host port `3001` into the container’s network namespace on port `3000`.

The biggest similarity to VMs:

- Both package an isolated environment.
- Both help avoid “works on my machine.”
- Both can run services with their own filesystem/network view.

The biggest differences:

| Thing | VM | Container |
|---|---|---|
| Virtualizes | Hardware | OS environment |
| Kernel | Has its own guest kernel | Shares host/kernel VM’s kernel |
| Startup | Slower, boots OS | Faster, starts process |
| Size | Usually GBs | Often MBs-100s MBs |
| Isolation | Stronger boundary | Lighter boundary |
| Best for | Full OS isolation | App/service packaging |

On macOS specifically, Docker still needs a lightweight Linux VM because containers rely on Linux kernel features. So on your Mac the real stack is more like:

```text
macOS
-> Docker Desktop Linux VM
-> Linux containers
-> your service process
```

So: Docker containers are not VMs, but on Mac they run inside a Linux VM because macOS is not a Linux kernel.

For this course, the practical mental model:

> A Docker image is a layered filesystem plus a default command. A container is an isolated Linux process started from that image, with its own filesystem/network view and optional host port/env mappings.

content.text: ok so it uses the same kernel on your machine that it pulls and downloads to run the code like a vm, but its usually a lot smaller and only needs certina packages to run so it takes advantage of that and only abstracts the execution layer and the supporting package layer

payload.message: ok so it uses the same kernel on your machine that it pulls and downloads to run the code like a vm, but its usually a lot smaller and only needs certina packages to run so it takes advantage of that and only abstracts the execution layer and the supporting package layer

Close, but one wording fix:

Docker does **not** pull/download a kernel as part of each image. Images contain userspace stuff: files, binaries, libraries, Node, npm packages, your code, etc. The container uses an already-running Linux kernel.

On Linux:

```text
host Linux kernel
-> container process
-> image filesystem layers
-> your app
```

On macOS:

```text
macOS
-> Docker Desktop Linux VM
-> Linux kernel inside that VM
-> container process
-> image filesystem layers
-> your app
```

So the better version is:

> Docker packages the userspace environment needed to run the app, like Node, system libraries, dependencies, and code. It does not boot a full guest OS per app. The container runs as an isolated process on an existing Linux kernel, using image layers as its filesystem and Docker features for networking, env vars, ports, and resource isolation.

Your intuition is right that it is smaller because it only carries the pieces needed above the kernel. It abstracts/isolate things like:

- filesystem
- process view
- networking
- environment variables
- resource limits
- installed runtime/dependencies

But it shares the kernel rather than bundling and booting a whole OS per service.

content.text: so docker desktop download has the linux kernel loaded into ememory?

payload.message: so docker desktop download has the linux kernel loaded into ememory?

Yes, basically.

On macOS, Docker Desktop runs a lightweight Linux VM in the background. That VM boots a Linux kernel into memory. Your containers then run inside that Linux VM and share that VM’s Linux kernel.

So the stack is:

```text
Mac hardware
-> macOS
-> Docker Desktop lightweight Linux VM
-> Linux kernel loaded in that VM
-> containers sharing that Linux kernel
-> your app processes
```

Important distinction:

- Docker Desktop includes/manages the Linux VM.
- The Linux kernel is part of that VM environment.
- Individual Docker images do not each include their own kernel.
- Individual containers do not each boot a kernel.

So if you run 10 containers, you do **not** have 10 Linux kernels. You have one Docker Desktop Linux VM kernel, shared by the containers.

- default command metadata

OKay now add this for unit05Unit 05: Docker Compose
Introduction
Chapter 2 of the textbook introduces the idea of an orchestrator: a system responsible for taking a declared desired state and ensuring the real state of the application matches it. In production, that role is played by Kubernetes. At the scale of a single developer or a small team, Docker Compose fills the same conceptual role. Instead of a sequence of imperative commands that must be typed in the right order with the right flags every time, Compose lets you declare what containers you want, how they are connected, and what volumes they share, then brings the whole arrangement up or down with a single command.

Unit 4 built one container from a Dockerfile and ran it with docker run. The moment you need two containers sharing a volume, that one command becomes four, each one with flags that must match exactly, in the right order, every time you want to bring the system up. This unit introduces Compose as the tool that replaces that sequence with a file you can read, share, and check into version control. Every multi-container setup from Unit 6 onward will be expressed as a docker-compose.yml, so the goal here is to make that format completely familiar before the patterns begin.

Before You Start
Read: Docker's Compose overview — https://docs.docker.com/compose/Links to an external site.
References
Compose file reference — https://docs.docker.com/reference/compose-file/Links to an external site.
docker compose CLI — https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/compose/Links to an external site.
Named volumes — https://docs.docker.com/engine/storage/volumes/Links to an external site.
Notes
The starting problem
Here are two small scripts. One writes a timestamp to a shared file every five seconds. The other serves whatever is currently in that file over HTTP.

// writer.js
import fs from 'node:fs';

setInterval(() => {
  fs.writeFileSync(
    '/data/message.txt',
    `Last updated: ${new Date().toISOString()}\n`,
  );
}, 5000);
// reader-server.js
import http from 'node:http';
import fs from 'node:fs';

http.createServer((req, res) => {
  const message = fs.existsSync('/data/message.txt')
    ? fs.readFileSync('/data/message.txt', 'utf8')
    : 'no data yet\n';
  res.writeHead(200, { 'Content-Type': 'text/plain' });
  res.end(message);
}).listen(3000, () => console.log('Listening on port 3000'));
Using what you learned in Unit 4, running both of these as containers that share a volume takes a sequence like this:

docker build -t demo-app .
docker volume create shared-data
docker run -d --name writer -v shared-data:/data demo-app node writer.js
docker run -d --name reader -p 3000:3000 -v shared-data:/data demo-app node reader-server.js
That's already four commands, each one easy to get slightly wrong, and you'd have to remember this exact sequence, in this exact order, every single time you wanted to bring this up again. Tearing it down means stopping and removing two containers and a volume by hand too.

Extending the example
Describe the same two containers and the volume they share in a single file instead.

# docker-compose.yml
services:
  writer:
    build: .
    command: node writer.js
    volumes:
      - shared-data:/data

  reader:
    build: .
    command: node reader-server.js
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
    volumes:
      - shared-data:/data

volumes:
  shared-data:
Now bring both containers up with one command:

docker compose up
Visit localhost:3000 a few times over thirty seconds and watch the timestamp update. When you're done, docker compose down removes both containers and cleans up after itself. Same two containers, same shared volume, same result as the four commands above — but now the whole arrangement lives in a file you can read top to bottom, hand to a teammate, and check into version control.

You also need a Dockerfile so Compose knows how to build the image:

FROM node:24
WORKDIR /usr/src/app
COPY . .
There's no CMD here — each service in docker-compose.yml provides its own command, so the Dockerfile just handles the image and leaves the command to Compose.

Managing a Compose project
docker compose up runs in the foreground — all service output streams to your terminal. To start in the background instead, add -d:

docker compose up -d
Check the status of every service in the project:

docker compose ps
To stream logs as they arrive:

docker compose logs -f           # all services
docker compose logs -f writer    # one service only
To restart a single service without touching the others:

docker compose restart writer
To stop all services without removing the containers:

docker compose stop
docker compose down goes further — it stops and removes all containers. By default it leaves named volumes alone. To remove volumes too and wipe all stored data:

docker compose down --volumes
To open a shell inside a running service for debugging:

docker compose exec reader sh
Naming the pattern
docker-compose.yml is a declarative description of a multi-container application. Each entry under services is one container's blueprint: where to build it from, what command to run, which ports to expose, which volumes to mount. A named volume like shared-data is declared once under volumes and referenced by any service that needs it — which is how two otherwise unrelated containers end up sharing the same files.

Compose itself isn't a new pattern. It's a tool for describing an arrangement of containers that you've already decided on, the same way a recipe describes a dish without being the dish. The patterns themselves — sidecar, ambassador, and the ones still ahead — are about why containers are arranged a certain way. Compose is just how that arrangement gets written down in one place instead of typed by hand every time.

From Unit 6 onward, every multi-container example in this course will be expressed as a docker-compose.yml.

Exercise
Task: Add a third service, logger, that prints the contents of /data/message.txt to its own console every five seconds. It reuses the same image as the other two services, but with a different command. It shares the shared-data volume but doesn't expose any port — it only reads from the shared file and logs to its own console.

// logger.js
import fs from 'node:fs';

setInterval(() => {
  const message = fs.existsSync('/data/message.txt')
    ? fs.readFileSync('/data/message.txt', 'utf8')
    : 'no data yet';
  console.log(message.trim());
}, 5000);
Starting point: The docker-compose.yml and Dockerfile from the Notes above, plus the logger.js file. Add a logger service to docker-compose.yml.

You'll know it works when:

docker compose up -d --build
docker compose ps — all three services listed as running
docker compose logs logger — shows the same timestamp the reader is serving over HTTP, updating every five seconds
curl localhost:3000 — the reader responds with that same timestamp
Cleanup: docker compose down
Real World
Volume sharing is one way containers cooperate. Another is the network: every service in a Compose project can reach every other service by its service name as a hostname.

Here's a two-service example. One service generates data; the other fetches from it and serves it externally.

// data.js — internal service, port 3001, not exposed to the host
import http from 'node:http';

http.createServer((req, res) => {
  res.writeHead(200, { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' });
  res.end(JSON.stringify({ message: 'data from internal service', timestamp: new Date().toISOString() }));
}).listen(3001, () => console.log('Data service on port 3001'));
// app.js — calls data by service name, serves on port 3000
import http from 'node:http';

http.createServer(async (req, res) => {
  const response = await fetch('http://data:3001/');
  const body = await response.json();
  res.writeHead(200, { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' });
  res.end(JSON.stringify(body));
}).listen(3000, () => console.log('App on port 3000'));
The URL http://data:3001/ uses the service name data as the hostname. Docker Compose creates a private network for the project and registers each service's name as a DNS entry on that network. No IP addresses, no service discovery configuration — just service names.

# docker-compose.yml
services:
  app:
    build: .
    command: node app.js
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
    depends_on:
      - data

  data:
    build: .
    command: node data.js
depends_on: data tells Compose to start the data container before starting app. The data service has no ports: entry — it's internal to the Compose network. Nothing on your host machine can reach it directly; only app can.

Run it:

docker compose up --build
curl localhost:3000
curl localhost:3000 hits the app container, which calls http://data:3001/ on the internal network, gets a response, and forwards it. The data service is invisible to the outside world.

Home Exercise
Task: Make the data service's message configurable without rebuilding the image. Read process.env.DATA_MESSAGE in data.js (defaulting to 'data from internal service') and set the value in docker-compose.yml using the environment: key.

Starting point: The two-service Compose setup from the Real World section above.

You'll know it works when: Running docker compose up --build followed by curl localhost:3000 returns your configured message — and changing the value in docker-compose.yml and restarting with docker compose up changes the response without rebuilding the image.

Looking Ahead
With a Dockerfile and a Compose file both behind you, Unit 6's sidecar example uses exactly these two tools to add a capability to a service without changing the service's own code.

+# Unit 5 Summary: Docker Compose
+
+Use this summary when working on Docker Compose, multi-container local systems,
+shared volumes, service-to-service networking, Compose commands, or
+`docker-compose.yml` files.
+
+## Integral Points
+
+- Docker Compose is local/small-team orchestration: declare the desired
+  multi-container setup, then bring it up/down with one command.
+- Compose replaces repeated `docker build`, `docker volume create`, and
+  `docker run` commands with a version-controlled `docker-compose.yml`.
+- A Compose file is declarative: it describes services, commands, ports,
+  volumes, environment variables, and relationships.
+- Each `services:` entry describes one container.
+- Named volumes are declared under top-level `volumes:` and mounted into
+  services that need shared persistent files.
+- Compose creates a private network where services can reach each other by
+  service name as hostname.
+- `ports:` exposes a service to the host; services without `ports:` are internal
+  to the Compose network.
+- `depends_on` controls startup ordering, not full application readiness.
+
+## Before Starting
+
+- Read: Docker Compose overview.
+- References:
+  - Compose file reference
+  - `docker compose` CLI
+  - Named volumes
+
+## Shared Volume Example
+
+Problem:
+
+- `writer.js` writes `/data/message.txt` every five seconds.
+- `reader-server.js` serves `/data/message.txt` over HTTP on port 3000.
+- Manually running this needs image build, volume creation, and two long
+  `docker run` commands.
+
+Compose version:
+
+```yaml
+services:
+  writer:
+    build: .
+    command: node writer.js
+    volumes:
+      - shared-data:/data
+
+  reader:
+    build: .
+    command: node reader-server.js
+    ports:
+      - "3000:3000"
+    volumes:
+      - shared-data:/data
+
+volumes:
+  shared-data:
+```
+
+Dockerfile can omit `CMD` when each Compose service supplies its own `command`.
+
+## Core Commands
+
+- Foreground startup: `docker compose up`
+- Detached startup: `docker compose up -d`
+- Rebuild while starting: `docker compose up --build`
+- Detached rebuild/start: `docker compose up -d --build`
+- Service status: `docker compose ps`
+- Logs for all services: `docker compose logs -f`
+- Logs for one service: `docker compose logs -f writer`
+- Restart one service: `docker compose restart writer`
+- Stop without removing containers: `docker compose stop`
+- Stop and remove containers: `docker compose down`
+- Stop/remove containers and named volumes: `docker compose down --volumes`
+- Shell into service: `docker compose exec reader sh`
+
+## Exercise
+
+Add `logger` service:
+
+- Uses same image.
+- Runs `node logger.js`.
+- Mounts `shared-data:/data`.
+- Exposes no ports.
+- Reads `/data/message.txt` every five seconds and logs it.
+
+Success:
+
+- `docker compose up -d --build`
+- `docker compose ps` lists writer, reader, logger.
+- `docker compose logs logger` shows the same timestamp reader serves.
+- `curl localhost:3000` returns that timestamp.
+
+## Service Networking Example
+
+Compose services can call each other by service name:
+
+- `data` listens on internal port 3001 and has no `ports:` entry.
+- `app` listens on host port 3000 and calls `http://data:3001/`.
+- `data` is invisible to the host; only other services on the Compose network
+  can reach it.
+
+Example relationship:
+
+```yaml
+services:
+  app:
+    build: .
+    command: node app.js
+    ports:
+      - "3000:3000"
+    depends_on:
+      - data
+
+  data:
+    build: .
+    command: node data.js
+```
+
+## Home Exercise
+
+Make `data.js` read `process.env.DATA_MESSAGE`, defaulting to
+`data from internal service`, then set it in `docker-compose.yml` with
+`environment:`.
+
+Expected:
+
+- `docker compose up --build`
+- `curl localhost:3000` returns configured message.
+- Changing the Compose environment value and restarting changes behavior without
+  rebuilding the image.
+
+## What To Look Closer At
+
+- Compose is not the pattern; it is the file format/tool for writing down a
+  chosen container arrangement.
+- Service names are hostnames on the Compose network.
+- `ports:` is only needed for host access; internal services can omit it.
+- Named volumes let otherwise isolated containers share files.
+- `docker compose down` leaves named volumes by default; use `--volumes` to wipe
+  stored data.
+
+## Looking Ahead
+
+Unit 6 uses Dockerfile plus Compose to implement the sidecar pattern: adding a
+capability to a service without changing the service's own code.
+

## Introduction

Chapter 2 of the textbook introduces the idea of an orchestrator: a system responsible for taking a declared desired state and ensuring the real state of the application matches it. # Unit 5 Summary: Docker Compose

Use this summary when working on Docker Compose, multi-container local systems,
shared volumes, service-to-service networking, Compose commands, or
`docker-compose.yml` files.

## Integral Points

- Docker Compose is local/small-team orchestration: declare the desired
  multi-container setup, then bring it up/down with one command.
- Compose replaces repeated `docker build`, `docker volume create`, and
  `docker run` commands with a version-controlled `docker-compose.yml`.
- A Compose file is declarative: it describes services, commands, ports,
  volumes, environment variables, and relationships.
- Each `services:` entry describes one container.
- Named volumes are declared under top-level `volumes:` and mounted into
  services that need shared persistent files.
- Compose creates a private network where services can reach each other by
  service name as hostname.
- `ports:` exposes a service to the host; services without `ports:` are internal
  to the Compose network.
- `depends_on` controls startup ordering, not full application readiness.

## Before Starting

- Read: Docker Compose overview.
- References:
  - Compose file reference
  - `docker compose` CLI
  - Named volumes

## Shared Volume Example

Problem:

- `writer.js` writes `/data/message.txt` every five seconds.
- `reader-server.js` serves `/data/message.txt` over HTTP on port 3000.
- Manually running this needs image build, volume creation, and two long
  `docker run` commands.

Compose version:

```yaml
services:
  writer:
    build: .
    command: node writer.js
    volumes:
      - shared-data:/data

  reader:
    build: .
    command: node reader-server.js
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
    volumes:
      - shared-data:/data

volumes:
  shared-data:
```

Dockerfile can omit `CMD` when each Compose service supplies its own `command`.

## Core Commands

- Foreground startup: `docker compose up`
- Detached startup: `docker compose up -d`
- Rebuild while starting: `docker compose up --build`
- Detached rebuild/start: `docker compose up -d --build`
- Service status: `docker compose ps`
- Logs for all services: `docker compose logs -f`
- Logs for one service: `docker compose logs -f writer`
- Restart one service: `docker compose restart writer`
- Stop without removing containers: `docker compose stop`
- Stop and remove containers: `docker compose down`
- Stop/remove containers and named volumes: `docker compose down --volumes`
- Shell into service: `docker compose exec reader sh`

## Exercise

Add `logger` service:

- Uses same image.
- Runs `node logger.js`.
- Mounts `shared-data:/data`.
- Exposes no ports.
- Reads `/data/message.txt` every five seconds and logs it.

Success:

- `docker compose up -d --build`
- `docker compose ps` lists writer, reader, logger.
- `docker compose logs logger` shows the same timestamp reader serves.
- `curl localhost:3000` returns that timestamp.

## Service Networking Example

Compose services can call each other by service name:

- `data` listens on internal port 3001 and has no `ports:` entry.
- `app` listens on host port 3000 and calls `http://data:3001/`.
- `data` is invisible to the host; only other services on the Compose network
  can reach it.

Example relationship:

```yaml
services:
  app:
    build: .
    command: node app.js
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
    depends_on:
      - data

  data:
    build: .
    command: node data.js
```

## Home Exercise

Make `data.js` read `process.env.DATA_MESSAGE`, defaulting to
`data from internal service`, then set it in `docker-compose.yml` with
`environment:`.

Expected:

- `docker compose up --build`
- `curl localhost:3000` returns configured message.
- Changing the Compose environment value and restarting changes behavior without
  rebuilding the image.

## What To Look Closer At

- Compose is not the pattern; it is the file format/tool for writing down a
  chosen container arrangement.
- Service names are hostnames on the Compose network.
- `ports:` is only needed for host access; internal services can omit it.
- Named volumes let otherwise isolated containers share files.
- `docker compose down` leaves named volumes by default; use `--volumes` to wipe
  stored data.

## Looking Ahead

Unit 6 uses Dockerfile plus Compose to implement the sidecar pattern: adding a
capability to a service without changing the service's own code.

# Unit 5 Summary: Docker Compose

Use this summary when working on Docker Compose, multi-container local systems,
shared volumes, service-to-service networking, Compose commands, or
`docker-compose.yml` files.

## Integral Points

- Docker Compose is local/small-team orchestration: declare the desired
  multi-container setup, then bring it up/down with one command.
- Compose replaces repeated `docker build`, `docker volume create`, and
  `docker run` commands with a version-controlled `docker-compose.yml`.
- A Compose file is declarative: it describes services, commands, ports,
  volumes, environment variables, and relationships.
- Each `services:` entry describes one container.
- Named volumes are declared under top-level `volumes:` and mounted into
  services that need shared persistent files.
- Compose creates a private network where services can reach each other by
  service name as hostname.
- `ports:` exposes a service to the host; services without `ports:` are internal
  to the Compose network.
- `depends_on` controls startup ordering, not full application readiness.

## Before Starting

- Read: Docker Compose overview.
- References:
  - Compose file reference
  - `docker compose` CLI
  - Named volumes

## Shared Volume Example

Problem:

- `writer.js` writes `/data/message.txt` every five seconds.
- `reader-server.js` serves `/data/message.txt` over HTTP on port 3000.
- Manually running this needs image build, volume creation, and two long
  `docker run` commands.

Compose version:

```yaml
services:
  writer:
    build: .
    command: node writer.js
    volumes:
      - shared-data:/data

  reader:
    build: .
    command: node reader-server.js
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
    volumes:
      - shared-data:/data

volumes:
  shared-data:
```

Dockerfile can omit `CMD` when each Compose service supplies its own `command`.

## Core Commands

- Foreground startup: `docker compose up`
- Detached startup: `docker compose up -d`
- Rebuild while starting: `docker compose up --build`
- Detached rebuild/start: `docker compose up -d --build`
- Service status: `docker compose ps`
- Logs for all services: `docker compose logs -f`
- Logs for one service: `docker compose logs -f writer`
- Restart one service: `docker compose restart writer`
- Stop without removing containers: `docker compose stop`
- Stop and remove containers: `docker compose down`
- Stop/remove containers and named volumes: `docker compose down --volumes`
- Shell into service: `docker compose exec reader sh`

## Exercise

Add `logger` service:

- Uses same image.
- Runs `node logger.js`.
- Mounts `shared-data:/data`.
- Exposes no ports.
- Reads `/data/message.txt` every five seconds and logs it.

Success:

- `docker compose up -d --build`
- `docker compose ps` lists writer, reader, logger.
- `docker compose logs logger` shows the same timestamp reader serves.
- `curl localhost:3000` returns that timestamp.

## Service Networking Example

Compose services can call each other by service name:

- `data` listens on internal port 3001 and has no `ports:` entry.
- `app` listens on host port 3000 and calls `http://data:3001/`.
- `data` is invisible to the host; only other services on the Compose network
  can reach it.

Example relationship:

```yaml
services:
  app:
    build: .
    command: node app.js
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
    depends_on:
      - data

  data:
    build: .
    command: node data.js
```

## Home Exercise

Make `data.js` read `process.env.DATA_MESSAGE`, defaulting to
`data from internal service`, then set it in `docker-compose.yml` with
`environment:`.

Expected:

- `docker compose up --build`
- `curl localhost:3000` returns configured message.
- Changing the Compose environment value and restarting changes behavior without
  rebuilding the image.

## What To Look Closer At

- Compose is not the pattern; it is the file format/tool for writing down a
  chosen container arrangement.
- Service names are hostnames on the Compose network.
- `ports:` is only needed for host access; internal services can omit it.
- Named volumes let otherwise isolated containers share files.
- `docker compose down` leaves named volumes by default; use `--volumes` to wipe
  stored data.

## Looking Ahead

Unit 6 uses Dockerfile plus Compose to implement the sidecar pattern: adding a
capability to a service without changing the service's own code.

payload.message: Ok what do i need to know here? what i go from it is that docker compose is the orchastration layer between containers - it has likie rountine for docker to run that cand fine how containers communicate across enviroments. It seemsl iek you can map oports or shard parts of the file system, anything you'd like. This makes it so you dont have to run a bunch of different commands to coordinate code across different services?

You’re on base. Tighten it like this:

Docker Compose is the **local orchestration/config layer** for a multi-container app. It does not really “run routines”; it reads `docker-compose.yml`, then asks Docker to build/start/stop the containers with the declared settings.

What you need to know:

- **It replaces a pile of `docker run` commands.**
  Instead of manually starting app, worker, Redis, Caddy, etc. with the right flags, you declare them once in YAML.

- **Each `services:` entry is one container blueprint.**
  Example: app service, database service, logger service, proxy service.

- **Services can talk by name.**
  If you have:

  ```yaml
  services:
    app:
    data:
  ```

  then `app` can call:

  ```text
  http://data:3001
  ```

  Compose gives them a private network and DNS names.

- **`ports:` exposes a container to your host.**
  `3000:3000` means host port 3000 maps to container port 3000.
  If a service has no `ports:`, other containers can still reach it, but your laptop browser/curl cannot directly.

- **`volumes:` share or persist files.**
  Named volumes let containers share data or keep data after containers restart.

- **`environment:` passes runtime config.**
  Same image, different behavior without rebuild.

- **`depends_on` controls startup order.**
  It starts one service before another, but it does not guarantee the service is fully ready unless healthchecks are involved.

The course-level takeaway:

> Dockerfile packages one service. Docker Compose describes how multiple packaged services run together.

Your phrasing “so you don’t have to run a bunch of different commands to coordinate code across different services” is exactly the point. Just replace “code” with “containers/services,” because Compose coordinates the running service containers, not the source code itself.

Codex can one-shot most Dockerfiles and Compose files if you understand the service pattern. You do not need to grind YAML syntax.

- service-name networking like `http://redis:6379` or `http://data:3001`
- `environment:`
- `volumes:`
- `docker compose up --build`
- `docker compose down`

That’s it.

The only experiment worth doing from Unit 5 is the internal networking one:

```text
app -> calls http://data:3001
data -> no ports exposed
host -> only calls app on localhost:3000
```

Why that matters: it’s the mental model for almost every later unit. App talks to Redis by `redis`, app talks to backend by `backend`, Caddy talks to replicas by service name, etc.

You don’t need to hand-memorize Compose. The skill is being able to look at a Compose file and answer:

- What containers exist?
- Which ones are reachable from my laptop?
- Which ones are internal only?
- What hostnames do services use to call each other?
- What data/config is shared?
- What command starts each service?

If you can answer those, Codex can write the file and you can review it intelligently.

content.text: volumes are shared data?

payload.message: volumes are shared data?

Yes. In Compose/Docker, **volumes are mounted storage** that containers can read/write.

They’re used for two main things:

1. **Persist data**
   Data survives container deletion/recreation.

   Example: Redis/Postgres data lives in a volume so it does not vanish every time the container restarts.

2. **Share files between containers**
   Multiple containers mount the same volume at the same path.

   Example from Unit 5:

   ```yaml
   services:
     writer:
       volumes:
         - shared-data:/data

     reader:
       volumes:
         - shared-data:/data

   volumes:
     shared-data:
   ```

   Both containers see the same `/data` directory. If `writer` writes:

   ```text
   /data/message.txt
   ```

   then `reader` can read it.

Important distinction:

- **Image filesystem**: baked into the image, mostly read-only blueprint.
- **Container writable layer**: private to one container, temporary-ish.
- **Volume**: external mounted storage, can persist and/or be shared.

So yes: volumes are how Docker gives containers shared or persistent data.

content.text: the compuse up --build means it rebuilds all the things that have chagned?

payload.message: the compuse up --build means it rebuilds all the things that have chagned?

Yes, close.

`docker compose up --build` means:

> Before starting the services, rebuild the images for services that have a `build:` section.

Docker still uses its layer cache, so it does not blindly redo everything from scratch. It checks the Dockerfile steps and reuses unchanged layers.

So if your Compose file has:

```yaml
services:
  app:
    build: .
```

then:

```bash
docker compose up --build
```

will rebuild `app`’s image, then start/recreate containers as needed.

What “changed” means in practice:

- If source files changed after `COPY . .`, that layer rebuilds.
- If `package.json` changed before `RUN npm install`, dependency install rebuilds.
- If nothing relevant changed, Docker reuses cached layers and rebuild is fast.

Contrast:

```bash
docker compose up
```

starts services using existing images. It may not notice that source changed if the image needs rebuilding.

Useful commands:

```bash
docker compose up --build
```

Rebuild if needed and start.

```bash
docker compose build --no-cache
```

Force rebuild from scratch, ignoring cache.

```bash
docker compose down
```

Stop/remove containers.

So for course work, when in doubt after editing Dockerfile/source:

```bash
docker compose up --build
```

# Unit 6 Summary: The Sidecar Pattern

Use this summary when working on the sidecar pattern, Compose services that
share a volume, or designs that extend a primary service without modifying it.

## Integral Points

- A sidecar is a second process/container attached to a primary service to add a
  capability without changing the primary service code.
- The primary and sidecar are deployed/managed together, but each has one job.
- The sidecar pattern separates concerns and failure modes:
  - primary serves user traffic
  - sidecar handles auxiliary work such as syncing, logging, monitoring, or
    refreshing content
- In this unit, coordination happens through a shared volume, not HTTP calls.
- The containers do not need to know much about each other; they agree on a
  shared local resource.
- Sidecars are the first named single-node pattern in the course.

## Before Starting

- Read: Designing Distributed Systems, Chapter 3, Sidecar Pattern.
- References:
  - Node.js `fs` module
  - `setInterval`
  - Compose volumes
  - `docker compose restart`

## Notes Example

Starting problem:

- One `app.js` both serves HTTP and syncs content.
- That gives one file/process two unrelated reasons to change:
  - request serving logic
  - content refresh logic

Split version:

- `app.js`: reads `./content/index.html` and serves it on port 3000.
- `sync.js`: writes `./content/index.html` on an interval.
- They cooperate only through the shared `./content` directory.

Key observation:

- The timestamp updates without `app.js` calling `sync.js`.
- Sync behavior can change without modifying serving behavior.

## Exercise

Modify only `sync.js`:

- Change sync interval from 10 seconds to 3 seconds.
- Add a counter that increments on every sync.
- Page should show timestamp and sync count.

Success condition:

- Reloading `http://localhost:3000` shows count climbing every ~3 seconds.
- `app.js` is untouched.

## Real World / Compose Version

Use two containers and one named volume:

- `app` service:
  - runs `node app.js`
  - exposes `3000:3000`
  - mounts `content:/usr/src/app/content`
- `sync` service:
  - runs `node sync.js`
  - mounts the same `content` volume
- top-level named volume: `content:`

Dockerfile:

```Dockerfile
FROM node:24
WORKDIR /usr/src/app
COPY . .
RUN mkdir -p content
```

Compose proves the pattern:

- `docker compose up`
- Open `http://localhost:3000`
- `docker compose restart sync` pauses/restarts sync only; `app` keeps serving.

## Home Exercise

Add a second sidecar:

- `monitor.js` polls `index.html` every 2 seconds.
- It logs when content changes.
- Add `monitor` service to Compose.
- It uses the same image, runs `node monitor.js`, and mounts the same `content`
  volume.

Success:

- `docker compose logs monitor` shows a line whenever `sync` updates the file.
- No changes to `app.js` or `sync.js` are needed.

## What To Look Closer At

- Sidecar is about adding capability without editing the primary service.
- The shared resource here is a volume, not memory and not direct HTTP calls.
- Each container has a narrow job and can be restarted independently.
- Multiple sidecars can attach to one primary.
- This pattern is useful for sync, logging, monitoring, proxy helpers, and other
  auxiliary behavior.

## Looking Ahead

Unit 7 introduces the ambassador pattern: a helper container in front of
outgoing calls, used for proxying, sharding, or experimentation without the
primary service knowing.

# Unit 6 Summary: The Sidecar Pattern

Use this summary when working on the sidecar pattern, Compose services that
share a volume, or designs that extend a primary service without modifying it.

## Integral Points

- A sidecar is a second process/container attached to a primary service to add a
  capability without changing the primary service code.
- The primary and sidecar are deployed/managed together, but each has one job.
- The sidecar pattern separates concerns and failure modes:
  - primary serves user traffic
  - sidecar handles auxiliary work such as syncing, logging, monitoring, or
    refreshing content
- In this unit, coordination happens through a shared volume, not HTTP calls.
- The containers do not need to know much about each other; they agree on a
  shared local resource.
- Sidecars are the first named single-node pattern in the course.

## Before Starting

- Read: Designing Distributed Systems, Chapter 3, Sidecar Pattern.
- References:
  - Node.js `fs` module
  - `setInterval`
  - Compose volumes
  - `docker compose restart`

## Notes Example

Starting problem:

- One `app.js` both serves HTTP and syncs content.
- That gives one file/process two unrelated reasons to change:
  - request serving logic
  - content refresh logic

Split version:

- `app.js`: reads `./content/index.html` and serves it on port 3000.
- `sync.js`: writes `./content/index.html` on an interval.
- They cooperate only through the shared `./content` directory.

Key observation:

- The timestamp updates without `app.js` calling `sync.js`.
- Sync behavior can change without modifying serving behavior.

## Exercise

Modify only `sync.js`:

- Change sync interval from 10 seconds to 3 seconds.
- Add a counter that increments on every sync.
- Page should show timestamp and sync count.

Success condition:

- Reloading `http://localhost:3000` shows count climbing every ~3 seconds.
- `app.js` is untouched.

## Real World / Compose Version

Use two containers and one named volume:

- `app` service:
  - runs `node app.js`
  - exposes `3000:3000`
  - mounts `content:/usr/src/app/content`
- `sync` service:
  - runs `node sync.js`
  - mounts the same `content` volume
- top-level named volume: `content:`

Dockerfile:

```Dockerfile
FROM node:24
WORKDIR /usr/src/app
COPY . .
RUN mkdir -p content
```

Compose proves the pattern:

- `docker compose up`
- Open `http://localhost:3000`
- `docker compose restart sync` pauses/restarts sync only; `app` keeps serving.

## Home Exercise

Add a second sidecar:

- `monitor.js` polls `index.html` every 2 seconds.
- It logs when content changes.
- Add `monitor` service to Compose.
- It uses the same image, runs `node monitor.js`, and mounts the same `content`
  volume.

Success:

- `docker compose logs monitor` shows a line whenever `sync` updates the file.
- No changes to `app.js` or `sync.js` are needed.

## What To Look Closer At

- Sidecar is about adding capability without editing the primary service.
- The shared resource here is a volume, not memory and not direct HTTP calls.
- Each container has a narrow job and can be restarted independently.
- Multiple sidecars can attach to one primary.
- This pattern is useful for sync, logging, monitoring, proxy helpers, and other
  auxiliary behavior.

## Looking Ahead

Unit 7 introduces the ambassador pattern: a helper container in front of
outgoing calls, used for proxying, sharding, or experimentation without the
primary service knowing.

content.text: SO what do i need to know about he sidecar pattern? What evne ius it

payload.message: SO what do i need to know about he sidecar pattern? What evne ius it

Sidecar pattern = **put a helper container next to your main service container to add a capability without changing the main service.**

The main service keeps doing its core job. The sidecar handles some supporting job.

Example from Unit 6:

```text
app container:
  serves index.html over HTTP

sync sidecar container:
  updates index.html every 10 seconds

shared volume:
  both containers see /content
```

The app does not call the sidecar. The sidecar does not call the app. They coordinate through a shared resource, like a volume.

Why this matters:

- You avoid stuffing unrelated jobs into one service.
- You can change the helper behavior without touching the main app.
- You can restart the sidecar without restarting the primary service.
- You separate failure modes.
- You keep the primary service simpler.

Common real examples:

- log shipper sidecar
- metrics exporter sidecar
- file/content sync sidecar
- auth/proxy helper sidecar
- certificate refresher sidecar
- config reloader sidecar

The mental model:

```text
Primary container = does the main business function
Sidecar container = does auxiliary support work
Shared local resource = how they coordinate
```

For this course, the important version is:

```text
app reads from a shared volume
sidecar writes to that shared volume
```

You do not need to overthink it. A sidecar is just a helper service packaged next to the main service so the main service does not need to know how that helper work happens.

content.text: Ok so its like if it isnt racing something you should put in a sidecar

payload.message: Ok so its like if it isnt racing something you should put in a sidecar

Not exactly. “Not racing” is not the reason to use a sidecar.

Use a sidecar when there is **supporting behavior that should live beside the main service but is not the main service’s core job**.

Better rule:

> If a capability supports the service, shares the service’s local context, and can be changed/restarted independently, it may be a sidecar.

Examples that fit:

- app serves files, sidecar syncs files
- app writes logs, sidecar ships logs
- app exposes metrics, sidecar formats/exports metrics
- app needs certificates, sidecar refreshes certificates
- app needs config files, sidecar updates config files

The sidecar often avoids direct coordination/racing because it usually interacts through a clear boundary: file, socket, local proxy, logs, etc. But “no race” is a benefit of a good design, not the definition.

Don’t use a sidecar just because something is separate. If it is core business behavior, make it part of the service or another normal service. If it is auxiliary infrastructure-ish behavior tightly coupled to one service, sidecar is a good fit.

Quick test:

```text
Would the main service still make sense without this behavior?
Is this behavior mostly support/ops/integration work?
Does it need to be deployed next to this service?
Would I want to change/restart it separately?
```

If yes, sidecar is plausible.

payload.message: So sidecars specifically are like non-integral seperate?

Yes, with one nuance.

Sidecars are **separate auxiliary behavior** attached to a primary service.

They are usually not the primary business logic, but they may still be operationally important.

Example:

```text
Primary service:
  serves the web page

Sidecar:
  syncs the page content
```

The sidecar is not the “main point” of the app, but the app may still depend on it to stay fresh.

Better wording:

> A sidecar is a helper container/process that provides supporting capability for one primary service, while staying separate from the primary service’s code.

Usually sidecar work is:

- logging
- monitoring
- syncing files/config
- proxying local traffic
- refreshing certs
- exporting metrics
- adapting output formats

Not usually sidecar work:

- core user-facing business logic
- the main API behavior
- a totally independent service used by many apps
- a database/cache shared by the whole system

So “non-integral separate” is close, but I’d say:

> not core business logic, but often important support logic.

- shared volume/filesystem
- local network interface / localhost
- Unix socket
- logs/stdout stream
- config files
- certificates
- metrics endpoint

In Unit 6, the shared resource is a **volume**:

```text
app reads /content/index.html
sidecar writes /content/index.html
```

That is the easiest sidecar example.

But a sidecar can also be a local proxy:

```text
app sends HTTP request to localhost:9000
sidecar forwards it to external service
```

There the shared “thing” is not a file. It is the local network namespace/localhost-style communication.

So the rule is:

> A sidecar is coupled to one primary service and shares some local context or boundary with it, so it can support that service without being part of its code.

If it is just another service on the network used by many things, it is probably not a sidecar. If it is a helper living next to one primary service, it probably is.

payload.message: what does auxilairt mean

Auxiliary means **supporting** or **helping**, not the main thing.

In this course:

```text
main service = does the core job
auxiliary sidecar = helps the main service do that job better
```

Example:

```text
app:
  serves web pages to users

sync sidecar:
  updates the files that app serves
```

The sync sidecar is auxiliary because users are not directly asking it for the webpage. It supports the app behind the scenes.

Other examples:

```text
main app:
  handles API requests

logging sidecar:
  collects and forwards logs
```

```text
main app:
  serves traffic

metrics sidecar:
  formats/export metrics for monitoring
```

So auxiliary = helpful support role, not the primary business/user-facing role.

+# Unit 7 Summary: The Ambassador Pattern
+
+Use this summary when working on ambassador proxies, outgoing-call routing,
+sharding, canary experiments, Caddy reverse proxies, or Compose
+`network_mode: "service:..."`.
+
+## Integral Points
+
+- An ambassador is a proxy container placed in the path of a primary
+  container's outgoing calls.
+- The primary service keeps calling a fixed local address, usually
+  `localhost:<port>`.
+- The ambassador decides where the call actually goes: shard, backend version,
+  retry target, experiment group, or proxy destination.
+- This keeps routing, retries, sharding, and experimentation out of application
+  code.
+- In this unit, Compose `network_mode: "service:app"` lets ambassador share the
+  app container's network namespace, so both use the same localhost interface.
+- Ambassador differs from sidecar:
+  - sidecar adds auxiliary capability beside the primary
+  - ambassador intercepts/reshapes outgoing calls the primary already makes
+
+## Before Starting
+
+- Read: Designing Distributed Systems, Chapter 4, Ambassador Pattern.
+- References:
+  - Node.js `http` module
+  - Node.js global `fetch`
+  - Compose `network_mode`
+  - Caddy `reverse_proxy`
+
+## Notes Example
+
+Starting problem:
+
+- `app.js` calls `http://users-service:5000/users/:id` directly.
+- If user data is sharded or backend versions change, routing logic must be
+  edited into every caller.
+
+Ambassador version:
+
+- `app.js` calls `http://localhost:5000/users/:id`.
+- `ambassador.js` listens on port 5000 in the app's network namespace.
+- Ambassador routes:
+  - even user IDs to `users-service-a:5000`
+  - odd user IDs to `users-service-b:5000`
+- `backend.js` is reused by both backend services with `LABEL=A` or `LABEL=B`.
+- `app.js` does not know the backends exist.
+
+Compose requirement:
+
+```yaml
+ambassador:
+  build: .
+  command: node ambassador.js
+  network_mode: "service:app"
+```
+
+## Exercise
+
+Add canary routing to `ambassador.js`:
+
+- Keep existing even/odd sharding.
+- But randomly route 20% of all requests to `users-service-b`, regardless of
+  user ID.
+
+Success condition:
+
+- Repeated requests for the same even-numbered user mostly return `servedBy: A`
+  but sometimes return `servedBy: B`.
+- `app.js` is unchanged.
+
+## Real World / Caddy Ambassador
+
+Replace custom JavaScript ambassador with Caddy:
+
+```Caddyfile
+:5000 {
+  reverse_proxy users-service-a:5000 users-service-b:5000 {
+    lb_policy round_robin
+  }
+}
+```
+
+Compose:
+
+- `caddy` uses `image: caddy:2`
+- mounts `./Caddyfile:/etc/caddy/Caddyfile`
+- uses `network_mode: "service:app"`
+- app still calls localhost
+
+Expected:
+
+- Repeated requests through `localhost:3000` alternate/mix `servedBy: A` and
+  `servedBy: B`.
+- Caddy handles reverse proxying, load balancing, health behavior, and
+  connection pooling.
+
+## Home Exercise
+
+Add a third backend:
+
+- Add `users-service-c` with `LABEL=C`.
+- Add `users-service-c:5000` to the Caddyfile upstreams.
+
+Success:
+
+- 30 requests produce a mix of A, B, and C responses in roughly equal
+  proportions.
+- Only Caddyfile and `docker-compose.yml` change; `app.js` and `backend.js` do
+  not.
+
+## What To Look Closer At
+
+- Ambassador is about moving routing/traffic decisions out of app code.
+- The primary calls a stable local address even while backend topology changes.
+- `network_mode: "service:app"` is the Compose trick that lets ambassador bind
+  to localhost from the app's point of view.
+- Sharding routes by key; canary routes by percentage/probability.
+- Caddy is a real tool that can implement ambassador behavior without custom
+  proxy code.
+
+## Looking Ahead
+
+Unit 8 introduces the adapter pattern: a helper container that transforms what
+the primary already produces into a format another system expects.
