+# Unit 7: The Ambassador Pattern: Proxying, Sharding, and Experimentation
+
+Source: COMPSCI 426 Canvas page pasted by the user.
+
+## Introduction
+
+Suppose your application calls a users-service to look up user data. Traffic grows to the point where one instance cannot keep up, so your team splits the data across two servers: even-numbered user IDs go to one, odd-numbered IDs go to another. You update app.js to route each call to the right server. Three months later a third server is added, and you update app.js again. A second internal service also looks up users, so the routing logic is duplicated there too. Whenever the sharding strategy changes, every service that calls users-service has to change with it. This is the problem Chapter 4 of the textbook targets with the ambassador pattern: routing decisions, retries, and traffic shaping belong in the infrastructure, not inside every application that happens to make a call. The ambassador is a proxy container that intercepts a primary container's outgoing calls and makes those decisions on its behalf, while the primary keeps calling a fixed local address as if nothing has changed.
+
+Unit 6 introduced the sidecar: a helper container that adds capability beside the primary by sharing a named volume with it. The ambassador keeps the two-container shape but flips the concern: instead of adding something the primary was missing, it intercepts something the primary was already doing, its outgoing calls to other services, and takes over the routing. This unit uses network_mode: "service:..." in Docker Compose to give the ambassador container access to the primary container's localhost interface. By the end you will have a working sharding ambassador that routes traffic to two backend instances based on user ID, and you will extend it to run a canary experiment on top of the existing routing logic.
+
+## Before You Start
+
+Read: Designing Distributed Systems, Ch. 4 (Ambassador Pattern)
+
+## References
+
+Node.js http module: https://nodejs.org/api/http.htmlLinks to an external site.
+fetch global (Node.js 18+): https://nodejs.org/api/globals.html#fetchLinks to an external site.
+Compose network_mode: https://docs.docker.com/reference/compose-file/services/#network_modeLinks to an external site.
+Caddy reverse_proxy directive: https://caddyserver.com/docs/caddyfile/directives/reverse_proxyLinks to an external site.
+
+## Notes
+
+### The starting problem
+
+Your application calls users-service to look up user data. There is one instance, one hostname, and the call is direct.
+
+```js
+// app.js
+import http from 'node:http';
+
+const getUser = async (userId) => {
+  const res = await fetch(`http://users-service:5000/users/${userId}`);
+  return res.json();
+};
+
+http.createServer(async (req, res) => {
+  const userId = req.url.split('/').pop();
+  const user = await getUser(userId);
+  res.writeHead(200, { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' });
+  res.end(JSON.stringify(user));
+}).listen(3000, () => console.log('App listening on port 3000'));
+```
+
+This works as long as there is exactly one users-service to call. The moment you want to split requests across two backend instances, or send a fraction of traffic to a new version you are testing, you have nowhere to put that decision except inside app.js, mixed into code whose job is to handle requests, not manage routing.
+
+### Extending the example
+
+Change one line: instead of calling the real backend's hostname, app.js calls localhost. A separate container, the ambassador, listens on that same localhost interface and decides where each request actually goes.
+
+```js
+// app.js — now calls localhost instead of the real backend
+import http from 'node:http';
+
+const getUser = async (userId) => {
+  const res = await fetch(`http://localhost:5000/users/${userId}`);
+  return res.json();
+};
+
+http.createServer(async (req, res) => {
+  const userId = req.url.split('/').pop();
+  const user = await getUser(userId);
+  res.writeHead(200, { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' });
+  res.end(JSON.stringify(user));
+}).listen(3000, () => console.log('App listening on port 3000'));
+```
+
+```js
+// ambassador.js
+import http from 'node:http';
+
+const forwardTo = async (host, userId, res) => {
+  const r = await fetch(`http://${host}/users/${userId}`);
+  const data = await r.text();
+  res.writeHead(200, { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' });
+  res.end(data);
+};
+
+http.createServer((req, res) => {
+  const userId = parseInt(req.url.split('/').pop(), 10);
+  const host = userId % 2 === 0 ? 'users-service-a:5000' : 'users-service-b:5000';
+  console.log(`Routing user ${userId} to ${host}`);
+  forwardTo(host, userId, res);
+}).listen(5000, () => console.log('Ambassador listening on port 5000'));
+```
+
+```js
+// backend.js — used by both users-service-a and users-service-b
+import http from 'node:http';
+
+http.createServer((req, res) => {
+  const userId = req.url.split('/').pop();
+  res.writeHead(200, { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' });
+  res.end(JSON.stringify({ id: userId, servedBy: process.env.LABEL }));
+}).listen(5000, () => console.log(`Backend ${process.env.LABEL} listening on port 5000`));
+```
+
+Create a package.json to enable ES modules:
+
+```json
+{
+  "type": "module"
+}
+```
+
+```yaml
+# docker-compose.yml
+services:
+  app:
+    build: .
+    command: node app.js
+    ports:
+      - "3000:3000"
+
+  ambassador:
+    build: .
+    command: node ambassador.js
+    network_mode: "service:app"
+
+  users-service-a:
+    build: .
+    command: node backend.js
+    environment:
+      - LABEL=A
+
+  users-service-b:
+    build: .
+    command: node backend.js
+    environment:
+      - LABEL=B
+```
+
+```Dockerfile
+# Dockerfile
+FROM node:24
+WORKDIR /usr/src/app
+COPY . .
+```
+
+network_mode: "service:app" puts the ambassador inside the same network namespace as app, so they share localhost the same way containers in the same pod would in production. Run docker compose up, then try:
+
+```bash
+curl localhost:3000/users/42
+curl localhost:3000/users/43
+```
+
+One comes back with "servedBy": "A" and the other with "servedBy": "B", even though app.js only ever called localhost:5000 and has no idea two backends exist.
+
+### Naming the pattern
+
+This is the ambassador pattern: a proxy container placed in the path of a primary container's outgoing calls, making routing decisions on its behalf, while the primary container keeps calling a fixed local address and stays completely unaware of sharding, retries, or anything else the ambassador might be doing. The primary container's code does not change when you add sharding, retry logic, or an experiment.
+
+It is worth comparing this directly to Unit 6's sidecar. Both patterns deploy a helper container alongside a primary one and share a local resource with it. But a sidecar sits beside the primary doing auxiliary work the primary would otherwise have to do itself, like syncing content into a shared volume. An ambassador sits in the path of calls the primary was already going to make, intercepting and reshaping them. Sharding, what you just built, routes requests across multiple backend instances based on a key.
+
+The same shape supports a second use case called a canary deployment. The name comes from the mining practice of sending a canary into a coal mine ahead of workers: if the canary was harmed by toxic gas, miners knew to stay out. A canary deployment works the same way. When you have a new version of a service that you are not yet confident in, you route a small percentage of real production traffic to it, say 10%, and leave the rest on the stable version. If the new version has a bug or a performance problem, only that fraction of users is affected, and you can pull it back immediately. Ninety percent of traffic never touched it. Once you gain confidence, you raise the percentage until the new version handles everything.
+
+An ambassador makes this straightforward: instead of routing by user ID, it rolls a random number on each incoming request and sends a configurable fraction to the new version. The primary container's code never changes. The experiment can be started, adjusted, or cancelled by modifying the ambassador alone.
+
+## Exercise
+
+Task: Add a canary experiment to ambassador.js. On top of the existing even-or-odd sharding, make 20% of all requests, regardless of user ID, go to users-service-b instead, chosen at random.
+
+Starting point: The ambassador.js and docker-compose.yml from the Notes above.
+
+You'll know it works when: sending 20 requests for the same even-numbered user ID results in most responses showing "servedBy": "A", but a noticeable fraction showing "servedBy": "B", and app.js did not need a single line changed.
+
+## Real World
+
+The Notes version builds its own ambassador in JavaScript. In production, most teams use an existing reverse proxy for this role. This section replaces ambassador.js with Caddy, a lightweight web server and reverse proxy, to show that the ambassador pattern is not a coding exercise: it is an arrangement that already exists inside tools you can drop in.
+
+Create a Caddyfile that configures Caddy to listen on port 5000 and round-robin between two backends:
+
+```Caddyfile
+:5000 {
+  reverse_proxy users-service-a:5000 users-service-b:5000 {
+    lb_policy round_robin
+  }
+}
+```
+
+Replace the ambassador service in docker-compose.yml with a Caddy container. The network_mode entry stays the same:
+
+```yaml
+services:
+  app:
+    build: .
+    command: node app.js
+    ports:
+      - "3000:3000"
+
+  caddy:
+    image: caddy:2
+    volumes:
+      - ./Caddyfile:/etc/caddy/Caddyfile
+    network_mode: "service:app"
+
+  users-service-a:
+    build: .
+    command: node backend.js
+    environment:
+      - LABEL=A
+
+  users-service-b:
+    build: .
+    command: node backend.js
+    environment:
+      - LABEL=B
+```
+
+Run docker compose up, then send several requests:
+
+```bash
+for i in $(seq 1 10); do curl -s localhost:3000/users/2 | grep servedBy; done
+```
+
+You should see alternating A and B responses. app.js is unchanged; the only thing that changed is which container acts as the ambassador. Caddy's reverse_proxy directive handles round-robin distribution, health checking, and connection pooling that you would otherwise have to implement yourself.
+
+## Home Exercise
+
+Caddy's reverse_proxy accepts additional upstream addresses alongside the existing two. Add a third backend, users-service-c, to both the Caddyfile and docker-compose.yml:
+
+Update the Caddyfile:
+
+```Caddyfile
+:5000 {
+  reverse_proxy users-service-a:5000 users-service-b:5000 users-service-c:5000 {
+    lb_policy round_robin
+  }
+}
+```
+
+Add to docker-compose.yml:
+
+```yaml
+  users-service-c:
+    build: .
+    command: node backend.js
+    environment:
+      - LABEL=C
+```
+
+You'll know it works when: sending 30 requests for the same user ID produces a mix of A, B, and C responses in roughly equal proportions, and you made this change entirely in Caddyfile and docker-compose.yml without touching app.js or backend.js.
+
+## Looking Ahead
+
+Unit 8 introduces the third shape for a helper container. Unlike the sidecar, which adds capability beside the primary, or the ambassador, which intercepts the primary's outgoing calls, the adapter intercepts what the primary already produces and transforms it into a format that something else expects. This is how you expose a standard interface from a service that was never designed to provide one.
+

# Unit 7 Summary: The Ambassador Pattern

Use this summary when working on ambassador proxies, outgoing-call routing,
sharding, canary experiments, Caddy reverse proxies, or Compose
`network_mode: "service:..."`.

## Integral Points

- An ambassador is a proxy container placed in the path of a primary
  container's outgoing calls.
- The primary service keeps calling a fixed local address, usually
  `localhost:<port>`.
- The ambassador decides where the call actually goes: shard, backend version,
  retry target, experiment group, or proxy destination.
- This keeps routing, retries, sharding, and experimentation out of application
  code.
- In this unit, Compose `network_mode: "service:app"` lets ambassador share the
  app container's network namespace, so both use the same localhost interface.
- Ambassador differs from sidecar:
  - sidecar adds auxiliary capability beside the primary
  - ambassador intercepts/reshapes outgoing calls the primary already makes

## Before Starting

- Read: Designing Distributed Systems, Chapter 4, Ambassador Pattern.
- References:
  - Node.js `http` module
  - Node.js global `fetch`
  - Compose `network_mode`
  - Caddy `reverse_proxy`

## Notes Example

Starting problem:

- `app.js` calls `http://users-service:5000/users/:id` directly.
- If user data is sharded or backend versions change, routing logic must be
  edited into every caller.

Ambassador version:

- `app.js` calls `http://localhost:5000/users/:id`.
- `ambassador.js` listens on port 5000 in the app's network namespace.
- Ambassador routes:
  - even user IDs to `users-service-a:5000`
  - odd user IDs to `users-service-b:5000`
- `backend.js` is reused by both backend services with `LABEL=A` or `LABEL=B`.
- `app.js` does not know the backends exist.

Compose requirement:

```yaml
ambassador:
  build: .
  command: node ambassador.js
  network_mode: "service:app"
```

## Exercise

Add canary routing to `ambassador.js`:

- Keep existing even/odd sharding.
- But randomly route 20% of all requests to `users-service-b`, regardless of
  user ID.

Success condition:

- Repeated requests for the same even-numbered user mostly return `servedBy: A`
  but sometimes return `servedBy: B`.
- `app.js` is unchanged.

## Real World / Caddy Ambassador

Replace custom JavaScript ambassador with Caddy:

```Caddyfile
:5000 {
  reverse_proxy users-service-a:5000 users-service-b:5000 {
    lb_policy round_robin
  }
}
```

Compose:

- `caddy` uses `image: caddy:2`
- mounts `./Caddyfile:/etc/caddy/Caddyfile`
- uses `network_mode: "service:app"`
- app still calls localhost

Expected:

- Repeated requests through `localhost:3000` alternate/mix `servedBy: A` and
  `servedBy: B`.
- Caddy handles reverse proxying, load balancing, health behavior, and
  connection pooling.

## Home Exercise

Add a third backend:

- Add `users-service-c` with `LABEL=C`.
- Add `users-service-c:5000` to the Caddyfile upstreams.

Success:

- 30 requests produce a mix of A, B, and C responses in roughly equal
  proportions.
- Only Caddyfile and `docker-compose.yml` change; `app.js` and `backend.js` do
  not.

## What To Look Closer At

- Ambassador is about moving routing/traffic decisions out of app code.
- The primary calls a stable local address even while backend topology changes.
- `network_mode: "service:app"` is the Compose trick that lets ambassador bind
  to localhost from the app's point of view.
- Sharding routes by key; canary routes by percentage/probability.
- Caddy is a real tool that can implement ambassador behavior without custom
  proxy code.

## Looking Ahead

Unit 8 introduces the adapter pattern: a helper container that transforms what
the primary already produces into a format another system expects.

Yes, that’s pretty accurate. Tighten one phrase:

**Ambassadors sit in front of a service’s outgoing calls**, not usually in front of incoming user traffic.

In this unit:

```text
app -> calls localhost:5000
ambassador -> receives that call
ambassador -> routes to users-service-a or users-service-b
```

The app thinks it is always calling one stable local address. The ambassador hides the real backend topology.

Your “shared address space” idea is close. More precise:

> The ambassador shares the app container’s network namespace, so `localhost` from the app’s point of view can reach the ambassador.

That is what this does:

```yaml
network_mode: "service:app"
```

So the app and ambassador behave like they are on the same tiny local network interface.

What you need to know:

- Ambassador = proxy/helper for **outgoing traffic**.
- App keeps calling a stable local address like `localhost:5000`.
- Ambassador decides where the request actually goes.
- Routing logic lives outside app code.
- Useful for:
  - sharding
  - retries
  - load balancing
  - canary rollouts
  - experiments
  - swapping backend versions

Canary rollout: yes, exactly.

```text
90% -> stable service
10% -> new service
```

If the new version breaks, only that slice is affected, and you can route back without changing the app.

Difference from sidecar:

```text
sidecar:
  helps the app do extra support work

ambassador:
  intercepts app's outgoing calls and routes/proxies them
```

Your understanding is good. The main correction is: ambassador is usually about **outbound calls from the primary**, not “sitting in front of services” in the public load-balancer sense.

- Ambassador = proxy/helper for **outgoing traffic**.
- App keeps calling a stable local address like `localhost:5000`.
- Ambassador decides where the request actually goes.
- Routing logic lives outside app code.

  - retries
  - load balancing
  - canary rollouts
  - experiments
  - swapping backend versions

```text
90% -> stable service
10% -> new service
```

If the new version breaks, only that slice is affected, and you can route back without changing the app.

```text
sidecar:
  helps the app do extra support work

ambassador:
  intercepts app's outgoing calls and routes/proxies them
```

Your understanding is good. The main correction is: ambassador is usually about **outbound calls from the primary**, not “sitting in front of services” in the public load-balancer sense.

For Unit 7, the main exercise is:

Add **canary routing** to `ambassador.js`.

Starting point: the Unit 7 ambassador setup where:

```text
app -> localhost:5000
ambassador -> users-service-a for even IDs
ambassador -> users-service-b for odd IDs
```

Your task:

- Keep the even/odd sharding logic.
- Add a random canary rule:
  - 20% of all requests go to `users-service-b`
  - regardless of whether the user ID is even or odd
- Do **not** change `app.js`.

You know it works when:

```bash
for i in $(seq 1 20); do curl -s localhost:3000/users/42; echo; done
```

```json
"servedBy":"A"
```

and some should say:

```json
"servedBy":"B"
```

The point is to prove the app code stays dumb/stable while the ambassador changes traffic behavior.

Add this as the context fo rhomewokr 2 Homework 2: The Seaweed Farm Monitoring Network
Overview
In this assignment you will build a small multi-container system that ties together the four concepts from Week 2: containerizing a service (Unit 4), orchestrating multiple containers with Docker Compose (Unit 5), the sidecar pattern (Unit 6), and the ambassador pattern (Unit 7). The system uses only Express; no other libraries are needed.

This assignment is framed around real marine science: at the Marine Biological Laboratory in Woods Hole, Massachusetts, Associate Scientist Loretta Roberson researches large-scale offshore seaweed farming as a source of sustainable biomass, aimed at bioremediation and at protecting sensitive ecosystems like coral reefs. She leads a DOE ARPA-E-funded initiative farming tropical seaweed off Puerto Rico and works on refining Sargassum into an alternative biomass feedstock. A real deployment of that kind of research depends on exactly the kind of system you will build here: a network of monitoring stations, one per farm site, coordinated and routed reliably enough that no single site's software has to know about the others.

When you are done you will have one shared Docker image, one docker-compose.yml, and four small service files (a farm-monitoring service, a regional-aggregator sidecar, a routing ambassador, and a buoy gateway) — hands-on evidence that the patterns from class compose together into a real distributed system.

Setup
Inside your Gantry devcontainer, create a working directory for this homework:

mkdir hw02 && cd hw02
npm init -y
npm pkg set type=module
npm install express
You will create seven files: farm-service.js, sidecar-sync.js, ambassador.js, buoy-gateway.js, Dockerfile, .dockerignore, and docker-compose.yml.

Part 1: Containerizing a Farm Site (Unit 4)
Your farm monitoring service represents one offshore farm site. It must expose two endpoints, and be entirely configured through environment variables so the same image can run as any farm site.

Environment variables
PORT — port to listen on
FARM_ID — this farm's identifier (e.g. farm-a)
DATA_DIR — directory to persist readings to (default ./data)
CALIBRATION — sensor calibration version (default v1)
GET /status
Returns the farm's identity and every reading recorded so far.

200 OK
{ "farmId": "farm-a", "calibration": "v1", "readings": [] }
POST /reading
Records a sensor reading. The request body must include metric (a string, e.g. "growthRateCm") and value (a number). Appends the reading (with a server-generated timestamp) to an in-memory array and to ${DATA_DIR}/readings.json.

200 OK
{ "farmId": "farm-a", "calibration": "v1", "count": 1, "latest": { "metric": "growthRateCm", "value": 2.4, "timestamp": "2026-07-10T12:00:00.000Z" } }
The Dockerfile
Write a Dockerfile that builds an image any farm site can run from:

FROM node:24 (or a version you have installed)
WORKDIR set to your app directory
Copy package*.json first and run npm install, then copy the rest of your source — in that order, so Docker only reinstalls dependencies when package.json actually changes
EXPOSE the port your service listens on
A default CMD that starts farm-service.js
Add a .dockerignore that excludes node_modules.

You'll know it works when: running

docker build -t seagrid .
docker run -e FARM_ID=farm-a -p 3000:3000 seagrid
and then curl http://localhost:3000/status returns { "farmId": "farm-a", "calibration": "v1", "readings": [] }.

Part 2: Orchestrating the Farm Network (Unit 5)
Write a docker-compose.yml that runs the whole farm network as one system:

farm-a, farm-b, farm-c — three farm-service instances, each built from the same image, each with its own FARM_ID and DATA_DIR, each mapped to its own host port
farm-a-v2 — a fourth farm-service instance with FARM_ID=farm-a, a separate DATA_DIR, and CALIBRATION=v2 — a calibration trial running alongside farm-a itself
A single named volume mounted into every farm service (all four) so their data directories persist and can be read by the sidecar you will add in Part 3
You'll know it works when: running docker compose up --build starts all four farm containers, each independently reachable on its own host port, and a reading posted to farm-a never appears when you GET /status on farm-b or farm-c.

Part 3: The Regional Aggregator Sidecar (Unit 6)
Add sidecar-sync.js: a background process with no HTTP server of its own, that periodically reads every farm's readings.json from the shared volume and writes a rolled-up summary — without farm-service.js ever knowing it exists.

Environment variables
DATA_ROOT — the shared volume's mount path
FARM_IDS — comma-separated list of farm ids to summarize (e.g. farm-a,farm-b,farm-c)
SYNC_INTERVAL_MS — how often to re-read and rewrite the summary (default 5000)
Behavior
On every interval tick, for each farm id in FARM_IDS, read ${DATA_ROOT}/<farmId>/readings.json (treat a missing file as zero readings), then write ${DATA_ROOT}/regional-summary.json:

{
  "generatedAt": "2026-07-10T12:00:05.000Z",
  "farms": {
    "farm-a": { "count": 3, "avgValue": 2.1 },
    "farm-b": { "count": 1, "avgValue": 4.0 }
  },
  "regionalAvgValue": 2.35
}
regionalAvgValue is the mean of every reading from every farm pooled together — not the mean of the per-farm averages. (With farm-a's three readings averaging 2.1 and farm-b's one reading at 4.0, the pooled mean of all four numbers — not the average of 2.1 and 4.0 — is what belongs here.)

Add sidecar as a service in your docker-compose.yml, sharing the same named volume, with depends_on on the three farms.

You'll know it works when: after posting a few readings to two or more farms and waiting one sync interval, docker compose exec sidecar cat /data/regional-summary.json shows the correct per-farm count and avgValue, and a regionalAvgValue that matches the pooled-mean formula above.

Part 4: The Ambassador (Unit 7)
Add two more files:

buoy-gateway.js — the primary service a real buoy would talk to. Exposes POST /submit-reading (body: { "farmId", "metric", "value" }) and forwards it verbatim to a fixed AMBASSADOR_URL. It contains no routing logic of its own — it always calls the same local address, the same way Unit 7's own primary service did.
ambassador.js — shares buoy-gateway's network namespace (via network_mode: "service:buoy-gateway" in Compose) and makes the actual routing decision on buoy-gateway's behalf.
ambassador.js: POST /reading
Body: { "farmId", "metric", "value" }.

Unknown farmId → 404 { "error": "unknown farmId: farm-x" }
farmId === "farm-b" or "farm-c" → forwarded to that farm's fixed URL every time
farmId === "farm-a" → forwarded to farm-a-v2 roughly CANARY_PERCENT percent of the time (default 20), and to farm-a the rest of the time — a canary trial of the new calibration
Response (whichever farm actually handled it):

200 OK
{ "routedTo": "farm-a", "farmResponse": { "farmId": "farm-a", "calibration": "v1", "count": 1, "latest": { "metric": "growthRateCm", "value": 2.0, "timestamp": "2026-07-10T12:00:00.000Z" } } }
buoy-gateway.js: POST /submit-reading
Forwards the request body to ${AMBASSADOR_URL}/reading and returns:

200 OK
{ "receivedBy": "buoy-gateway", "routedTo": "farm-a", "farmResponse": { "...": "..." } }
Wiring it in docker-compose.yml
Add buoy-gateway and ambassador services. The ambassador must not declare its own ports: — network_mode: "service:buoy-gateway" and ports: cannot be used together on the same service; Compose will reject it. Expose the port through buoy-gateway instead.

You'll know it works when:

Repeatedly submitting readings for farm-b or farm-c always routes to that same farm.
Submitting around 100 readings for farm-a results in roughly 10-30 of them landing on farm-a-v2 (check GET /status on each afterward) — not exactly 20 every time, but in that range.
Testing your work locally
Start the whole system:

docker compose up --build
In another terminal:

# Submit a reading through the full path: buoy-gateway -> ambassador -> farm-b
curl -X POST http://localhost:4000/submit-reading \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"farmId": "farm-b", "metric": "growthRateCm", "value": 3.1}'

# Confirm it landed on farm-b specifically
curl http://localhost:3002/status

# Send 100 farm-a readings and see how the count splits across calibrations
for i in $(seq 1 100); do
  curl -s -X POST http://localhost:4000/submit-reading \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d '{"farmId": "farm-a", "metric": "growthRateCm", "value": 2.0}' > /dev/null
done
curl -s http://localhost:3001/status | grep -o '"count":[0-9]*'
curl -s http://localhost:3004/status | grep -o '"count":[0-9]*'

# Check the sidecar's regional summary
docker compose exec sidecar cat /data/regional-summary.json
Submission
Submit a zip file containing exactly these files (no subdirectories):

Dockerfile
.dockerignore
docker-compose.yml
farm-service.js
sidecar-sync.js
ambassador.js
buoy-gateway.js
package.json
From inside your hw02 directory, create the zip:

zip hw02.zip Dockerfile .dockerignore docker-compose.yml farm-service.js sidecar-sync.js ambassador.js buoy-gateway.js package.json
Upload hw02.zip to Gradescope. The autograder runs your service files directly against the endpoint shapes above, and checks your Dockerfile and docker-compose.yml for the required structur

+In this assignment you will build a small multi-container system that ties together the four concepts from Week 2: containerizing a service (Unit 4), orchestrating multiple containers with Docker Compose (Unit 5), the sidecar pattern (Unit 6), and the ambassador pattern (Unit 7). The system uses only Express; no other libraries are needed.
+
+This assignment is framed around real marine science: at the Marine Biological Laboratory in Woods Hole, Massachusetts, Associate Scientist Loretta Roberson researches large-scale offshore seaweed farming as a source of sustainable biomass, aimed at bioremediation and at protecting sensitive ecosystems like coral reefs. She leads a DOE ARPA-E-funded initiative farming tropical seaweed off Puerto Rico and works on refining Sargassum into an alternative biomass feedstock. A real deployment of that kind of research depends on exactly the kind of system you will build here: a network of monitoring stations, one per farm site, coordinated and routed reliably enough that no single site's software has to know about the others.
+
+When you are done you will have one shared Docker image, one docker-compose.yml, and four small service files (a farm-monitoring service, a regional-aggregator sidecar, a routing ambassador, and a buoy gateway) — hands-on evidence that the patterns from class compose together into a real distributed system.
+

+Inside your Gantry devcontainer, create a working directory for this homework:

+```bash
+mkdir hw02 && cd hw02
+npm init -y
+npm pkg set type=module

+```

+
+## Part 1: Containerizing a Farm Site (Unit 4)
+
+Your farm monitoring service represents one offshore farm site. It must expose two endpoints, and be entirely configured through environment variables so the same image can run as any farm site.
+
+### Environment variables
+
+PORT — port to listen on
+FARM_ID — this farm's identifier (e.g. farm-a)
+DATA_DIR — directory to persist readings to (default ./data)
+CALIBRATION — sensor calibration version (default v1)

+### GET /status
+
+Returns the farm's identity and every reading recorded so far.

+```text
+200 OK
+{ "farmId": "farm-a", "calibration": "v1", "readings": [] }
+```
+
+### POST /reading
+
+Records a sensor reading. The request body must include metric (a string, e.g. "growthRateCm") and value (a number). Appends the reading (with a server-generated timestamp) to an in-memory array and to ${DATA_DIR}/readings.json.
+
+```text
+200 OK
+{ "farmId": "farm-a", "calibration": "v1", "count": 1, "latest": { "metric": "growthRateCm", "value": 2.4, "timestamp": "2026-07-10T12:00:00.000Z" } }
+```

+Write a Dockerfile that builds an image any farm site can run from:

+FROM node:24 (or a version you have installed)
+WORKDIR set to your app directory

+EXPOSE the port your service listens on
+A default CMD that starts farm-service.js
+Add a .dockerignore that excludes node_modules.

+```

+
+## Part 2: Orchestrating the Farm Network (Unit 5)

+Write a docker-compose.yml that runs the whole farm network as one system:
+
+farm-a, farm-b, farm-c — three farm-service instances, each built from the same image, each with its own FARM_ID and DATA_DIR, each mapped to its own host port
+farm-a-v2 — a fourth farm-service instance with FARM_ID=farm-a, a separate DATA_DIR, and CALIBRATION=v2 — a calibration trial running alongside farm-a itself

+DATA_ROOT — the shared volume's mount path
+FARM_IDS — comma-separated list of farm ids to summarize (e.g. farm-a,farm-b,farm-c)

+  "generatedAt": "2026-07-10T12:00:05.000Z",
+  "farms": {

# Homework 2 Summary: The Seaweed Farm Monitoring Network

Use this summary when implementing, testing, packaging, or reviewing Homework 2.
Open `source.md` for exact assignment wording, response shapes, and commands.

## Objective

Build a multi-container Express system combining Week 2 concepts:

- Unit 4: containerizing services with a Dockerfile.
- Unit 5: orchestrating services with Docker Compose.
- Unit 6: regional aggregator sidecar using a shared volume.
- Unit 7: routing ambassador with canary behavior.

Only Express is needed; no other libraries.

## Required Files

Inside `hw02/`, create exactly:

- `farm-service.js`
- `sidecar-sync.js`
- `ambassador.js`
- `buoy-gateway.js`
- `Dockerfile`
- `.dockerignore`
- `docker-compose.yml`
- `package.json`

Submission zip must contain exactly these files and no subdirectories.

## Setup

Run inside the Gantry devcontainer:

```bash
mkdir hw02 && cd hw02
npm init -y
npm pkg set type=module
npm install express
```

## Part 1: Farm Service

`farm-service.js` represents one offshore farm site. It must be configured only
through environment variables so one image can run any farm.

Environment variables:

- `PORT`: port to listen on.
- `FARM_ID`: farm identifier, e.g. `farm-a`.
- `DATA_DIR`: directory to persist readings, default `./data`.
- `CALIBRATION`: sensor calibration version, default `v1`.

Endpoints:

- `GET /status`: returns `{ "farmId", "calibration", "readings" }`.
- `POST /reading`: body must include string `metric` and number `value`.

`POST /reading` must:

- generate a server timestamp
- append reading to in-memory array
- persist readings to `${DATA_DIR}/readings.json`
- return `{ farmId, calibration, count, latest }`

Dockerfile requirements:

- `FROM node:24` or installed Node version.
- Set `WORKDIR`.
- Copy `package*.json` first, run `npm install`, then copy source.
- `EXPOSE` service port.
- Default `CMD` starts `farm-service.js`.

`.dockerignore` must exclude `node_modules`.

## Part 2: Compose Farm Network

`docker-compose.yml` must run:

- `farm-a`
- `farm-b`
- `farm-c`
- `farm-a-v2`

All four are farm-service instances built from the same image.

Requirements:

- Each has its own `FARM_ID` and `DATA_DIR`.
- Each maps to its own host port.
- `farm-a-v2` uses `FARM_ID=farm-a`, separate `DATA_DIR`, and
  `CALIBRATION=v2`.
- A single named volume is mounted into every farm service so farm data persists
  and the sidecar can read it.

Success:

- `docker compose up --build` starts all four farms.
- Each farm is reachable on its own host port.
- Readings posted to one farm do not appear in another farm's `/status`.

## Part 3: Regional Aggregator Sidecar

`sidecar-sync.js` is a background process with no HTTP server.

Environment variables:

- `DATA_ROOT`: shared volume mount path.
- `FARM_IDS`: comma-separated farm IDs, e.g. `farm-a,farm-b,farm-c`.
- `SYNC_INTERVAL_MS`: sync interval, default `5000`.

Behavior on each interval:

- For each farm ID, read `${DATA_ROOT}/<farmId>/readings.json`.
- Missing file means zero readings.
- Write `${DATA_ROOT}/regional-summary.json`.

Summary shape:

```json
{
  "generatedAt": "2026-07-10T12:00:05.000Z",
  "farms": {
    "farm-a": { "count": 3, "avgValue": 2.1 },
    "farm-b": { "count": 1, "avgValue": 4.0 }
  },
  "regionalAvgValue": 2.35
}
```

Important formula:

- `regionalAvgValue` is the pooled mean of every reading across farms.
- It is not the mean of per-farm averages.

Compose:

- Add `sidecar` service.
- Mount same named volume.
- `depends_on` the three farms.

Success:

- After readings and one sync interval,
  `docker compose exec sidecar cat /data/regional-summary.json` has correct
  counts, per-farm averages, and pooled regional average.

## Part 4: Ambassador and Buoy Gateway

Files:

- `buoy-gateway.js`: primary service real buoys call.
- `ambassador.js`: routing proxy sharing buoy-gateway network namespace.

`buoy-gateway.js`:

- exposes `POST /submit-reading`
- body: `{ "farmId", "metric", "value" }`
- forwards body to `${AMBASSADOR_URL}/reading`
- contains no routing logic
- returns `{ "receivedBy": "buoy-gateway", "routedTo", "farmResponse" }`

- Ambassador must not declare `ports:`.
- Expose the ambassador path through `buoy-gateway` instead.

Success:

# Homework 2: The Seaweed Farm Monitoring Network

Source: COMPSCI 426 Canvas assignment pasted by the user.

## Overview

In this assignment you will build a small multi-container system that ties together the four concepts from Week 2: containerizing a service (Unit 4), orchestrating multiple containers with Docker Compose (Unit 5), the sidecar pattern (Unit 6), and the ambassador pattern (Unit 7). The system uses only Express; no other libraries are needed.

This assignment is framed around real marine science: at the Marine Biological Laboratory in Woods Hole, Massachusetts, Associate Scientist Loretta Roberson researches large-scale offshore seaweed farming as a source of sustainable biomass, aimed at bioremediation and at protecting sensitive ecosystems like coral reefs. She leads a DOE ARPA-E-funded initiative farming tropical seaweed off Puerto Rico and works on refining Sargassum into an alternative biomass feedstock. A real deployment of that kind of research depends on exactly the kind of system you will build here: a network of monitoring stations, one per farm site, coordinated and routed reliably enough that no single site's software has to know about the others.

When you are done you will have one shared Docker image, one docker-compose.yml, and four small service files (a farm-monitoring service, a regional-aggregator sidecar, a routing ambassador, and a buoy gateway) — hands-on evidence that the patterns from class compose together into a real distributed system.

## Setup

Inside your Gantry devcontainer, create a working directory for this homework:

```bash
mkdir hw02 && cd hw02
npm init -y
npm pkg set type=module
npm install express
```

You will create seven files: farm-service.js, sidecar-sync.js, ambassador.js, buoy-gateway.js, Dockerfile, .dockerignore, and docker-compose.yml.

## Part 1: Containerizing a Farm Site (Unit 4)

Your farm monitoring service represents one offshore farm site. It must expose two endpoints, and be entirely configured through environment variables so the same image can run as any farm site.

### Environment variables

PORT — port to listen on
FARM_ID — this farm's identifier (e.g. farm-a)
DATA_DIR — directory to persist readings to (default ./data)
CALIBRATION — sensor calibration version (default v1)

### GET /status

Returns the farm's identity and every reading recorded so far.

```text
200 OK
{ "farmId": "farm-a", "calibration": "v1", "readings": [] }
```

### POST /reading

Records a sensor reading. The request body must include metric (a string, e.g. "growthRateCm") and value (a number). Appends the reading (with a server-generated timestamp) to an in-memory array and to ${DATA_DIR}/readings.json.

```text
200 OK
{ "farmId": "farm-a", "calibration": "v1", "count": 1, "latest": { "metric": "growthRateCm", "value": 2.4, "timestamp": "2026-07-10T12:00:00.000Z" } }
```

### The Dockerfile

Write a Dockerfile that builds an image any farm site can run from:

FROM node:24 (or a version you have installed)
WORKDIR set to your app directory
Copy package*.json first and run npm install, then copy the rest of your source — in that order, so Docker only reinstalls dependencies when package.json actually changes
EXPOSE the port your service listens on
A default CMD that starts farm-service.js
Add a .dockerignore that excludes node_modules.

You'll know it works when: running

```bash
docker build -t seagrid .
docker run -e FARM_ID=farm-a -p 3000:3000 seagrid
```

and then curl http://localhost:3000/status returns { "farmId": "farm-a", "calibration": "v1", "readings": [] }.

## Part 2: Orchestrating the Farm Network (Unit 5)

Write a docker-compose.yml that runs the whole farm network as one system:

farm-a, farm-b, farm-c — three farm-service instances, each built from the same image, each with its own FARM_ID and DATA_DIR, each mapped to its own host port
farm-a-v2 — a fourth farm-service instance with FARM_ID=farm-a, a separate DATA_DIR, and CALIBRATION=v2 — a calibration trial running alongside farm-a itself
A single named volume mounted into every farm service (all four) so their data directories persist and can be read by the sidecar you will add in Part 3

You'll know it works when: running docker compose up --build starts all four farm containers, each independently reachable on its own host port, and a reading posted to farm-a never appears when you GET /status on farm-b or farm-c.

## Part 3: The Regional Aggregator Sidecar (Unit 6)

Add sidecar-sync.js: a background process with no HTTP server of its own, that periodically reads every farm's readings.json from the shared volume and writes a rolled-up summary — without farm-service.js ever knowing it exists.

### Environment variables

DATA_ROOT — the shared volume's mount path
FARM_IDS — comma-separated list of farm ids to summarize (e.g. farm-a,farm-b,farm-c)
SYNC_INTERVAL_MS — how often to re-read and rewrite the summary (default 5000)

### Behavior

On every interval tick, for each farm id in FARM_IDS, read ${DATA_ROOT}/<farmId>/readings.json (treat a missing file as zero readings), then write ${DATA_ROOT}/regional-summary.json:

```json
{
  "generatedAt": "2026-07-10T12:00:05.000Z",
  "farms": {
    "farm-a": { "count": 3, "avgValue": 2.1 },
    "farm-b": { "count": 1, "avgValue": 4.0 }
  },
  "regionalAvgValue": 2.35
}
```

regionalAvgValue is the mean of every reading from every farm pooled together — not the mean of the per-farm averages. (With farm-a's three readings averaging 2.1 and farm-b's one reading at 4.0, the pooled mean of all four numbers — not the average of 2.1 and 4.0 — is what belongs here.)

Add sidecar as a service in your docker-compose.yml, sharing the same named volume, with depends_on on the three farms.

You'll know it works when: after posting a few readings to two or more farms and waiting one sync interval, docker compose exec sidecar cat /data/regional-summary.json shows the correct per-farm count and avgValue, and a regionalAvgValue that matches the pooled-mean formula above.

## Part 4: The Ambassador (Unit 7)

Add two more files:

buoy-gateway.js — the primary service a real buoy would talk to. Exposes POST /submit-reading (body: { "farmId", "metric", "value" }) and forwards it verbatim to a fixed AMBASSADOR_URL. It contains no routing logic of its own — it always calls the same local address, the same way Unit 7's own primary service did.
ambassador.js — shares buoy-gateway's network namespace (via network_mode: "service:buoy-gateway" in Compose) and makes the actual routing decision on buoy-gateway's behalf.

### ambassador.js: POST /reading

Body: { "farmId", "metric", "value" }.

Unknown farmId → 404 { "error": "unknown farmId: farm-x" }
farmId === "farm-b" or "farm-c" → forwarded to that farm's fixed URL every time
farmId === "farm-a" → forwarded to farm-a-v2 roughly CANARY_PERCENT percent of the time (default 20), and to farm-a the rest of the time — a canary trial of the new calibration

Response (whichever farm actually handled it):

```text
200 OK
{ "routedTo": "farm-a", "farmResponse": { "farmId": "farm-a", "calibration": "v1", "count": 1, "latest": { "metric": "growthRateCm", "value": 2.0, "timestamp": "2026-07-10T12:00:00.000Z" } } }
```

### buoy-gateway.js: POST /submit-reading

Forwards the request body to ${AMBASSADOR_URL}/reading and returns:

```text
200 OK
{ "receivedBy": "buoy-gateway", "routedTo": "farm-a", "farmResponse": { "...": "..." } }
```

### Wiring it in docker-compose.yml

Add buoy-gateway and ambassador services. The ambassador must not declare its own ports: — network_mode: "service:buoy-gateway" and ports: cannot be used together on the same service; Compose will reject it. Expose the port through buoy-gateway instead.

You'll know it works when:

Repeatedly submitting readings for farm-b or farm-c always routes to that same farm.
Submitting around 100 readings for farm-a results in roughly 10-30 of them landing on farm-a-v2 (check GET /status on each afterward) — not exactly 20 every time, but in that range.

- `GET /status`: returns `{ "farmId", "calibration", "readings" }`.
- `POST /reading`: body must include string `metric` and number `value`.

`POST /reading` must:

- generate a server timestamp
- append reading to in-memory array
- persist readings to `${DATA_DIR}/readings.json`
- return `{ farmId, calibration, count, latest }`

Dockerfile requirements:

- `FROM node:24` or installed Node version.
- Set `WORKDIR`.
- Copy `package*.json` first, run `npm install`, then copy source.
- `EXPOSE` service port.
- Default `CMD` starts `farm-service.js`.

`.dockerignore` must exclude `node_modules`.

## Part 2: Compose Farm Network

`docker-compose.yml` must run:

- `farm-a`
- `farm-b`
- `farm-c`
- `farm-a-v2`

All four are farm-service instances built from the same image.

Requirements:

- Each has its own `FARM_ID` and `DATA_DIR`.
- Each maps to its own host port.
- `farm-a-v2` uses `FARM_ID=farm-a`, separate `DATA_DIR`, and
  `CALIBRATION=v2`.
- A single named volume is mounted into every farm service so farm data persists
  and the sidecar can read it.

Success:

- `docker compose up --build` starts all four farms.
- Each farm is reachable on its own host port.
- Readings posted to one farm do not appear in another farm's `/status`.

## Part 3: Regional Aggregator Sidecar

`sidecar-sync.js` is a background process with no HTTP server.

Environment variables:

- `DATA_ROOT`: shared volume mount path.
- `FARM_IDS`: comma-separated farm IDs, e.g. `farm-a,farm-b,farm-c`.
- `SYNC_INTERVAL_MS`: sync interval, default `5000`.

Behavior on each interval:

- For each farm ID, read `${DATA_ROOT}/<farmId>/readings.json`.
- Missing file means zero readings.
- Write `${DATA_ROOT}/regional-summary.json`.

Summary shape:

```json
{
  "generatedAt": "2026-07-10T12:00:05.000Z",
  "farms": {
    "farm-a": { "count": 3, "avgValue": 2.1 },
    "farm-b": { "count": 1, "avgValue": 4.0 }
  },
  "regionalAvgValue": 2.35
}
```

Important formula:

- `regionalAvgValue` is the pooled mean of every reading across farms.
- It is not the mean of per-farm averages.

Compose:

- Add `sidecar` service.
- Mount same named volume.
- `depends_on` the three farms.

Success:

- After readings and one sync interval,
  `docker compose exec sidecar cat /data/regional-summary.json` has correct
  counts, per-farm averages, and pooled regional average.

## Part 4: Ambassador and Buoy Gateway

Files:

- `buoy-gateway.js`: primary service real buoys call.
- `ambassador.js`: routing proxy sharing buoy-gateway network namespace.

`buoy-gateway.js`:

- exposes `POST /submit-reading`
- body: `{ "farmId", "metric", "value" }`
- forwards body to `${AMBASSADOR_URL}/reading`
- contains no routing logic
- returns `{ "receivedBy": "buoy-gateway", "routedTo", "farmResponse" }`

`ambassador.js`:

- exposes `POST /reading`
- body: `{ "farmId", "metric", "value" }`
- unknown farm: `404 { "error": "unknown farmId: farm-x" }`
- `farm-b` and `farm-c`: always forward to fixed farm URL
- `farm-a`: route to `farm-a-v2` roughly `CANARY_PERCENT` percent of the time,
  default 20; otherwise route to `farm-a`
- returns `{ "routedTo", "farmResponse" }`

Compose:

- Add `buoy-gateway` and `ambassador`.
- Ambassador must use `network_mode: "service:buoy-gateway"`.
- Ambassador must not declare `ports:`.
- Expose the ambassador path through `buoy-gateway` instead.

Success:

- farm-b/farm-c readings always route to that farm.
- Around 100 farm-a readings produce roughly 10-30 on `farm-a-v2`.

## Local Test Commands

Start:

```bash
docker compose up --build
```

Submit through full path:

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:4000/submit-reading \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"farmId": "farm-b", "metric": "growthRateCm", "value": 3.1}'
```

Check sidecar:

```bash
docker compose exec sidecar cat /data/regional-summary.json
```

## Submission

From inside `hw02/`:

```bash
zip hw02.zip Dockerfile .dockerignore docker-compose.yml farm-service.js sidecar-sync.js ambassador.js buoy-gateway.js package.json
```

Upload `hw02.zip` to Gradescope.

payload.message: Without doing the assignment yet, is it valuable for me to know implementation wise how to od all of this stuff? Or is it calm

It’s calm. You do **not** need to deeply memorize implementation syntax before doing the assignment.

For Homework 2, the valuable understanding is architectural:

- One image can run multiple farm services because behavior comes from env vars.
- Compose runs all services together.
- The sidecar reads shared files from a volume and writes a regional summary.
- The buoy gateway is dumb: it forwards to one fixed local ambassador URL.
- The ambassador owns routing:
  - farm-b -> farm-b
  - farm-c -> farm-c
  - farm-a -> mostly farm-a, sometimes farm-a-v2
- `network_mode: "service:buoy-gateway"` lets the ambassador share localhost with the gateway.
- The regional average is pooled across all readings, not an average of averages.

Implementation-wise, Codex can write most of this. What you need to be able to review is:

- Are endpoint names and JSON shapes exact?
- Are files persisted in the right paths?
- Is every farm using its own `DATA_DIR`?
- Is the sidecar reading the same mounted volume?
- Is the ambassador free of `ports:` when using `network_mode`?
- Is the gateway free of routing logic?
- Does the zip contain exactly the required files?

So don’t pre-study the syntax. When you start, we should build it straight from the summary and then verify behavior with the required curl/Compose checks.

⚖️ 426 U26 Syllabus (Summer Session II)
COMPSCI 426 Scalable Web Systems
Number: COMPSCI 426
Title: Scalable Web Systems
Instructor: Tim Richards
Canvas: https://umamherst.instructure.com/courses/38093
Semester: Summer Session II 2026
Mode: Online, Asynchronous
Scheduled Meetings: There are no scheduled meetings for this course. It is online and asynchronous.
Exams: There are no exams in this course
Groups: There is group work in this course
Credits: 3
Prerequisites: COMPSCI 320 or COMPSCI 326 with a grade of C or better. If you are from another academic institution or have unique circumstances, you must submit an override requestLinks to an external site. to be considered for enrollment.
Description
The web has become a large and complex area for application development. Access to an abundance of open source languages, libraries, and frameworks has led to the quick and easy construction of a variety of applications with several moving parts working in coordination to present to the user the illusion of a single program. In reality, web applications are extremely difficult to get right. They involve a large collection of coordinated services, multiple databases, complicated user interfaces, security and performance issues, and ever changing third party services, spread across physical and virtual machines. These complications are further stressed by the large number of concurrent users that access these applications every second. This course investigates several well known web-based applications and the technology and software architecture used to scale them. We will also study specific topics related to scalability in software design in the context of web application architecture. This course is hands-on and heavily project-based; students will build, monitor, and load test a distributed system composed of coordinated services. This course counts as an Elective for the CS and INFORM Majors.

This course is concept-first and experiential. You will build and break real scalable systems before we put names to the patterns you discover. The vocabulary of the field, sidecars, ambassadors, sharding, scatter/gather, comes after you have already felt why each pattern exists.

Staff
Instructor: Tim Richards
Email: tdr@umass.edu
Office Hours: By appointment, via Google Meet
Teaching Assistant: Miles (Mingzhe) Li
Email: mingzhel@umass.edu
Learning Objectives
By the end of this course, students will be able to:

Configure and use a devcontainer-based development environment with Docker and VS Code for a reproducible, team-consistent workspace.

Explain the core properties of distributed systems, including latency, reliability, idempotency, and delivery semantics, and reason about the trade-offs between them.

Containerize an application with Docker and orchestrate multiple coordinated services with Docker Compose.

Apply single-node patterns, including the sidecar, ambassador, and adapter patterns, to extend services without modifying them.

Design and reason about serving patterns, including replication, caching, sharding with consistent hashing, and scatter/gather.

Measure system behavior under load using k6, and interpret latency percentiles, throughput, and error rates.

Build event-driven and queue-based systems, including work queues, pub/sub pipelines, and dead letter queues.

Reason about distributed coordination, including locks, leases, ownership election, and concurrent data manipulation.

Instrument a system for observability using structured logging, metrics, and tracing.

Diagnose common distributed failure patterns, including thundering herd, versioning errors, and cascading failure.

Use Git and GitHub for version control, branching, and pull request workflows on a shared team repository.

Plan, build, and present a complete, scalable web system simulation as a team.

Time Commitment
A three credit course does not get smaller when you compress it into six weeks; it gets denser. Plan for roughly twenty-two to twenty-three hours a week.

UMass Amherst defines course workload by a standard credit hour rule. The guiding rule is forty five hours of work per semester for each unit of credit, on the assumption that each credit hour generates two hours of assigned work for every hour of in class contact. By that rule a three credit course represents about one hundred thirty five hours of total work, and the University expects the total workload for a three credit course to be at least 135 hours. That total is fixed. It is the same whether the course runs across a full semester or across a summer.

What changes is how those hours are distributed. In a normal fifteen week semester, one hundred thirty five hours works out to about nine hours per week. This section is taught asynchronously over six weeks, so the same one hundred thirty five hours are compressed into roughly six weeks of effort, which comes to about twenty-two to twenty-three hours per week. There is no reduction in scope to go with the shorter calendar; you are doing a full three credit course in forty percent of the usual time, so the weekly pace is about two and a half times what the same course would demand in the fall or spring.

Twenty-two hours a week is a serious commitment, and you should plan your summer around that reality. Spread across six working days it is just under four hours a day. Because each day's material builds directly on the day before, and because this is a systems course where one misconfigured service can block everything downstream, the work does not compress well into a weekend burst. Students who treat this as a part time effort fall behind quickly, and in a six week term there is very little room to recover. For that reason I strongly advise against pairing this course with another demanding summer course or with full time employment. If your situation makes twenty-two hours a week difficult, email me at tdr@umass.edu before the term begins so we can be honest about whether the timing works for you.

To make the number concrete, your weekly hours go toward the same components described elsewhere in this syllabus: working through several Knowledge Units, since the eighteen KUs are spread across the six weeks, including their preparatory reading, the activity, and the exercises; and steadily advancing your team's sprint project, which on its own accounts for a substantial share of your time over the term. The weekly quizzes are the clearest early signal of whether you are keeping pace. If you find yourself consistently spending far more than this, or far less and still finishing everything, let me know, because that is useful feedback on the course and may also be a sign we should look at how you are approaching the work.

Course Structure Synopsis
Asynchronous Delivery
This course is offered in an online, asynchronous format. All course materials will be available online on the course website. You are expected to engage with the content and complete assignments on your own schedule within the given deadlines. This course is designed to be experiential, meaning that you will learn by doing, and the course structure is built around active participation and hands-on activities.

Knowledge Units (KUs)
The primary way in which learning takes place is through knowledge units (KUs). Each KU is a self-contained module that includes preparatory reading, hands-on activities, and exercises. You are expected to complete each KU in order, as they build upon one another. The course is deliberately concept-first: most units ask you to build or observe something before the underlying pattern is named, so that the name lands on an experience you already have rather than on an abstraction. Each KU will have a set of activities that you must complete, including coding and load-testing exercises.

Canvas
Canvas is where you will find links to all of the course material. The syllabus and schedule can be found on Canvas. All assignments will be posted on Canvas. Grades will be posted to Canvas. Announcements will be posted on Canvas. If in doubt, go to Canvas to find what you are looking for and follow links from there.

Gradescope
Homework assignments are submitted through Gradescope and graded automatically. When you submit, an autograder runs your code against a test suite and reports a score immediately; you do not have to wait for manual review to see how you did. If a test fails, the output includes enough information to diagnose and fix the issue before the deadline. You may resubmit as many times as you like before the deadline, and only your final submission is graded. Gradescope is accessible through Canvas.

Communication
Email the instructor at tdr@umass.edu for all course-related questions and requests. Every email must include [426] at the start of the subject line — for example, [426] Sprint 3 question. Emails without this prefix may be missed. See the full Communication section for guidance on what to include in your message.

Spire
Final grades will be posted to Canvas before they are submitted to Spire. You are expected to check your grades in both places to ensure that everything adds up. You are responsible for ensuring that your grades are accurate and that you have received credit for all assignments that you submitted by the posted deadline. If you notice any discrepancies, you should contact the course staff immediately.

Required Books, Equipment, and Technology
One textbook, one container that carries the entire stack, and a machine capable of running it.

This course uses one textbook: Designing Distributed Systems, 2nd EditionLinks to an external site., by Brendan Burns (O'Reilly). You have free access to the book by logging in using your UMass credentials under “Other login options” and selecting “Affiliated with a school or institution?” The book frames containers as the vehicle for every pattern we study, and its treatment of patterns like the sidecar, the work queue, and dead letter queues is unusually thorough. Preparatory reading for the Knowledge Units draws directly from it. Beyond the textbook, everything you need to read is provided through as Knowledge Units, primers, and linked documentation. Where you need a reference for a specific tool, the course points you to that tool's official documentation.

What this course also requires is a computer you control and that is capable of running a containerized development environment. You need a reasonably current laptop or desktop running macOS, Windows, or Linux, with enough memory and disk space to run Docker comfortably; eight gigabytes of RAM is a practical minimum and sixteen is more comfortable, along with several gigabytes of free disk space for container images and your project. A Chromebook or a tablet is not sufficient for this course, because neither can run the local development environment. If your only computer cannot meet these requirements, email the course staff at tdr@umass.edu during the first few days so we can help you find an alternative such as a loaner machine through the University. We will try, but we can't guarantee.

Nearly all of the software for this course is delivered through a single prepared development environment, a Dev Container that bundles the entire technology stack so you do not have to install or configure each piece by hand.

Development Environment
This course uses development containers (devcontainers) to provide a uniform and consistent development environment for all students. Devcontainers are a way to package and distribute development environments using Docker containers. This allows you to have a consistent environment across different machines and operating systems, and ensures that you have all the necessary tools and dependencies installed.

You are not required to know much about Docker or devcontainers to begin, but you will need to have Docker installed on your machine, and over the course of the term you will come to understand containers deeply, since they are the central building block of the entire course. You will be required to use the devcontainer for all course-related work, including coding exercises, load tests, and the project.

The core software you will need to install is VS Code, Docker Desktop, and the VS Code Remote Containers extension. The devcontainer is configured to include the tools and dependencies for the course, including Node.js, npm, the Docker CLI and Compose, the k6 load testing tool, and Caddy as a reverse proxy and load balancer. Services and worker processes in this course are written in Node.js and JavaScript. You should not install this software right now, as you will be instructed on how to do so as part of the course setup unit.

Assignments
We use several different methods to scaffold your learning and assess your understanding of the material covered in this course. We outline the various methods and the kind of assessment below so you can better understand and plan your learning path. We categorize assignments as either being formative (F), summative (S), or a combination (FS). A purely formative assignment is designed to build your understanding, low stakes, and doesn't have any or very little impact on your grade. A summative assignment is designed to measure your understanding of the material. A combination of formative/summative contains aspects of low stakes assessment with measurement.

Exercises
Practice embedded in every unit, not graded, but expected.

Exercises are short activities built into each Knowledge Unit. They are not submitted and they do not count toward your grade. Many ask you to run a service under load with k6, observe a latency percentile or an error rate, and interpret what you see. The goal is practice: try something, get it wrong safely, and learn from it. You are expected to do the exercises; they exist to make the hands-on work in the Knowledge Units land rather than to generate a score.

Participation
Small, low-stakes tasks spread across the term that keep you engaged with the course and your teammates-to-be.

Each of the six weeks, Week 0 through Week 5, carries one participation task delivered natively on Canvas: Week 0 is a public discussion where you introduce yourself before project teams form; Weeks 1 through 5 are a short, private reflection survey connecting that week's Knowledge Units to your own experience. Both are graded on completion, not correctness or length, and both are generated directly from this repository rather than written by hand in Canvas. Together the six tasks make up five percent of your final grade.

Weekly Quizzes
A timed, summative check on the week's material, taken at your own pace within 3 days after the week's completion.

After each of the six content weeks you complete a timed quiz covering that week's Knowledge Units. Each quiz is multiple choice, approximately twenty questions, and you have forty-five minutes. You may take each quiz up to three times; your highest score is recorded. The quiz for the final week is cumulative across the full course. Together the six quizzes make up twenty percent of your final grade. Quizzes are available on Canvas.

Homework
Four hands-on assignments that build the skills the project depends on.

There are four homework assignments across the term, one roughly every week and a half. Each is a hands-on task that involves creating parts of a simulated distributed system using real tools and services: k6 for load testing, JavaScript for building services, and existing services such as Caddy, Redis, MongoDB, PostgreSQL, Prometheus, and Grafana. Homework is submitted through Gradescope and graded automatically against a rubric; you will see your score as soon as the autograder runs. Together the four assignments make up thirty percent of your final grade. Your scores from Gradescope will be periodically synced to Canvas.

Sprints
A simulated scalable system built incrementally: each sprint applies only what the previous week taught.

The Sprints are the team project itself, carried forward in stages rather than assembled at the end. Each sprint is due during the week after the Knowledge Units that inform it are covered, so the system grows in lockstep with the course material. You cannot design the full architecture at the start; you do not yet know the patterns. Instead the simulation is extended one layer at a time: Sprint 0 forms the team and stakes out a domain idea; Sprint 1 frames the scalability problem using the distributed systems vocabulary from Week 1; Sprint 2 produces the first containerized services running under Docker Compose; Sprint 3 adds serving patterns (replication, caching, load balancing) and a first k6 load test; Sprint 4 introduces async processing and resilience; and Sprint 5 instruments the system with observability, runs a final load test, and delivers the four capstone artifacts.

The system you build throughout is a simulation: data is synthetic, latency is injected, failures are scripted, and computation is modeled. This is a deliberate choice, not a shortcut. Building a production system from scratch in six weeks is not realistic, and the goal of this course is not deployment; it is design, engineering, and measurement. Simulation lets you practice every pattern the course covers, instrument and break the system intentionally, and measure it under realistic load, without the operational complexity of real data pipelines or live traffic. The skills you develop, structuring services, reasoning about coordination, interpreting latency percentiles, are the same ones a team would use on a real system.

Sprints introduce no new instruction. They are where you apply the current state of the Knowledge Units to the simulated system your team is building. Teams are assigned by the instructor and are 2–3 members for this six-week section. Because this course has no separate lab sequence, the professional workflow skills that labs would otherwise carry, clean commits, pull requests, code review, conflict resolution, are practiced and assessed directly inside the sprints. Because impressions are unreliable, your sprint contribution is assessed against objective GitHub evidence, your commits, the pull requests you authored and reviewed, and the merge history, rather than against anyone's sense of who did what. Sprints 0 and 1 are half-weight (each worth half a full sprint); Sprints 2, 3, and 4 are full-weight. Sprint 5 is graded as the Project Final (20%) rather than as part of the Sprints category.

Sprint 0: Team Formation and Project Concept
Week 0 covered setting up the development environment and GitHub. Sprint 0 is about getting organized as a team and staking out a project idea while that setup is still fresh. No architecture decisions are required yet; students do not have the vocabulary for them.

Shared GitHub repository created with all team members added as collaborators
README with team roster
A short paragraph describing the domain the team wants to simulate and a first guess at what makes it interesting from a scalability standpoint: what would a real system in this domain need to handle that a single server could not?
Sprint 1: Project Definition and Scalability Framing
Week 1 covered why distributed systems exist, the core trade-offs between latency and reliability, and the semantics of idempotency and message delivery. Sprint 1 asks the team to apply that vocabulary to their chosen domain. No code is expected yet; this is design thinking grounded in the concepts just studied.

A refined project description: what domain, what scalability problem, and why this problem is meaningful (the Computing for the Common Good framing)
An initial list of services the simulation might include, with one sentence on what each does; this is a first guess, not a commitment, and it will evolve as more patterns are introduced
A short statement of the system's latency and reliability requirements: what does "fast enough" mean for this domain, and what happens if a component fails?
Sprint 2: First Containerized System
Week 2 covered Docker fundamentals, Docker Compose, the sidecar pattern, and the ambassador pattern. Sprint 2 is the first time the team writes code. The goal is a multi-service simulation running under Docker Compose with at least one pattern from Week 2 applied.

At least two services containerized and running under Docker Compose, each with its own HTTP endpoint returning domain-relevant simulated data
At least one sidecar or ambassador pattern applied alongside a primary service as a separate container
A docker-compose.yml committed to the repository that starts the whole system with a single command
Sprint 3: Serving Patterns and First Load Test
Week 3 covered the adapter pattern, replicated services with load balancing and caching, sharded services, and scatter/gather. Sprint 3 extends the existing simulation with at least one serving pattern and adds the first measurement.

At least one service running with multiple replicas behind Caddy as a load balancer
A caching layer (Redis) integrated into at least one service path, with simulated cache hits and misses
A k6 load test script that exercises the replicated service, with a written summary of the p50, p95, and p99 latency results
Sprint 4: Async Processing and Resilience
Week 4 covered resilience and failure modes, event-driven processing, work queue systems, and pub/sub pipelines. Sprint 4 adds an asynchronous processing path to the simulation and introduces controlled failures to show the system can handle them.

At least one async processing path: a work queue or pub/sub channel backed by Redis
Health check endpoints on all services, wired into Docker Compose healthcheck configuration
At least one scripted failure scenario: a service that can be made to fail or slow down, with a brief written description of how the system responds
Sprint 5: Observability, Final Measurement, and Delivery
Week 5 covered coordinated batch processing, ownership election, and observability. Sprint 5 instruments the simulation, produces the final load test evidence, and assembles the four capstone deliverables.

Prometheus metrics exposed by all custom services, scraped by a Prometheus instance defined in Docker Compose
A Grafana dashboard showing at minimum: request rate, error rate, and p95 latency for the main service path
Structured JSON log output from all custom services
A final k6 load test with a written interpretation: what the latency distribution shows, how it compares to the Sprint 3 baseline, and where the bottleneck appears to be
GitHub repository URL: code committed, README complete, system starts with a single command
Recorded video demonstration (10 minutes or less): the system starting with docker compose up, at least one endpoint responding, the Grafana dashboard live during a k6 load test, and an explanation of one design decision and its trade-off
Project poster: the problem, the architecture, the patterns demonstrated, and the key trade-offs, formatted as a one-page PDF
Individual reflection: submitted separately by each team member covering what you contributed, what you learned, and what you would do differently
Project
The capstone: a simulated scalable system that demonstrates the design, engineering, and measurement skills of the course.

The Project is the summative destination the entire course is aimed at, and in this section it is fully asynchronous. Working in a team, you choose a problem domain in the spirit of Computing for the Common Good and design a meaningful but achievable scalable application. You then build a simulation of that application: services that model realistic behavior using synthetic data, injected latency, and scripted failures, orchestrated with Docker Compose and measured under load with k6. The simulation is not a stripped-down version of a real system; it is the full architecture, with coordinated services, asynchronous pipelines, caching, and observability, implemented in a way that makes every pattern visible and every failure intentional. The goal is to demonstrate that you understand how such a system is designed, how its components interact, and how its behavior changes under load.

You submit four deliverables: the source code in your shared GitHub repository, a recorded video walkthrough of the running system, a poster presenting the problem, the architecture, and the trade-offs you made, and an individual written reflection from each team member on their own contribution and what they learned. You are assessed on collaborative practice, on meeting the sprint deliverable deadlines that pace the project from Week 1, and on professional conduct throughout, with contribution again read from objective GitHub evidence and the grade trajectory-weighted across the term. Deployment to a public host is not required and is not taught here; the destination is a complete, multi-service simulation running under Docker Compose in the dev container and demonstrated on video.

Communication
One address, one required prefix, enough detail to get a useful answer on the first reply.

Email tdr@umass.edu for all course-related questions and requests. Every email must include [426] at the start of the subject line — for example, [426] Sprint 3 docker-compose question. Emails without this prefix may be missed or delayed. Send from your verified UMass email address; replies go there.

In the body of your message, name the category that fits your request so it can be routed and answered efficiently: Logistics for course mechanics, scheduling, and enrollment; Assignment for the content or requirements of a Knowledge Unit or Sprint; Technical for the dev environment, Docker, Compose, k6, Git, GitHub, or tooling; Grading for score discrepancies or rubric questions; Extension for late work and deadline changes; Accommodation for disability services, religious observance, and similar arrangements; Personal for private matters such as illness or anything that does not fit a label.

When your request concerns a specific deliverable, name it exactly — for example Sprint 3, or KU 11 Sharded Services — rather than a vague reference. For Assignment, Technical, and Grading requests, paste direct links to your repository and to the specific pull request, commit, or failing Gradescope run. Copy any error message verbatim rather than describing it, and tell us what you have already tried so we do not suggest it back to you. End with the precise question you want answered.

Reach out early. A request about a deadline, an accommodation, or a situation that may affect your work should arrive before the deadline passes, not after. The staff aim to respond within one business day on weekdays; do not expect responses on weekends or University holidays. We are glad to help when we hear from you in time.

Course Policies
Engagement, late work, incompletes, and exemptions are handled in an accelerated term.

This is a fully asynchronous course delivered over six weeks, so there are no scheduled class meetings and there is no attendance taken in the traditional sense. What replaces attendance is engagement on time. The course moves quickly, each day builds on the one before it, and because this is a systems course, one misconfigured or missing service can block everything downstream. Falling a few days behind in a six week term is the equivalent of falling two weeks behind in a normal semester. Your engagement is measured by the on time completion of weekly quizzes and homework, and by steady, visible contribution to your team's sprint work in GitHub.

Late work is handled differently depending on what kind of work it is. Homework assignments may be turned in late for up to two days past the due date, with a deduction of ten percent per day; after two days they are no longer accepted and are scored as zero. Sprint deliverables and the final capstone submission are hard deadlines and are not eligible for the late allowance, because your teammates and the staff depend on that work being in place on time and because the schedule has no slack to absorb a slipped project milestone. If something is going to prevent you from meeting any deadline, email an Extension request to tdr@umass.edu before the deadline passes. Proactive communication is the rule in this course, not a courtesy. We are far more able to help a student who writes before the deadline than one who writes after it.

Incomplete grades follow university policy. An Incomplete (INC) may be granted only when a student who has been in good standing and has completed a substantial portion of the coursework is prevented by serious circumstances beyond their control from finishing on time. An Incomplete is never a substitute for a low grade and must be arranged with the instructor through a written agreement before the end of the term that specifies the remaining work and the completion date.

There are no exemptions from individual assignments. Every student completes the same work, with the single exception of arrangements made through Disability Services or for documented religious observance, both of which are described in the sections below.

Academic Honesty and Collaboration
