Development Environment Setup
Welcome! This guide will get your development environment up and running, even if you have never used Docker or a dev container before. Read through each section in order the first time, it only takes about 10 minutes.

What is this, exactly?
When you open the development environment folder in VS Code, it automatically builds a Linux environment that runs inside your computer. Think of it like a virtual machine, but lighter and faster. Inside that environment you get:

Node.js (latest LTS) and all the tools you need for web development
Optional databases (PostgreSQL, Redis, MongoDB, MySQL, and more) that you can turn on with a single command
A pre-configured terminal with shortcuts that make common tasks faster
Everything needed for web development, no manual installation required
No matter whether you are on macOS, Windows, or Linux, everyone on the team gets the exact same environment. "It works on my machine" stops being an excuse.

A note before you dive in: This document covers a lot of ground, and that is intentional. It is meant to be a reference you return to throughout the course, not something you need to absorb all at once. You will not use everything here, and that is completely fine. Many of the services, shortcuts, and tools listed are available if and when a homework or exercise calls for them. If you have never touched a terminal or typed a command before, do not worry. The terminal may look unfamiliar at first, but you will get comfortable with it gradually as we work through things together. Just follow the steps in order, and if something is confusing, set it aside for now. It will make more sense in context when we get there.

Step 1: Install the prerequisites
You need three things installed on your computer before you start. Click each link and follow the instructions for your operating system.

Docker DesktopLinks to an external site. Docker is the engine that runs the dev environment. The Desktop app gives you a graphical dashboard too.

Windows users: during installation, choose "Use WSL 2" if asked. After installing, open Docker Desktop once and let it finish starting up before moving on.

Visual Studio CodeLinks to an external site. The code editor.

Dev Containers extensionLinks to an external site. This VS Code extension makes the "open in container" magic work. Click the link, then click Install, and VS Code will open and install it automatically.

Once all three are installed, make sure Docker Desktop is running (look for the Docker whale icon in your taskbar or menu bar) before continuing.

Step 2: Download the development environment
Go to the Gantry Dev Container ReleasesLinks to an external site.. Under "Assets," download the latest release by selecting the file named gantry-<version>.zip. Do not download the "Source code" archives, that is not the release build. Save the file somewhere you can find it, such as your Desktop or your own folder for this course.

Step 3: Extract the archive
Extract gantry-<version>.zip to your chosen folder location. Do not leave it in your Downloads folder, the container will store your course work inside this folder, so treat it as your course workspace.

On macOS: double-click gantry-<version>.zip to extract it. A folder named gantry-<version> will appear alongside the archive.

On Windows: right-click gantry-<version>.zip and choose "Extract All." Select your destination folder and click Extract. A folder named gantry-<version> will appear in the destination folder.

On Linux: open a terminal and run unzip gantry-<version>.zip. A folder named gantry-<version> will appear in the destination folder. You may also use a zip extracting application provided by the particular Linux distribution you are using (e.g., Ubuntu, Fedora, Arch)

Step 4: Open the Development Environment in VS Code
Open VS Code.

Go to File → Open Folder and select the development environment folder.

VS Code will show a notification in the bottom-right corner (this may take a moment).

Click "Reopen in Container". If you missed the notification, open the Command Palette (Ctrl+Shift+P on Windows/Linux, Cmd+Shift+P on Mac), type "Reopen in Container", and press Enter.

Wait for the build to finish. The first time takes 3–5 minutes while it downloads everything. You will see a progress bar in the bottom-right corner. Subsequent openings are almost instant. It is helpful to be on a fast WiFi connection for this part.

When the build finishes, VS Code reloads and you are now inside the development environment.

Step 5: Open the terminal
The terminal is how you run code and commands. Inside VS Code:

Go to Terminal → New Terminal in the menu bar, or press Ctrl+` (backtick).
The Gantry banner confirms everything is working. The $ at the end of the last line is the prompt, it is waiting for you to type a command.

New to the terminal? The terminal works by typing a command and pressing Enter. Commands are case-sensitive. If something goes wrong, you can usually press Ctrl+C to stop whatever is running.

Common Tasks
The following examples cover common tasks. Run them in the VS Code terminal (Terminal → New Terminal in the menu bar, or press Ctrl+` (backtick)).

Run a Node.js script
Let's confirm Node.js is ready.

node --version
You should see something like v22.x.x. Now create and run a tiny script:

echo 'console.log("Hello from the dev container!")' > hello.js
node hello.js
Expected output:

Hello from the dev container!
Install npm packages and run a project
If you have a package.json file in your workspace:

npm install
npm run dev
The npm run dev command starts your project (exact behavior depends on the project). Press Ctrl+C to stop it.

Shortcuts that save typing:

Instead of	You can type
npm install	ni
npm run dev	nrd
npm run	nr
npm start	ns
npm test	nt
Start a database and connect to it
Databases are off by default to save memory. Turn one on when you need it.

Start PostgreSQL:

dc-up postgres
You will see Docker pulling the image and starting the container. Once it says the container is healthy, connect to it:

psql-dev
You are now inside the PostgreSQL shell. Try a quick command:

\l
This lists all databases. You should see devdb in the list. Type \q to exit.

Start Redis:

dc-up redis
redis-dev ping
Expected output: PONG

Start MongoDB:

dc-up mongo
mongo-dev
You are now in the MongoDB shell. Type show dbs to list databases. Type exit to leave.

Stop everything when you're done:

dc-down
Check what is running
dps
This shows all running containers in a tidy table format. If nothing is running, you will see an empty table. To see the logs from a running service (like postgres), use:

dc-logs postgres
Press Ctrl+C to stop watching logs.

Make an HTTP request and read JSON
The environment comes with several tools for working with HTTP APIs.

curl https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/todos/1
The output is JSON but it is hard to read. Pipe it through jq to pretty-print it:

curl https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/todos/1 | jq .
Or use the built-in shortcut jcurl which does both steps at once:

jcurl https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/todos/1
You can also use xh (a friendlier HTTP tool):

xh https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/todos/1
Check what ports are listening
When your app is running, you might want to see what ports are in use:

ports
This lists every port that has something listening on it.

Customizing Your Terminal
You can add your own aliases, functions, and environment variables without touching any shared files and without restarting the container.

Open the file .bashrc.user in your workspace root (VS Code's Explorer panel, it is a hidden file, so look for it there or open it from the terminal).

Add your customizations. Example:

# My personal shortcuts
alias serve='npx http-server . -p 8080'
alias cls='clear'
export MY_API_KEY="abc123"
Apply changes without restarting by running:
reload-env
Your changes are now active in the current terminal.

Troubleshooting
The "Reopen in Container" notification never appeared
Open the Command Palette (Cmd+Shift+P / Ctrl+Shift+P), type Dev Containers: Reopen in Container, and press Enter. If that option doesn't appear, make sure the Dev Containers extension is installed and Docker Desktop is running.

The build failed or got stuck
Make sure Docker Desktop is open and running (check the taskbar/menu bar icon).
Open the Command Palette and choose Dev Containers: Rebuild Container.
If it fails again, open Docker Desktop and check that you have at least 4 GB of memory allocated to Docker (Settings → Resources).
A service won't start
Check Docker is running, then try:

dc-logs <service>
This shows the service's error output. Common fix: the service might need a moment to initialize. Try dc-up <service> again after 10 seconds.

psql-dev / redis-dev says "connection refused"
The service is not running yet. Start it first:

dc-up postgres   # or redis, mongo, etc.
Wait a few seconds for it to become ready, then try again.

My app can't connect to the database
Make sure you are using the service name as the host (e.g. postgres, redis, mongo), not localhost. Inside the dev container, services talk to each other by name. See the connection table above.

I can't push to GitHub
Run this inside the container terminal:

gh auth status
If it says you are not authenticated, run:

gh auth login
Follow the prompts. After authenticating, git push will work automatically.

I accidentally ran something and the terminal is frozen
Press Ctrl+C to cancel the current command. If that doesn't work, close the terminal tab and open a new one from Terminal → New Terminal.

Everything is broken, I want to start fresh
Open the Command Palette and choose Dev Containers: Rebuild Container. This rebuilds the environment from scratch. Your files in the workspace folder are never deleted.

The Terminal: A Primer
Talk to your computer with words, not clicks

You have probably spent most of your computing life using a graphical interface — clicking icons, dragging windows, navigating menus. The terminal is a completely different way of talking to your computer, and it requires a different mental model. This primer explains what the terminal is, why it exists, why it matters for a course like this one, and what you need to know to use it without confusion.

What the Terminal Is
Your operating system — macOS, Windows, Linux — is a layer of software that manages the hardware underneath your applications. Every time you create a file, open a browser, or install a program, the operating system is doing the actual work. A graphical interface gives you buttons and menus to make requests to the operating system. The terminal does the same thing, but through text.

When you open a terminal, you see a cursor waiting for input. That interface is called the command line. You type a command, press Enter, and the operating system executes it. The output, if there is any, appears as text below your command. Then the cursor reappears and waits for the next one. That is the entire interaction model.

The program that reads your input and coordinates with the operating system is called a shell. On macOS and Linux, the default shell is usually bash or zsh. On Windows with WSL, you also get bash. The shell is not the terminal window itself — the terminal is the visual container, and the shell is the program running inside it. The distinction rarely matters in practice, but you will see both words used in documentation.

Why the Terminal Exists and Why It Matters
The terminal is not a relic from before graphical interfaces were invented. It is still the primary tool for technical work because it is fast, precise, scriptable, and universal.

Most of the tools used in professional software development — version control, build systems, test runners, package managers, servers, deployment scripts — are built to be operated from the command line. They have no graphical interface at all, or their graphical interface exposes far less than the command line does. git, npm, node, docker, psql: every tool you will use in this course is a command-line program. You will install packages by typing npm install. You will run your server by typing node server.js. You will interact with a database by typing commands. None of this happens through a menu.

There is a second reason the terminal matters: it is the same everywhere. A command that works on your laptop works on your classmates' laptops and on a remote server in a data center. When you deploy an application to production, there is no graphical interface available — there is only a shell. Learning to work in the terminal now means the jump to professional environments is not a surprise later.

Terminology You Need to Know
Before touching any commands, you need a shared vocabulary.

The file system is the structure your operating system uses to organize all stored data. Everything — your documents, your code, your programs — lives somewhere in the file system.

A directory is a container that holds files and other directories. You may know this concept as a "folder." In the terminal, the word "directory" is standard. Directories nest inside each other, forming a tree.

The root directory is the top of that tree. On macOS and Linux it is written as /. On Windows with WSL it is also / inside the Linux environment. Everything else in the file system is inside the root directory, directly or indirectly.

Your home directory is the directory assigned to your user account. On macOS it is typically /Users/yourname. On Linux it is typically /home/yourname. The ~ character is shorthand for your home directory in most shells.

The working directory is the directory the terminal is currently "inside." When you open a terminal, it starts in your home directory. When you run a command, the command executes relative to the working directory unless you specify otherwise. Understanding what your working directory is at any moment is one of the most important habits in terminal use.

A path is the address of a file or directory in the file system. An absolute path starts from the root and describes the full address: /home/yourname/cs326/project/server.js. A relative path starts from the current working directory: if your working directory is /home/yourname/cs326, then project/server.js is a relative path to the same file.

A command is a text instruction you give to the shell. Commands are usually short programs that live somewhere on your file system. When you type a command name, the shell searches a list of known locations to find and run it.

An argument is additional information passed to a command. When you type node server.js, node is the command and server.js is an argument telling it which file to run.

A flag (also called an option) is a special kind of argument that modifies a command's behavior. Flags usually start with - or --. For example, ls -l runs ls with the -l flag, which changes the output format.

A script is a text file containing a sequence of commands. Instead of typing ten commands manually, you put them in a script file and run the whole file at once. Scripts are how automation works in the terminal.

Permissions control who is allowed to read, write, or execute a file. Every file and directory in the file system has a set of permissions attached to it. Permissions matter when you try to run a script or access a file and the operating system refuses — understanding permissions tells you why and how to fix it.

Standard output (stdout) is where a command sends its normal output — the text you see printed in the terminal after a command runs. Standard error (stderr) is a separate channel for error messages. Both appear in the terminal by default, but they can be separated and redirected independently.

A process is a running instance of a program. When you run node server.js, you start a process. That process runs until it finishes or you stop it. Pressing Ctrl+C in the terminal sends a signal to the current process telling it to stop.

The Commands You Need First
These are the commands you will use constantly. Learn what they do before you need them in an activity.

pwd: Print the working directory.
Outputs the absolute path of the directory the terminal is currently in. When you are disoriented, run this first.

pwd
ls: List files and directories.
Shows the files and directories inside the working directory. Running ls -l shows a detailed view including permissions, owner, size, and modification date.

ls
ls -l
cd: Change directory.
Moves the terminal's working directory to the path you specify.

cd cs326
cd ..
cd ~
cd /home/yourname/cs326
cd .. moves up one level to the parent directory. cd ~ moves to your home directory. cd with no argument also moves to your home directory.

mkdir: Make a directory.
Creates a new directory with the name you provide.

cat: Concatenate a file.

Shows the contents of a file one screen at a time, letting you scroll through output that is too long to read in a single terminal view. Unlike cat, it does not dump everything at once. Use the arrow keys or j/k to scroll, space to jump a full page, and q to exit.

man: Manual.
Open the manual page for a command. On macOS and Linux, nearly every command has a manual page. Use the arrow keys or j/k to scroll, space to jump a full page, and q to exit. Press q to exit.

man cp
Running a Script
Basics
A script is an executable text file. To run one, you call it like a command:

node server.js
Some scripts are written for the shell directly, not for a runtime like Node. Those files typically end in .sh. To run a shell script, you first need to make sure it has execute permission, then call it:

chmod +x setup.sh
./setup.sh
chmod +x adds execute permission to the file. The ./ prefix tells the shell to look for the file in the current directory — without it, the shell only searches its known program locations and will not find your script.

The Shebang (#!)
The first line of a shell script that tells the operating system which interpreter to use to run the file. When you execute a script, the operating system reads the first two characters. If they are #!, it treats the rest of that line as the path to the program that should run the script.

#!/bin/bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
#!/usr/bin/env node
#!/usr/bin/env python3
Without a shebang, the operating system does not know what kind of script it is looking at. It may refuse to run it, or it may guess wrong. With a shebang, running ./setup.sh works exactly the same as running bash setup.sh — the shebang makes the file self-describing.

The second form, #!/usr/bin/env node, is more portable than a hardcoded path like #!/usr/local/bin/node. The env program searches your PATH for the named interpreter, so the script works regardless of where Node is installed on a given machine. You will see this form in most modern scripts that target Node or Python.

The shebang line is ignored as a comment by the interpreter itself, # starts a comment in bash, Python, and most scripting languages, so it causes no errors when the interpreter processes the rest of the file.

Here is a simple Node script that prints a greeting to the terminal:

#!/usr/bin/env node
const name = process.argv[2] ?? "stranger";
console.log(`Hello, ${name}!`);
Save this as greet.js, make it executable, and run it:

chmod +x greet.js
./greet.js
./greet.js Alice
Output:

Hello, stranger!
Hello, Alice!
process.argv is an array Node populates with the command-line arguments passed to the script. The first two entries are always the path to Node and the path to the script itself, so index 2 is where your first real argument lives. The ?? operator supplies a default if no argument was given.

Without the shebang, you would have to type node greet.js Alice every time. With it, ./greet.js Alice works -- the script knows how to run itself.

Permissions in Brief
When you run ls -l, each entry starts with a string like -rwxr-xr--. That string encodes the permissions on the file. The characters map to three groups: the owner, the group, and everyone else. For each group, there are three possible permissions: read (r), write (w), and execute (x). A - means that permission is not granted.

You will encounter permissions issues most often when trying to run a script that the operating system refuses to execute. The fix is usually chmod +x filename, which adds execute permission for the owner. The course activities will tell you when this is necessary.

What Happens When Something Goes Wrong
The terminal is unforgiving in one specific way: it does what you say, not what you meant. If you mistype a filename, it will tell you the file does not exist. If you run a command in the wrong directory, the results will be wrong. If you delete something with rm, it is gone.

Developing three habits will prevent most problems. First, always know your working directory. Run pwd whenever you are uncertain. Second, use ls before and after operations that create or move files. Third, read error messages carefully -- they almost always tell you exactly what went wrong. "No such file or directory" means your path is wrong. "Permission denied" means you do not have the right access level. "Command not found" means the program is not installed or not on your PATH.

There is no way to learn the terminal except by using it. The commands above will get you through everything in this course. You will be slow at first and faster within a week.

A Note on This Course
In this course you will use the terminal constantly. Every activity, every project sprint, every interaction with git, npm, node, and the Gantry container runs through the command line. If you setup the development environment and reach the integrated terminal inside VS Code, you are already in the right place. The shell running there is the same shell described in this primer. Every command here works exactly the same inside that terminal as it would in a standalone terminal application.

The Project
What You Are Building
The capstone of this course is a simulated scalable web system built by your team over six weeks. The system is a simulation: its data is synthetic, its latency is injected, its failures are scripted, and its computation is modeled. This is a deliberate design choice, not a shortcut. A production system built from scratch in six weeks is not realistic, and that is not the goal. The goal is design, engineering, and measurement. Simulation lets your team practice every pattern covered in the course, break the system intentionally, and measure it under realistic load, without the operational complexity of real data pipelines or live traffic.

Every pattern you study in the units is first presented as a simulation. By the time you reach the project, you will know exactly how to model latency, inject failures, and observe behavior, because the units showed you how. The project is where those techniques are applied to a coherent system of your team's own design.

Computing for the Common Good
Your project domain must serve a real community or address a genuine societal need. This is not a theme layer on top of the technical work; it shapes what services exist, what the latency and reliability requirements mean, and who is affected when the system fails. A system that routes community food pantry inventory across multiple locations has different failure consequences than one that serves movie recommendations, and reasoning about those consequences is part of the design work.

Domains that fit this framing include, for example: a public health outbreak alert and notification service; a community library catalog with digital resource lending; a municipal transit real-time information and disruption alert system; an emergency shelter capacity and resource tracking system; or a neighborhood mutual aid request coordination platform. Domains that do not fit include commercial recommendation engines, advertising platforms, social media analytics, or entertainment applications.

When choosing a domain, ask: who benefits if this system is reliable and fast, and who is harmed when it is not? If the answer involves a specific real community, you are in the right territory.

What the System Must Demonstrate
Every project, regardless of domain, must demonstrate the following:

Reliability: Services have health check endpoints. The system can recover from at least one scripted failure scenario.
Latency: At least one service path is measured under load with k6. Results are reported as p50, p95, and p99 percentiles.
Resiliency: The system handles at least one simulated failure (a slow service, a crashing service, or a queue backlog) without total collapse.
Observability: At least two services expose Prometheus metrics. A Grafana dashboard displays request rate, error rate, and p95 latency. At least one service writes structured log output.
Patterns: The system must implement patterns covered in the course across its services. [TBD: minimum required pattern list and count]
Technical Constraints
The same constraints that apply to the course units apply to the project:

JavaScript only, using the course subset: arrow functions, no classes, ES6 modules, functional iteration preferred.
All services and infrastructure are orchestrated with Docker Compose. The entire system must start with a single docker compose up command.
Services are written in Node.js with Express for HTTP.
Load testing uses k6. Caching and async processing use Redis. Reverse proxying and load balancing use Caddy.
No new tools may be introduced unless approved in advance.
Team Structure
Teams are assigned by the instructor. Team size depends on the course version: 2–3 members in the 6-week summer or winter version, 3–7 members in the 13-week regular semester. Each team targets one custom service per team member plus one shared service (team_size + 1, minimum 3): a 2-person summer team targets 3 services; a 3-person team targets 4; a 5-person semester team targets 6. Infrastructure containers (Caddy, Redis, Prometheus, Grafana) do not count. Services are added incrementally: 2 in Sprint 2, at least one more in Sprint 4, reaching the full target by Sprint 5.

Each team member is expected to contribute meaningfully and independently. Contribution is assessed from objective GitHub evidence: commits, pull requests authored and reviewed, and merge history. Homework 1: A Reliable Request Handler
Overview
In this assignment you will build a small HTTP service that ties together the three concepts from Week 1: a concurrency-safe shared counter (Unit 1), measured with k6 (Unit 2), and an idempotent transaction endpoint (Unit 3). The service uses only Express; no other libraries are needed.

When you are done you will have one server file, one load test file, and hands-on evidence that the patterns from class work the way the notes described.

Setup
Inside your Gantry devcontainer, create a working directory for this homework:

mkdir hw01 && cd hw01
npm init -y
npm pkg set type=module
npm install express
You will create two files: server.js and loadtest.js.

Part 1: The Counter Service
Your server must expose three endpoints for a shared in-memory counter.

GET /counter
Returns the current counter value.

200 OK
{ "count": 7 }
POST /increment
Increments the counter by one and returns the new value. This endpoint must simulate a brief async operation (5 ms) to model real-world work such as a database write. Use the createLock helper from Unit 1 to protect the read-delay-write sequence from concurrent interleaving.

200 OK
{ "count": 8 }
POST /reset
Resets the counter to zero and returns the new value.

200 OK
{ "count": 0 }
You'll know it works when: running 20 concurrent POST /increment requests (after a reset) and then GET /counter always returns { "count": 20 }.

Part 2: The Transaction Service
Your server must also expose two endpoints for idempotent transaction recording, using the pattern from Unit 3.

POST /transaction
Records a transaction. The client must include an Idempotency-Key header with a unique string. The request body must include an amount field (a number).

First call with a given key:

200 OK
{ "id": "order-001", "amount": 50, "duplicate": false }
Repeat call with the same key (any body):

200 OK
{ "id": "order-001", "amount": 50, "duplicate": true }
Missing Idempotency-Key header:

400 Bad Request
{ "error": "Idempotency-Key header is required" }
GET /transactions
Returns all recorded transactions (one entry per unique key, regardless of how many times each key was submitted).

200 OK
{ "transactions": [ { "id": "order-001", "amount": 50 }, ... ] }
You'll know it works when: submitting the same key three times and then GET /transactions returns exactly one entry for that key.

Part 3: Load Testing with k6
Create loadtest.js. It should test the /increment endpoint with 10 virtual users running for 10 seconds, and define thresholds that require:

95th-percentile response time under 200 ms
Error rate under 1%
Run the test while your server is running:

node server.js &
k6 run loadtest.js
Watch the http_req_duration output. Compare the p50 and p95 values to what you computed by hand in Unit 2.

You'll know it works when: k6 exits with all thresholds shown as passing (green checkmarks).

Testing your work locally
Start your server in one terminal:

node server.js
In another terminal, run a few manual checks:

# Counter should start at 0
curl http://localhost:3000/counter

# Increment a few times
curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/increment
curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/increment

# Record a transaction
curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/transaction \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Idempotency-Key: order-001" \
  -d '{"amount": 50}'

# Retry same key — should return duplicate: true
curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/transaction \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Idempotency-Key: order-001" \
  -d '{"amount": 50}'

# Verify only one entry
curl http://localhost:3000/transactions
Submission
Submit a zip file containing exactly these three files (no subdirectories):

server.js
loadtest.js
package.json
From inside your hw01 directory, create the zip:

zip hw01.zip server.js loadtest.js package.json
Upload hw01.zip to Gradescope. The autograder will install your dependencies, start your server on port 3000, and run tests against it. It will also run your loadtest.js with k6.

Add this to the context Unit 04: Docker Fundamentals
Introduction
Chapter 1 of the textbook positions containers as the foundational technology that makes distributed system patterns possible. Before containers, the patterns the book describes existed as ideas but not as reusable, portable artifacts: you could implement a sidecar in code, but the deployment unit was just "some process" that had to be configured, versioned, and reproduced by hand on every machine it ran on. Containers changed that. When a service and everything it depends on are packaged into a single image, you have something that runs identically anywhere Docker is installed, that can be composed with other services by name, and that other teams can depend on without knowing what it is built from.

Units 1 through 3 covered the logical challenges of distributed services: concurrency, measurement, and safe retries. Before any of those patterns can run in production, each service needs to be packaged as an image. A Node.js server that works on your machine may fail on a teammate's machine, in CI, or in production, because none of its dependencies are written down anywhere. This unit fixes that. You will write a Dockerfile, build it into an image, and run it as a container. By the end, those words stop being vocabulary and become two specific things you watched happen.

Before You Start
Read: Docker's overview of images and containers — https://docs.docker.com/get-started/docker-overview/Links to an external site.
References
Dockerfile reference — https://docs.docker.com/engine/reference/builder/Links to an external site.
docker build — https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/image/build/Links to an external site.
docker run — https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/container/run/Links to an external site.
docker ps / docker logs / docker rm — https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/container/Links to an external site.
Notes
The starting problem
Here's a tiny web server.

// server.js
import http from 'node:http';

http.createServer((req, res) => {
  res.writeHead(200, { 'Content-Type': 'text/plain' });
  res.end('Hello from a plain Node process\n');
}).listen(3000, () => console.log('Listening on port 3000'));
You also need a package.json so Node treats the file as an ES module:

{
  "type": "module"
}
Run it with node server.js, then visit localhost:3000 or run curl localhost:3000. It works, but notice everything it's quietly depending on: this exact machine has Node installed, at some version, with nothing else conflicting. None of that is written down anywhere. If you sent server.js to a teammate, it would either work by luck or fail in some way that has nothing to do with the code itself.

Extending the example
Write down exactly what this code needs to run, in a file called a Dockerfile, then build that description into an image.

# Dockerfile
FROM node:24
WORKDIR /usr/src/app
COPY . .
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
Each line does one specific thing. FROM node:24 starts from a base image that already has Node 24 installed. WORKDIR sets the directory inside the image where the following commands run. COPY . . brings everything from your current directory into the image. EXPOSE documents which port the container expects to be reached on. CMD is the command that runs when a container starts from this image.

Build it, then run it:

docker build -t hello-server .
docker run -p 3000:3000 hello-server
docker build reads the Dockerfile and produces an image named hello-server. docker run starts a container — a running instance of that image — and -p 3000:3000 connects port 3000 on your machine to port 3000 inside the container. Visit localhost:3000 again. Same response as before, but now it's coming from inside an isolated container built from a file that says exactly what it needs.

Managing containers and images
docker run blocks your terminal because the container's output goes there. To start a container in the background, add -d (detached mode). Give it a name with --name so you can refer to it by something other than its ID:

docker run -d --name my-server -p 3000:3000 hello-server
Check what's running:

docker ps
docker ps lists every running container: its ID, image, when it started, and the port mapping. To include containers that have stopped, use docker ps -a.

To see the output from a detached container:

docker logs my-server
When you're done, stop the container and remove it:

docker stop my-server
docker rm my-server
docker stop sends a signal that gives the process a moment to shut down cleanly. docker rm removes the stopped container — until you do this, the container still exists on disk (visible in docker ps -a) even after it stops. To skip the two steps, docker rm -f my-server stops and removes in one command.

Images accumulate too. To see what images are installed on your machine:

docker images
To remove an image (only works if no containers — running or stopped — are using it):

docker rmi hello-server
To remove all unused images at once:

docker image prune
Naming the pattern
An image is a packaged, read-only blueprint: your code plus everything it depends on to run, frozen into a single artifact. A container is a running instance of that image, the way a process is a running instance of a program. You can start several containers from the same image at once, and they won't interfere with each other — each one gets its own isolated filesystem and process space.

The Dockerfile is the recipe that produces the image, and each instruction in it becomes a layer that Docker can cache. That's why rebuilding an image after a small code change is usually much faster than the first build: Docker reuses unchanged layers and only reruns the steps that changed.

Two things worth keeping straight: EXPOSE just documents intent inside the Dockerfile. The -p flag on docker run is what actually connects a port on your machine to a port inside the running container. EXPOSE without -p doesn't open anything.

This is the foundation everything from Unit 6 onward sits on top of. Multi-container patterns — sidecars, proxies, workers — are just multiple containers, each one a running instance of some image, deliberately sharing a little while staying isolated in every other way.

Exercise
Task: Make the port configurable without rebuilding the image. Update server.js to read the port from process.env.PORT, defaulting to 3000 if it isn't set. Then run two containers from the same image at once, on two different host ports.

Starting point: server.js and Dockerfile from the Notes above.

You'll know it works when:

docker run -d --name server-3000 -e PORT=3000 -p 3000:3000 hello-server
docker run -d --name server-3001 -e PORT=3001 -p 3001:3001 hello-server
docker ps — both containers are listed as running
docker logs server-3000 — shows "Listening on port 3000"
docker logs server-3001 — shows "Listening on port 3001"
curl localhost:3000 and curl localhost:3001 both return a response
Cleanup: docker stop server-3000 server-3001 then docker rm server-3000 server-3001
Real World
Most Node.js projects have npm dependencies. That changes the Dockerfile in one important way: you need to install them inside the image before copying your source code.

Create an Express app:

// server.js
import express from 'express';

const app = express();
const port = process.env.PORT || 3000;

app.get('/', (req, res) => {
  res.send('Hello from Express in a container\n');
});

app.listen(port, () => console.log(`Listening on port ${port}`));
{
  "type": "module",
  "dependencies": {
    "express": "^4.18.0"
  }
}
Run npm install once locally to generate package-lock.json. Then write the Dockerfile:

FROM node:24
WORKDIR /usr/src/app
COPY package*.json .
RUN npm install
COPY . .
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
The key change is the order: copy package*.json first, run npm install, then copy the rest of the source. Docker caches each layer — so as long as package.json doesn't change, npm install is skipped on every subsequent rebuild. If you copied everything first and then ran npm install, any change to any file would invalidate the install layer and force a full reinstall.

Add a .dockerignore file to prevent the local node_modules from being copied into the image (which would overwrite what npm install just put there):

node_modules
Build and run:

npm install
docker build -t hello-express .
docker run -p 3000:3000 hello-express
curl localhost:3000 returns the response from Express running inside the container. The image contains Node, Express, and your code — nothing else — and it will run identically anywhere Docker is installed.

Home Exercise
Task: Make the greeting in the Express app configurable without rebuilding the image. Read a GREETING environment variable (defaulting to Hello) and include it in the response. Run the same image twice with different greetings.

Starting point: The Express app from the Real World section above.

You'll know it works when:

docker run -e GREETING=Hello -p 3000:3000 hello-express
docker run -e GREETING=Hola -p 3001:3000 hello-express
produces different responses:

curl localhost:3000   # Hello from Express in a container
curl localhost:3001   # Hola from Express in a container
Looking Ahead

Introduction
Chapter 2 of the textbook introduces the idea of an orchestrator: a system responsible for taking a declared desired state and ensuring the real state of the application matches it. In production, that role is played by Kubernetes. At the scale of a single developer or a small team, Docker Compose fills the same conceptual role. Instead of a sequence of imperative commands that must be typed in the right order with the right flags every time, Compose lets you declare what containers you want, how they are connected, and what volumes they share, then brings the whole arrangement up or down with a single command.

Unit 4 built one container from a Dockerfile and ran it with docker run. The moment you need two containers sharing a volume, that one command becomes four, each one with flags that must match exactly, in the right order, every time you want to bring the system up. This unit introduces Compose as the tool that replaces that sequence with a file you can read, share, and check into version control. Every multi-container setup from Unit 6 onward will be expressed as a docker-compose.yml, so the goal here is to make that format completely familiar before the patterns begin.

Before You Start
Read: Docker's Compose overview — https://docs.docker.com/compose/Links to an external site.
References
Compose file reference — https://docs.docker.com/reference/compose-file/Links to an external site.
docker compose CLI — https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/compose/Links to an external site.
Named volumes — https://docs.docker.com/engine/storage/volumes/Links to an external site.
Notes
The starting problem
Here are two small scripts. One writes a timestamp to a shared file every five seconds. The other serves whatever is currently in that file over HTTP.

// writer.js
import fs from 'node:fs';

setInterval(() => {
  fs.writeFileSync(
    '/data/message.txt',
    `Last updated: ${new Date().toISOString()}\n`,
  );
}, 5000);
// reader-server.js
import http from 'node:http';
import fs from 'node:fs';

http.createServer((req, res) => {
  const message = fs.existsSync('/data/message.txt')
    ? fs.readFileSync('/data/message.txt', 'utf8')
    : 'no data yet\n';
  res.writeHead(200, { 'Content-Type': 'text/plain' });
  res.end(message);
}).listen(3000, () => console.log('Listening on port 3000'));
Using what you learned in Unit 4, running both of these as containers that share a volume takes a sequence like this:

docker build -t demo-app .
docker volume create shared-data
docker run -d --name writer -v shared-data:/data demo-app node writer.js
docker run -d --name reader -p 3000:3000 -v shared-data:/data demo-app node reader-server.js
That's already four commands, each one easy to get slightly wrong, and you'd have to remember this exact sequence, in this exact order, every single time you wanted to bring this up again. Tearing it down means stopping and removing two containers and a volume by hand too.

Extending the example
Describe the same two containers and the volume they share in a single file instead.

# docker-compose.yml
services:
  writer:
    build: .
    command: node writer.js
    volumes:
      - shared-data:/data

  reader:
    build: .
    command: node reader-server.js
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
    volumes:
      - shared-data:/data

volumes:
  shared-data:
Now bring both containers up with one command:

docker compose up
Visit localhost:3000 a few times over thirty seconds and watch the timestamp update. When you're done, docker compose down removes both containers and cleans up after itself. Same two containers, same shared volume, same result as the four commands above — but now the whole arrangement lives in a file you can read top to bottom, hand to a teammate, and check into version control.

You also need a Dockerfile so Compose knows how to build the image:

FROM node:24
WORKDIR /usr/src/app
COPY . .
There's no CMD here — each service in docker-compose.yml provides its own command, so the Dockerfile just handles the image and leaves the command to Compose.

Managing a Compose project
docker compose up runs in the foreground — all service output streams to your terminal. To start in the background instead, add -d:

docker compose up -d
Check the status of every service in the project:

docker compose ps
To stream logs as they arrive:

docker compose logs -f           # all services
docker compose logs -f writer    # one service only
To restart a single service without touching the others:

docker compose restart writer
To stop all services without removing the containers:

docker compose stop
docker compose down goes further — it stops and removes all containers. By default it leaves named volumes alone. To remove volumes too and wipe all stored data:

docker compose down --volumes
To open a shell inside a running service for debugging:

docker compose exec reader sh
Naming the pattern
docker-compose.yml is a declarative description of a multi-container application. Each entry under services is one container's blueprint: where to build it from, what command to run, which ports to expose, which volumes to mount. A named volume like shared-data is declared once under volumes and referenced by any service that needs it — which is how two otherwise unrelated containers end up sharing the same files.

Compose itself isn't a new pattern. It's a tool for describing an arrangement of containers that you've already decided on, the same way a recipe describes a dish without being the dish. The patterns themselves — sidecar, ambassador, and the ones still ahead — are about why containers are arranged a certain way. Compose is just how that arrangement gets written down in one place instead of typed by hand every time.

From Unit 6 onward, every multi-container example in this course will be expressed as a docker-compose.yml.

Exercise
Task: Add a third service, logger, that prints the contents of /data/message.txt to its own console every five seconds. It reuses the same image as the other two services, but with a different command. It shares the shared-data volume but doesn't expose any port — it only reads from the shared file and logs to its own console.

// logger.js
import fs from 'node:fs';

setInterval(() => {
  const message = fs.existsSync('/data/message.txt')
    ? fs.readFileSync('/data/message.txt', 'utf8')
    : 'no data yet';
  console.log(message.trim());
}, 5000);
Starting point: The docker-compose.yml and Dockerfile from the Notes above, plus the logger.js file. Add a logger service to docker-compose.yml.

You'll know it works when:

docker compose up -d --build
docker compose ps — all three services listed as running
docker compose logs logger — shows the same timestamp the reader is serving over HTTP, updating every five seconds
curl localhost:3000 — the reader responds with that same timestamp
Cleanup: docker compose down
Real World
Volume sharing is one way containers cooperate. Another is the network: every service in a Compose project can reach every other service by its service name as a hostname.

Here's a two-service example. One service generates data; the other fetches from it and serves it externally.

// data.js — internal service, port 3001, not exposed to the host
import http from 'node:http';

http.createServer((req, res) => {
  res.writeHead(200, { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' });
  res.end(JSON.stringify({ message: 'data from internal service', timestamp: new Date().toISOString() }));
}).listen(3001, () => console.log('Data service on port 3001'));
// app.js — calls data by service name, serves on port 3000
import http from 'node:http';

http.createServer(async (req, res) => {
  const response = await fetch('http://data:3001/');
  const body = await response.json();
  res.writeHead(200, { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' });
  res.end(JSON.stringify(body));
}).listen(3000, () => console.log('App on port 3000'));
The URL http://data:3001/ uses the service name data as the hostname. Docker Compose creates a private network for the project and registers each service's name as a DNS entry on that network. No IP addresses, no service discovery configuration — just service names.

# docker-compose.yml
services:
  app:
    build: .
    command: node app.js
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
    depends_on:
      - data

  data:
    build: .
    command: node data.js
depends_on: data tells Compose to start the data container before starting app. The data service has no ports: entry — it's internal to the Compose network. Nothing on your host machine can reach it directly; only app can.

Run it:

docker compose up --build
curl localhost:3000
curl localhost:3000 hits the app container, which calls http://data:3001/ on the internal network, gets a response, and forwards it. The data service is invisible to the outside world.

Home Exercise
Task: Make the data service's message configurable without rebuilding the image. Read process.env.DATA_MESSAGE in data.js (defaulting to 'data from internal service') and set the value in docker-compose.yml using the environment: key.

Starting point: The two-service Compose setup from the Real World section above.

You'll know it works when: Running docker compose up --build followed by curl localhost:3000 returns your configured message — and changing the value in docker-compose.yml and restarting with docker compose up changes the response without rebuilding the image.

Looking Ahead
With a Dockerfile and a Compose file both behind you, Unit 6's sidecar example uses exactly these two tools to add a capability to a service without changing the service's own code.

Overview
In this assignment you will build a small multi-container system that ties together the four concepts from Week 2: containerizing a service (Unit 4), orchestrating multiple containers with Docker Compose (Unit 5), the sidecar pattern (Unit 6), and the ambassador pattern (Unit 7). The system uses only Express; no other libraries are needed.

This assignment is framed around real marine science: at the Marine Biological Laboratory in Woods Hole, Massachusetts, Associate Scientist Loretta Roberson researches large-scale offshore seaweed farming as a source of sustainable biomass, aimed at bioremediation and at protecting sensitive ecosystems like coral reefs. She leads a DOE ARPA-E-funded initiative farming tropical seaweed off Puerto Rico and works on refining Sargassum into an alternative biomass feedstock. A real deployment of that kind of research depends on exactly the kind of system you will build here: a network of monitoring stations, one per farm site, coordinated and routed reliably enough that no single site's software has to know about the others.

When you are done you will have one shared Docker image, one docker-compose.yml, and four small service files (a farm-monitoring service, a regional-aggregator sidecar, a routing ambassador, and a buoy gateway) — hands-on evidence that the patterns from class compose together into a real distributed system.

Setup
Inside your Gantry devcontainer, create a working directory for this homework:

mkdir hw02 && cd hw02
npm init -y
npm pkg set type=module
npm install express
You will create seven files: farm-service.js, sidecar-sync.js, ambassador.js, buoy-gateway.js, Dockerfile, .dockerignore, and docker-compose.yml.

Part 1: Containerizing a Farm Site (Unit 4)
Your farm monitoring service represents one offshore farm site. It must expose two endpoints, and be entirely configured through environment variables so the same image can run as any farm site.

Environment variables
PORT — port to listen on
FARM_ID — this farm's identifier (e.g. farm-a)
DATA_DIR — directory to persist readings to (default ./data)
CALIBRATION — sensor calibration version (default v1)
GET /status
Returns the farm's identity and every reading recorded so far.

200 OK
{ "farmId": "farm-a", "calibration": "v1", "readings": [] }
POST /reading
Records a sensor reading. The request body must include metric (a string, e.g. "growthRateCm") and value (a number). Appends the reading (with a server-generated timestamp) to an in-memory array and to ${DATA_DIR}/readings.json.

200 OK
{ "farmId": "farm-a", "calibration": "v1", "count": 1, "latest": { "metric": "growthRateCm", "value": 2.4, "timestamp": "2026-07-10T12:00:00.000Z" } }
The Dockerfile
Write a Dockerfile that builds an image any farm site can run from:

FROM node:24 (or a version you have installed)
WORKDIR set to your app directory
Copy package*.json first and run npm install, then copy the rest of your source — in that order, so Docker only reinstalls dependencies when package.json actually changes
EXPOSE the port your service listens on
A default CMD that starts farm-service.js
Add a .dockerignore that excludes node_modules.

You'll know it works when: running

docker build -t seagrid .
docker run -e FARM_ID=farm-a -p 3000:3000 seagrid
and then curl http://localhost:3000/status returns { "farmId": "farm-a", "calibration": "v1", "readings": [] }.

Part 2: Orchestrating the Farm Network (Unit 5)
Write a docker-compose.yml that runs the whole farm network as one system:

farm-a, farm-b, farm-c — three farm-service instances, each built from the same image, each with its own FARM_ID and DATA_DIR, each mapped to its own host port
farm-a-v2 — a fourth farm-service instance with FARM_ID=farm-a, a separate DATA_DIR, and CALIBRATION=v2 — a calibration trial running alongside farm-a itself
A single named volume mounted into every farm service (all four) so their data directories persist and can be read by the sidecar you will add in Part 3
You'll know it works when: running docker compose up --build starts all four farm containers, each independently reachable on its own host port, and a reading posted to farm-a never appears when you GET /status on farm-b or farm-c.

Part 3: The Regional Aggregator Sidecar (Unit 6)
Add sidecar-sync.js: a background process with no HTTP server of its own, that periodically reads every farm's readings.json from the shared volume and writes a rolled-up summary — without farm-service.js ever knowing it exists.

Environment variables
DATA_ROOT — the shared volume's mount path
FARM_IDS — comma-separated list of farm ids to summarize (e.g. farm-a,farm-b,farm-c)
SYNC_INTERVAL_MS — how often to re-read and rewrite the summary (default 5000)
Behavior
On every interval tick, for each farm id in FARM_IDS, read ${DATA_ROOT}/<farmId>/readings.json (treat a missing file as zero readings), then write ${DATA_ROOT}/regional-summary.json:

{
  "generatedAt": "2026-07-10T12:00:05.000Z",
  "farms": {
    "farm-a": { "count": 3, "avgValue": 2.1 },
    "farm-b": { "count": 1, "avgValue": 4.0 }
  },
  "regionalAvgValue": 2.35
}
regionalAvgValue is the mean of every reading from every farm pooled together — not the mean of the per-farm averages. (With farm-a's three readings averaging 2.1 and farm-b's one reading at 4.0, the pooled mean of all four numbers — not the average of 2.1 and 4.0 — is what belongs here.)

Add sidecar as a service in your docker-compose.yml, sharing the same named volume, with depends_on on the three farms.

You'll know it works when: after posting a few readings to two or more farms and waiting one sync interval, docker compose exec sidecar cat /data/regional-summary.json shows the correct per-farm count and avgValue, and a regionalAvgValue that matches the pooled-mean formula above.

Part 4: The Ambassador (Unit 7)
Add two more files:

buoy-gateway.js — the primary service a real buoy would talk to. Exposes POST /submit-reading (body: { "farmId", "metric", "value" }) and forwards it verbatim to a fixed AMBASSADOR_URL. It contains no routing logic of its own — it always calls the same local address, the same way Unit 7's own primary service did.
ambassador.js — shares buoy-gateway's network namespace (via network_mode: "service:buoy-gateway" in Compose) and makes the actual routing decision on buoy-gateway's behalf.
ambassador.js: POST /reading
Body: { "farmId", "metric", "value" }.

Unknown farmId → 404 { "error": "unknown farmId: farm-x" }
farmId === "farm-b" or "farm-c" → forwarded to that farm's fixed URL every time
farmId === "farm-a" → forwarded to farm-a-v2 roughly CANARY_PERCENT percent of the time (default 20), and to farm-a the rest of the time — a canary trial of the new calibration
Response (whichever farm actually handled it):

200 OK
{ "routedTo": "farm-a", "farmResponse": { "farmId": "farm-a", "calibration": "v1", "count": 1, "latest": { "metric": "growthRateCm", "value": 2.0, "timestamp": "2026-07-10T12:00:00.000Z" } } }
buoy-gateway.js: POST /submit-reading
Forwards the request body to ${AMBASSADOR_URL}/reading and returns:

200 OK
{ "receivedBy": "buoy-gateway", "routedTo": "farm-a", "farmResponse": { "...": "..." } }
Wiring it in docker-compose.yml
Add buoy-gateway and ambassador services. The ambassador must not declare its own ports: — network_mode: "service:buoy-gateway" and ports: cannot be used together on the same service; Compose will reject it. Expose the port through buoy-gateway instead.

You'll know it works when:

Repeatedly submitting readings for farm-b or farm-c always routes to that same farm.
Submitting around 100 readings for farm-a results in roughly 10-30 of them landing on farm-a-v2 (check GET /status on each afterward) — not exactly 20 every time, but in that range.
Testing your work locally
Start the whole system:

docker compose up --build
In another terminal:

# Submit a reading through the full path: buoy-gateway -> ambassador -> farm-b
curl -X POST http://localhost:4000/submit-reading \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"farmId": "farm-b", "metric": "growthRateCm", "value": 3.1}'

# Confirm it landed on farm-b specifically
curl http://localhost:3002/status

# Send 100 farm-a readings and see how the count splits across calibrations
for i in $(seq 1 100); do
  curl -s -X POST http://localhost:4000/submit-reading \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d '{"farmId": "farm-a", "metric": "growthRateCm", "value": 2.0}' > /dev/null
done
curl -s http://localhost:3001/status | grep -o '"count":[0-9]*'
curl -s http://localhost:3004/status | grep -o '"count":[0-9]*'

# Check the sidecar's regional summary
docker compose exec sidecar cat /data/regional-summary.json

# Austin's Global Development Environment

## Package Management

- Prefer `uv` for Python projects.
- Never use `pip install` directly unless explicitly required.
- Use:

```bash
uv venv
uv sync
uv add <package>
uv run python file.py
```

## Python

- Prefer Python 3.12+
- Use virtual environments for every project.
- Do not install project dependencies globally.

## JavaScript

- Prefer `pnpm` over npm.
- Use existing project package manager if already configured.

## Git

- Use git worktrees when appropriate.
- Never commit secrets.
- Show a diff summary before large changes.

## Terminal Tools

Prefer the following tools when available:

- rg (ripgrep) instead of grep
- fd instead of find
- jq for JSON processing
- tree for directory visualization

## Remote Development

- Assume this machine is accessed remotely via SSH.
- Long running processes should be run inside tmux.
- Create or reuse tmux sessions for multi-step workflows.

## Docker

- Prefer Docker Compose when multiple services are involved.
- Do not install databases directly on the host machine unless requested.

## Agent/Model Usage Guidelines

- GPT models are the orchestrators: use them for planning, coordination, trusted full-feature work, and final decision-making.
- OpenRouter models are for very simple coding tasks or small refactors. Keep their tasks narrow and low-risk.
- DeepSeek models are worker models for harder implementation that needs more reasoning, especially parallel feature work. Still give DeepSeek explicit, well-defined tasks, scope, acceptance criteria, and instructions.
- Reviewer role: prefer GPT. DeepSeek R1/R-series style reasoning models can also work as reviewers when GPT is not available or cost needs to be lower.
- Full feature work can be done by GPT 5.4 or GPT 5.5 low for cheaper execution. Optimize prompts/tasks for cost, but these models can be trusted more than cheaper worker models.

## Development Philosophy

- Keep solutions simple.
- Prefer maintainability over cleverness.
- Minimize dependencies.
- Explain tradeoffs when introducing infrastructure.

## Machine Purpose

This machine is a persistent development workstation used for:

- ML experimentation
- Optimization projects
- Full-stack applications
- Long-running Codex sessions
- Data processing

Treat it as a desktop-first machine with always-on capabilities, not as a dedicated server.

# COMPSCI 426 Agent Instructions

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

topic="${1:-session}"
source_file="${2:-}"
safe_topic="$(printf '%s' "$topic" | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]' | tr -cs 'a-z0-9._-' '-' | sed 's/^-//; s/-$//')"
if [ -z "$safe_topic" ]; then
  safe_topic="session"
fi

mkdir -p ai/chats
stamp="$(date '+%Y-%m-%d-%H%M%S')"
out="ai/chats/${stamp}-${safe_topic}.jsonl"

find_latest_codex_session() {
  local sessions_root="${CODEX_HOME:-$HOME/.codex}/sessions"
  if [ ! -d "$sessions_root" ]; then
    return 1
  fi

  find "$sessions_root" -type f -name '*.jsonl' -print0 2>/dev/null \
    | xargs -0 ls -t 2>/dev/null \
    | while IFS= read -r candidate; do
        if grep -Fq "\"cwd\":\"$PWD\"" "$candidate"; then
          printf '%s\n' "$candidate"
          return 0
        fi
      done
}

if [ -n "$source_file" ]; then
  cp "$source_file" "$out"
elif [ -t 0 ]; then
  latest_session="$(find_latest_codex_session || true)"
  if [ -z "${latest_session:-}" ]; then
    {
      echo "No Codex JSONL session log found for $PWD."
      echo "Pass the raw session log explicitly:"
      echo "  scripts/save-chat.sh \"$topic\" ~/.codex/sessions/YYYY/MM/DD/rollout-...jsonl"
    } >&2
    exit 1
  fi
  cp "$latest_session" "$out"
else
  tee "$out" >/dev/null
fi

printf '%s\n' "$out"
# Homework 2 Summary: The Seaweed Farm Monitoring Network

Use this summary when implementing, testing, packaging, or reviewing Homework 2.
Open `source.md` for exact assignment wording, response shapes, and commands.

## Objective

Build a multi-container Express system combining Week 2 concepts:

- Unit 4: containerizing services with a Dockerfile.
- Unit 5: orchestrating services with Docker Compose.
- Unit 6: regional aggregator sidecar using a shared volume.
- Unit 7: routing ambassador with canary behavior.

Only Express is needed; no other libraries.

## Required Files

Inside `hw02/`, create exactly:

- `farm-service.js`
- `sidecar-sync.js`
- `ambassador.js`
- `buoy-gateway.js`
- `Dockerfile`
- `.dockerignore`
- `docker-compose.yml`
- `package.json`

Submission zip must contain exactly these files and no subdirectories.

## Setup

Run inside the Gantry devcontainer:

```bash
mkdir hw02 && cd hw02
npm init -y
npm pkg set type=module
npm install express
```

## Part 1: Farm Service

`farm-service.js` represents one offshore farm site. It must be configured only
through environment variables so one image can run any farm.

Environment variables:

- `PORT`: port to listen on.
- `FARM_ID`: farm identifier, e.g. `farm-a`.
- `DATA_DIR`: directory to persist readings, default `./data`.
- `CALIBRATION`: sensor calibration version, default `v1`.

Endpoints:

- `GET /status`: returns `{ "farmId", "calibration", "readings" }`.
- `POST /reading`: body must include string `metric` and number `value`.

`POST /reading` must:

- generate a server timestamp
- append reading to in-memory array
- persist readings to `${DATA_DIR}/readings.json`
- return `{ farmId, calibration, count, latest }`

Dockerfile requirements:

- `FROM node:24` or installed Node version.
- Set `WORKDIR`.
- Copy `package*.json` first, run `npm install`, then copy source.
- `EXPOSE` service port.
- Default `CMD` starts `farm-service.js`.

`.dockerignore` must exclude `node_modules`.

## Part 2: Compose Farm Network

`docker-compose.yml` must run:

- `farm-a`
- `farm-b`
- `farm-c`
- `farm-a-v2`

All four are farm-service instances built from the same image.

Requirements:

- Each has its own `FARM_ID` and `DATA_DIR`.
- Each maps to its own host port.
- `farm-a-v2` uses `FARM_ID=farm-a`, separate `DATA_DIR`, and
  `CALIBRATION=v2`.
- A single named volume is mounted into every farm service so farm data persists
  and the sidecar can read it.

Success:

- `docker compose up --build` starts all four farms.
- Each farm is reachable on its own host port.
- Readings posted to one farm do not appear in another farm's `/status`.

## Part 3: Regional Aggregator Sidecar

`sidecar-sync.js` is a background process with no HTTP server.

Environment variables:

- `DATA_ROOT`: shared volume mount path.
- `FARM_IDS`: comma-separated farm IDs, e.g. `farm-a,farm-b,farm-c`.
- `SYNC_INTERVAL_MS`: sync interval, default `5000`.

Behavior on each interval:

- For each farm ID, read `${DATA_ROOT}/<farmId>/readings.json`.
- Missing file means zero readings.
- Write `${DATA_ROOT}/regional-summary.json`.

Summary shape:

```json
{
  "generatedAt": "2026-07-10T12:00:05.000Z",
  "farms": {
    "farm-a": { "count": 3, "avgValue": 2.1 },
    "farm-b": { "count": 1, "avgValue": 4.0 }
  },
  "regionalAvgValue": 2.35
}
```

Important formula:

- `regionalAvgValue` is the pooled mean of every reading across farms.
- It is not the mean of per-farm averages.

Compose:

- Add `sidecar` service.
- Mount same named volume.
- `depends_on` the three farms.

Success:

- After readings and one sync interval,
  `docker compose exec sidecar cat /data/regional-summary.json` has correct
  counts, per-farm averages, and pooled regional average.

## Part 4: Ambassador and Buoy Gateway

Files:

- `buoy-gateway.js`: primary service real buoys call.
- `ambassador.js`: routing proxy sharing buoy-gateway network namespace.

`buoy-gateway.js`:

- exposes `POST /submit-reading`
- body: `{ "farmId", "metric", "value" }`
- forwards body to `${AMBASSADOR_URL}/reading`
- contains no routing logic
- returns `{ "receivedBy": "buoy-gateway", "routedTo", "farmResponse" }`

`ambassador.js`:

- exposes `POST /reading`
- body: `{ "farmId", "metric", "value" }`
- unknown farm: `404 { "error": "unknown farmId: farm-x" }`
- `farm-b` and `farm-c`: always forward to fixed farm URL
- `farm-a`: route to `farm-a-v2` roughly `CANARY_PERCENT` percent of the time,
  default 20; otherwise route to `farm-a`
- returns `{ "routedTo", "farmResponse" }`

Compose:

- Add `buoy-gateway` and `ambassador`.
- Ambassador must use `network_mode: "service:buoy-gateway"`.
- Ambassador must not declare `ports:`.
- Expose the ambassador path through `buoy-gateway` instead.

Success:

- farm-b/farm-c readings always route to that farm.
- Around 100 farm-a readings produce roughly 10-30 on `farm-a-v2`.

## Local Test Commands

Start:

```bash
docker compose up --build
```

Submit through full path:

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:4000/submit-reading \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"farmId": "farm-b", "metric": "growthRateCm", "value": 3.1}'
```

Check sidecar:

```bash
docker compose exec sidecar cat /data/regional-summary.json
```

## Submission

From inside `hw02/`:

```bash
zip hw02.zip Dockerfile .dockerignore docker-compose.yml farm-service.js sidecar-sync.js ambassador.js buoy-gateway.js package.json
```

Upload `hw02.zip` to Gradescope.

## Implementation Priorities

- Match endpoint names and JSON shapes exactly.
- Use only Express.
- Keep all farm behavior environment-driven.
- Persist each farm's readings in its own subdirectory under the shared volume.
- Compute regional average as pooled average.
- Keep buoy gateway routing-free; put routing/canary in ambassador.
- Do not put `ports:` on the ambassador service when using
  `network_mode: "service:buoy-gateway"`.

# Homework 2: The Seaweed Farm Monitoring Network

Source: COMPSCI 426 Canvas assignment pasted by the user.

## Overview

In this assignment you will build a small multi-container system that ties together the four concepts from Week 2: containerizing a service (Unit 4), orchestrating multiple containers with Docker Compose (Unit 5), the sidecar pattern (Unit 6), and the ambassador pattern (Unit 7). The system uses only Express; no other libraries are needed.

This assignment is framed around real marine science: at the Marine Biological Laboratory in Woods Hole, Massachusetts, Associate Scientist Loretta Roberson researches large-scale offshore seaweed farming as a source of sustainable biomass, aimed at bioremediation and at protecting sensitive ecosystems like coral reefs. She leads a DOE ARPA-E-funded initiative farming tropical seaweed off Puerto Rico and works on refining Sargassum into an alternative biomass feedstock. A real deployment of that kind of research depends on exactly the kind of system you will build here: a network of monitoring stations, one per farm site, coordinated and routed reliably enough that no single site's software has to know about the others.

When you are done you will have one shared Docker image, one docker-compose.yml, and four small service files (a farm-monitoring service, a regional-aggregator sidecar, a routing ambassador, and a buoy gateway) — hands-on evidence that the patterns from class compose together into a real distributed system.

## Setup

Inside your Gantry devcontainer, create a working directory for this homework:

```bash
mkdir hw02 && cd hw02
npm init -y
npm pkg set type=module
npm install express
```

You will create seven files: farm-service.js, sidecar-sync.js, ambassador.js, buoy-gateway.js, Dockerfile, .dockerignore, and docker-compose.yml.

## Part 1: Containerizing a Farm Site (Unit 4)

Your farm monitoring service represents one offshore farm site. It must expose two endpoints, and be entirely configured through environment variables so the same image can run as any farm site.

### Environment variables

PORT — port to listen on
FARM_ID — this farm's identifier (e.g. farm-a)
DATA_DIR — directory to persist readings to (default ./data)
CALIBRATION — sensor calibration version (default v1)

### GET /status

Returns the farm's identity and every reading recorded so far.

```text
200 OK
{ "farmId": "farm-a", "calibration": "v1", "readings": [] }
```

### POST /reading

Records a sensor reading. The request body must include metric (a string, e.g. "growthRateCm") and value (a number). Appends the reading (with a server-generated timestamp) to an in-memory array and to ${DATA_DIR}/readings.json.

```text
200 OK
{ "farmId": "farm-a", "calibration": "v1", "count": 1, "latest": { "metric": "growthRateCm", "value": 2.4, "timestamp": "2026-07-10T12:00:00.000Z" } }
```

### The Dockerfile

Write a Dockerfile that builds an image any farm site can run from:

FROM node:24 (or a version you have installed)
WORKDIR set to your app directory
Copy package*.json first and run npm install, then copy the rest of your source — in that order, so Docker only reinstalls dependencies when package.json actually changes
EXPOSE the port your service listens on
A default CMD that starts farm-service.js
Add a .dockerignore that excludes node_modules.

You'll know it works when: running

```bash
docker build -t seagrid .
docker run -e FARM_ID=farm-a -p 3000:3000 seagrid
```

and then curl http://localhost:3000/status returns { "farmId": "farm-a", "calibration": "v1", "readings": [] }.

## Part 2: Orchestrating the Farm Network (Unit 5)

Write a docker-compose.yml that runs the whole farm network as one system:

farm-a, farm-b, farm-c — three farm-service instances, each built from the same image, each with its own FARM_ID and DATA_DIR, each mapped to its own host port
farm-a-v2 — a fourth farm-service instance with FARM_ID=farm-a, a separate DATA_DIR, and CALIBRATION=v2 — a calibration trial running alongside farm-a itself
A single named volume mounted into every farm service (all four) so their data directories persist and can be read by the sidecar you will add in Part 3

You'll know it works when: running docker compose up --build starts all four farm containers, each independently reachable on its own host port, and a reading posted to farm-a never appears when you GET /status on farm-b or farm-c.

## Part 3: The Regional Aggregator Sidecar (Unit 6)

Add sidecar-sync.js: a background process with no HTTP server of its own, that periodically reads every farm's readings.json from the shared volume and writes a rolled-up summary — without farm-service.js ever knowing it exists.

### Environment variables

DATA_ROOT — the shared volume's mount path
FARM_IDS — comma-separated list of farm ids to summarize (e.g. farm-a,farm-b,farm-c)
SYNC_INTERVAL_MS — how often to re-read and rewrite the summary (default 5000)

### Behavior

On every interval tick, for each farm id in FARM_IDS, read ${DATA_ROOT}/<farmId>/readings.json (treat a missing file as zero readings), then write ${DATA_ROOT}/regional-summary.json:

```json
{
  "generatedAt": "2026-07-10T12:00:05.000Z",
  "farms": {
    "farm-a": { "count": 3, "avgValue": 2.1 },
    "farm-b": { "count": 1, "avgValue": 4.0 }
  },
  "regionalAvgValue": 2.35
}
```

regionalAvgValue is the mean of every reading from every farm pooled together — not the mean of the per-farm averages. (With farm-a's three readings averaging 2.1 and farm-b's one reading at 4.0, the pooled mean of all four numbers — not the average of 2.1 and 4.0 — is what belongs here.)

Add sidecar as a service in your docker-compose.yml, sharing the same named volume, with depends_on on the three farms.

You'll know it works when: after posting a few readings to two or more farms and waiting one sync interval, docker compose exec sidecar cat /data/regional-summary.json shows the correct per-farm count and avgValue, and a regionalAvgValue that matches the pooled-mean formula above.

## Part 4: The Ambassador (Unit 7)

Add two more files:

buoy-gateway.js — the primary service a real buoy would talk to. Exposes POST /submit-reading (body: { "farmId", "metric", "value" }) and forwards it verbatim to a fixed AMBASSADOR_URL. It contains no routing logic of its own — it always calls the same local address, the same way Unit 7's own primary service did.
ambassador.js — shares buoy-gateway's network namespace (via network_mode: "service:buoy-gateway" in Compose) and makes the actual routing decision on buoy-gateway's behalf.

### ambassador.js: POST /reading

Body: { "farmId", "metric", "value" }.

Unknown farmId → 404 { "error": "unknown farmId: farm-x" }
farmId === "farm-b" or "farm-c" → forwarded to that farm's fixed URL every time
farmId === "farm-a" → forwarded to farm-a-v2 roughly CANARY_PERCENT percent of the time (default 20), and to farm-a the rest of the time — a canary trial of the new calibration

Response (whichever farm actually handled it):

```text
200 OK
{ "routedTo": "farm-a", "farmResponse": { "farmId": "farm-a", "calibration": "v1", "count": 1, "latest": { "metric": "growthRateCm", "value": 2.0, "timestamp": "2026-07-10T12:00:00.000Z" } } }
```

### buoy-gateway.js: POST /submit-reading

Forwards the request body to ${AMBASSADOR_URL}/reading and returns:

```text
200 OK
{ "receivedBy": "buoy-gateway", "routedTo": "farm-a", "farmResponse": { "...": "..." } }
```

### Wiring it in docker-compose.yml

Add buoy-gateway and ambassador services. The ambassador must not declare its own ports: — network_mode: "service:buoy-gateway" and ports: cannot be used together on the same service; Compose will reject it. Expose the port through buoy-gateway instead.

You'll know it works when:

Repeatedly submitting readings for farm-b or farm-c always routes to that same farm.
Submitting around 100 readings for farm-a results in roughly 10-30 of them landing on farm-a-v2 (check GET /status on each afterward) — not exactly 20 every time, but in that range.

## Testing your work locally

Start the whole system:

```bash
docker compose up --build
```

In another terminal:

```bash
# Submit a reading through the full path: buoy-gateway -> ambassador -> farm-b
curl -X POST http://localhost:4000/submit-reading \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"farmId": "farm-b", "metric": "growthRateCm", "value": 3.1}'

# Confirm it landed on farm-b specifically
curl http://localhost:3002/status

# Send 100 farm-a readings and see how the count splits across calibrations
for i in $(seq 1 100); do
  curl -s -X POST http://localhost:4000/submit-reading \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d '{"farmId": "farm-a", "metric": "growthRateCm", "value": 2.0}' > /dev/null
done
curl -s http://localhost:3001/status | grep -o '"count":[0-9]*'
curl -s http://localhost:3004/status | grep -o '"count":[0-9]*'

# Check the sidecar's regional summary
docker compose exec sidecar cat /data/regional-summary.json
```

## Submission

Submit a zip file containing exactly these files (no subdirectories):

Dockerfile
.dockerignore
docker-compose.yml
farm-service.js
sidecar-sync.js
ambassador.js
buoy-gateway.js
package.json

From inside your hw02 directory, create the zip:

```bash
zip hw02.zip Dockerfile .dockerignore docker-compose.yml farm-service.js sidecar-sync.js ambassador.js buoy-gateway.js package.json
```

Upload hw02.zip to Gradescope. The autograder runs your service files directly against the endpoint shapes above, and checks your Dockerfile and docker-compose.yml for the required structure.

# Escalation Requests

Commands are run outside the sandbox if they are approved by the user, or match an existing rule that allows it to run unrestricted. The command string is split into independent command segments at shell control operators, including but not limited to:

- Pipes: |
- Logical operators: &&, ||
- Command separators: ;
- Subshell boundaries: (...), $(...)

Each resulting segment is evaluated independently for sandbox restrictions and approval requirements.

Example:

git pull | tee output.txt

This is treated as two command segments:

["git", "pull"]

["tee", "output.txt"]

Commands that use more advanced shell features like redirection (>, >>, <), substitutions ($(...), ...), environment variables (FOO=bar), or wildcard patterns (*, ?) will not be evaluated against rules, to limit the scope of what an approved rule allows.

## How to request escalation

IMPORTANT: To request approval to execute a command that will require escalated privileges:

- Provide the `sandbox_permissions` parameter with the value `"require_escalated"`
- Include a short question asking the user if they want to allow the action in `justification` parameter. e.g. "Do you want to download and install dependencies for this project?"
- Optionally suggest a `prefix_rule` - this will be shown to the user with an option to persist the rule approval for future sessions.

ALWAYS proceed to use the `justification` parameter - do not message the user before requesting approval for the command.

## When to request escalation

While commands are running inside the sandbox, here are some scenarios that will require escalation outside the sandbox:

- You need to run a command that writes to a directory that requires it (e.g. running tests that write to /var)
- You need to run a GUI app (e.g., open/xdg-open/osascript) to open browsers or files.

## prefix_rule guidance

When choosing a `prefix_rule`, request one that will allow you to fulfill similar requests from the user in the future without re-requesting escalation. It should be categorical and reasonably scoped to similar capabilities. You should rarely pass the entire command into `prefix_rule`.

NEVER provide a prefix_rule if your command uses a heredoc or herestring.
