content.text:
Ok Sprint 1: Project Definition and Scalability Framing
Schedule: Week 2 (Jul 13–17)

Grade entry: Sprint 2 (half weight)

Purpose
Week 1 introduced the vocabulary of distributed systems: why latency and reliability are the two properties you measure first, what idempotency means and why it matters when services retry, and how concurrency creates coordination problems that do not exist on a single machine. Sprint 1 asks your team to apply that vocabulary to your chosen domain.

No code is expected in this sprint. This is design thinking grounded in the concepts just studied. The deliverables are written artifacts that demonstrate you can reason about your system before you build it.

Deliverables
All three deliverables are committed to the team repository under a docs/ directory and linked from the README.md.

1. Refined project description (docs/PROJECT.md)
Write a short document called docs/PROJECT.md (roughly one page) that refines the domain paragraph from Sprint 0 into a complete project description. It must address:

Domain: What kind of system is this, and who does it serve?
Scalability problem: What specific load or coordination challenge makes this domain require a scalable distributed web system? Be concrete: what happens when demand spikes, when a service goes down, or when data must be shared across multiple nodes?
Computing for the Common Good framing: Who benefits when this system works correctly? Who is harmed when it fails or is slow? This framing should motivate the latency and reliability requirements you will define below.
2. Initial service list (docs/SERVICES.md)
Write a document called docs/SERVICES.md containing a bulleted list of the services your simulation will likely include, with one sentence describing what each service does. This is a first guess and will change as you learn more patterns in subsequent weeks.

Each service entry should name the service and describe its role in one sentence:

inventory-service: Manages stock levels for each pantry location and accepts update and query requests from the coordinator.
coordinator-service: Routes incoming distribution requests to the appropriate pantry location based on availability.
The target is team_size + 1 custom services: 3 for 2-person teams, 4 for 3-person teams, and one more per additional member. The extra service beyond per-member ownership is a shared component — a coordinator, gateway, or API layer that multiple members contribute to. Infrastructure containers (Caddy, Redis, Prometheus, Grafana) do not count. This list is a projection — you will not build all services in Sprint 1. Sprint 2 begins with 2; Sprint 4 adds at least one more.

3. Service level objectives (docs/SLO.md)
Write a document called docs/SLO.md. It should be roughly half a page and define the system's service level objectives: the specific, measurable targets that describe what "good enough" looks like for your domain.

For each service you listed above, define at least two SLOs:

Latency SLO: A percentile target and a threshold. For example: "The inventory lookup endpoint must respond within 500 ms at the 95th percentile." Tie the target to the domain: name who is waiting and what happens when the threshold is exceeded.
Reliability SLO: A success rate target. For example: "The distribution request endpoint must succeed at least 99% of the time." Reason about what at-least-once and at-most-once delivery semantics mean for each operation: a failed lookup is annoying; a double-counted distribution is a data integrity problem.
These SLOs do not need to be precise engineering targets yet. They are commitments that will inform your design decisions in later sprints and that you will measure against in Sprint 3 and Sprint 5. Write them as if you intend to hold your system to them.

Grading
Sprint 1 is worth 50 points. It counts as half a sprint grade toward the Sprints total (30%).

Team (30 pts)
Criterion	Points
docs/PROJECT.md, docs/SERVICES.md, and docs/SLO.md all exist in a docs/ directory and are linked from README.md	5
docs/PROJECT.md: names a specific domain and community (5 pts); describes a concrete scalability problem with at least one named condition (5 pts); CFTCG framing names specific beneficiaries and a specific harm — not a restatement of the domain (5 pts)	15
docs/SERVICES.md: lists team_size + 1 services; every entry has a formatted name (service-name) and a one-sentence role description	5
docs/SLO.md: contains at least one latency SLO and at least one reliability SLO	5
Award 0 pts for a docs/PROJECT.md criterion if the content is absent or entirely generic (e.g. "high traffic" without a named condition). For docs/SERVICES.md, deduct 1 pt per entry missing a name or description, down to 0.

Individual (20 pts)
Graded per student based on commit history and service ownership.

Criterion	Points
Student has authored at least one commit to any of the three Sprint 1 documents before the deadline	5
docs/SERVICES.md includes a service this student owns (identifiable by commit authorship in Sprint 2 onward) with a formatted name and one-sentence description	5
docs/SLO.md contains both a latency SLO and a reliability SLO for their service; latency SLO names an endpoint, a percentile, and a threshold with units	10
A latency SLO without a percentile scores 5/10. A reliability SLO without a success rate percentage scores 0 for that half.

Submission
Commit all three deliverables to the team repository and submit the repository URL through Canvas by the Sprint 1 deadline. this is the sprint 0 assignment

## Domain Description

Our system simulates a distributed mobile blue-light emergency response network that routes emergency requests across multiple regions, including university campuses, transit hubs, stadiums, shopping centers, and other public venues. Users submit requests through a mobile application, and the system is responsible for determining the appropriate response, routing the request to the correct regional service, and keeping responders and users updated throughout the incident.

A single server becomes insufficient when the system experiences sudden spikes in demand, such as during large public events, severe weather, or multiple simultaneous emergencies. During these periods, the system must rapidly process incoming requests, determine user locations, prioritize incidents based on severity, and notify the appropriate local responders without introducing delays. Distributing the workload across multiple servers allows the system to remain responsive and available even under heavy load.

From a Computing for the Common Good perspective, a reliable emergency response system directly improves public safety. Students, commuters, event attendees, employees, and other members of the public all benefit from fast and dependable access to emergency services. When the system performs well, people receive timely police, medical, security, or crisis-response assistance. When it fails or becomes overloaded, delayed or misrouted requests can increase response times and potentially place people in dangerous situations. There are also inherent flaws with physical blue light alarms as they may not always be accessible during times of need, which makes being able to use blue light systems from one's phone the natural way to improve accesibilty.

payload.message:
For a three-person team, I’d keep it to exactly four custom services: one shared service plus one clear ownership area per person. This is the cleanest fit for Blue Light:

```text
Mobile user
  -> emergency-gateway
  -> incident-service
  -> regional-routing-service
  -> responder-dispatch-service
```

- `emergency-gateway`: Shared service that receives mobile emergency requests, validates them, accepts an idempotency key, and forwards each request into the incident workflow.

- `incident-service`: Creates and tracks simulated emergency incidents, assigns a severity level, and provides the authoritative incident ID and current state.

- `regional-routing-service`: Determines the relevant campus, transit hub, stadium, or other venue region and selects the eligible local response group for an incident.

- `responder-dispatch-service`: Simulates notifying and assigning the appropriate security, medical, police, or crisis-response team, then records dispatch and responder-status updates.

This structure gives you a really natural build path later:

- Replicate `emergency-gateway` or `regional-routing-service` behind Caddy.
- Cache venue and regional-routing data in Redis.
- Make `incident-service -> responder-dispatch-service` asynchronous through a Redis queue or pub/sub pipeline.
- Add failures such as a slow routing lookup, an unavailable regional responder, or a backed-up dispatch queue.
- Measure the main path: “submit emergency request until dispatch confirmation.”

Do not count Caddy, Redis, Prometheus, or Grafana in the four. They are infrastructure, not the custom domain services Sprint 1 wants.

For ownership, I’d claim `regional-routing-service` or `incident-service`. Both give you a strong data-model and coordination angle, while still making it easy to point to clear commits later.

# AI Disclosure Skill

Use this skill when AI helps with submitted coursework, especially code,
configuration, scripts, project docs, or analysis that will be turned in.

## Goal

Satisfy the COMPSCI 426 AI policy:

- Save the relevant raw Codex JSONL transcript.
- Identify code generated or substantially modified by AI.
- Make majority-AI files obvious to graders and future agents.

## Required Workflow

1. Run `scripts/save-chat.sh "<deliverable-topic>"`.
2. Confirm the generated file is a `.jsonl` file copied from the raw Codex
   session log under `${CODEX_HOME:-$HOME/.codex}/sessions`.
3. Do not replace the raw log with a hand-written summary. If notes are needed,
   create a separate Markdown note in addition to the JSONL, never instead of
   it.
4. For files that are majority generated or majority substantially modified by
   AI, add AI disclosure comments at both the top and bottom of the file.
5. For smaller AI edits, add inline comments at the specific AI-generated or
   substantially modified code.
6. Include the raw `.jsonl` transcript in the assignment submission artifact
   whenever the course submission expects AI disclosure files.

## Majority-AI File Comments

Use the language below, adjusted only for comment syntax and transcript path.

JavaScript/TypeScript/CSS:

```js
// AI DISCLOSURE: This file was generated or substantially modified with AI assistance. See ai/chats/<chat-file>.jsonl.
// ... file content ...
// END AI DISCLOSURE: AI-assisted file. See ai/chats/<chat-file>.jsonl.
```

Shell/Python/Dockerfile:

```bash
# AI DISCLOSURE: This file was generated or substantially modified with AI assistance. See ai/chats/<chat-file>.jsonl.
# ... file content ...
# END AI DISCLOSURE: AI-assisted file. See ai/chats/<chat-file>.jsonl.
```

Markdown/HTML:

```md
<!-- AI DISCLOSURE: This file was generated or substantially modified with AI assistance. See ai/chats/<chat-file>.jsonl. -->
<!-- ... file content ... -->
<!-- END AI DISCLOSURE: AI-assisted file. See ai/chats/<chat-file>.jsonl. -->
```

## Syntax Rules

- If a file has a shebang, keep the shebang as line 1 and put the top AI
  disclosure comment immediately after it.
- Do not add comments to strict JSON files such as `package.json`; JSON does not
  allow comments. The raw JSONL transcript still serves as the disclosure
  record.
- Keep comments truthful: use top/bottom comments only for files that are
  majority AI-generated or majority AI-modified.
- If a grader requires exact output text, keep disclosure comments outside
  runtime output paths and avoid changing API responses.

## Before Submission

- Confirm every AI-assisted submission has a raw `.jsonl` transcript in
  `ai/chats/`.
- Confirm majority-AI files have top and bottom disclosure comments where the
  file syntax supports comments.
- Confirm smaller AI-generated sections have local inline comments.
- Confirm `package.json` or other no-comment formats are covered by the raw
  JSONL transcript if AI helped create or modify them.
- Inspect the final zip contents with `zipinfo -1 <submission>.zip` and verify
  the raw `.jsonl` transcript is present when required.
